News.title: ‘Much-loved’ grandma, 61, found dead at home as man arrested in ‘murder’ probe & family pay heartbreaking tribute
News.content:
'MURDER' PROBE ‘Much-loved’ grandma, 61, found dead at home as man arrested in ‘murder’ probe & family pay heartbreaking tribute

A HEARTBROKEN family have paid moving tribute to a “much-loved” grandma after she was found dead in a home.

Susan Watson, 61, was found dead at a property in Carlisle, Cumbria, on Sunday August 2.

A man in his 60s was arrested in connection with the investigation, but has since been released on bail while enquiries continue.

Detectives are working to establish the full circumstances surrounding the woman’s death and enquiries remain ongoing.





Cops had previously asked people to “refrain from speculation whilst the investigation is ongoing”.

Susan’s family said she was a “much-loved” sister, mum, grandma and friend who was “always the first to offer a helping hand”.

A moving tribute read: “Family meant everything to her, and she was never happier than when she had the people she loved around her.

“She absolutely adored being a Grandma and treasured every moment she spent with her grandchildren.

“Helping people was simply who Susan was. She always put other people before herself and was the first to offer a helping hand, whether it was family, friends, neighbours or complete strangers.

“She never expected anything in return and never wanted recognition. She just believed that if someone needed help, you helped them.”

Susan was a committed volunteer with the Samaritans, dedicating “countless evenings,” providing a listening ear “to anyone who needed someone to talk to at Carlisle railway station”.

She also volunteered at the Samaritans charity’s shop.



Susan was known for her compassion and willingness to listen to anyone in need.

As a foot practitioner in Carlisle, kind-hearted Susan developed lasting friendships with many of her patients.

“Looking after other people came naturally to her,” her family said of the foot practitioner.

“She often went far beyond what anyone would expect, picking up shopping for people who couldn’t get out, checking in on those who were struggling, and making sure nobody felt alone or forgotten.

“If someone was going through a difficult time, she would open her home and do whatever she could to help.”



The family also said if someone had nowhere to go at Christmas, “there was always a place at her table”.

News.title: Body found in desperate search for missing man, 47, in sea after he went rock climbing and disappeared
News.content:
SEARCH TRAGEDY Body found in desperate search for missing man, 47, in sea after he went rock climbing and disappeared

COPS have found a body after a frantic search was launched for a missing 47-year-old man who vanished.

Ben, 47, is thought to have intended to go rock climbing when he left his home in St Davids in Wales, at around midday on Wednesday.

Loved ones raised the alarm with the emergency services when they didn’t hear from him for hours.

Cops have now confirmed that a body has sadly been found in the coastal area of Caer Bwdy, Pembrokeshire.





Dyfed-Powys Police said that formal identification has not yet taken place.

The family of the deceased have been notified, said the force.

Cops confirmed that enquiries are still underway.

In a statement issued on Thursday evening, the force said: “Formal identification has not yet taken place, and while the family have been informed of this development, we are not in a position to confirm the identity of the deceased at this time.



“They are being supported by specially trained officers.

“We ask that the family’s privacy is respected while enquiries continue.”

It is believed he intended to head to either Carreg y Barcud area, near Trelerw, or Caer Bwdy Bay, outside St Davids in Pembrokeshire.

Ben was previously described as around 5ft 11in tall, of athletic build, with short brown/greying hair and brown eyes.



He was carrying an orange bag and wearing black climbing shoes with an orange strap when he disappeared.

The Coastguard boat and helicopter were both involved in the search.

News.title: Teenage girl ‘sexually assaulted multiple times’ in city centre as police release CCTV of man
News.content:
MANHUNT Teenage girl ‘sexually assaulted multiple times’ in city centre as police release CCTV of man

COPS have released CCTV of a man they would like to speak to after a teenage girl was allegedly sexually assaulted multiple times in a city centre.

Cheshire Police said that the reported assault took place in the early hours of the morning in Chester on Saturday, May 30.

A teenage girl was approached by an unknown man in Chester city centre, said police.

During the encounter, the man is reported to have sexually assaulted the victim multiple times, cops said.





The force has now released a CCTV image of a man it wants to question over the incident.

Cheshire Police believe he can help with the investigation.

Detective Constable Niall Dudley urged anyone with information to contact the force immediately.

He said: “Enquiries have been carried out since the incident was reported, and we have now released CCTV images of a man we would like to speak to.

“If anyone has any information as to the identity of the man pictured, please get in touch with us. We would also urge the man to contact us directly.

“The same goes for anyone with any further information about the incident.

“You can contact Cheshire Police by calling 101 or visit the website quoting 26000461032.”

News.title: School shooter, 14, ‘kills 8 after opening fire on students and gunning down grandparents’ in Thailand
News.content:
AT LEAST eight people have been killed by a teen gunman who went on a rampage inside a school after murdering his grandparents, police say.

The lone shooter, believed to be a 14-year-old, reportedly stole his grandad’s gun and opened fire inside his own secondary school killing three teachers and three students.



At least 15 people were injured at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School on the outskirts of Bangkok including three who are in a critical condition.

The deadly attack started at around 10.40am local time and saw the shooter fire 26 rounds across multiple classrooms.





Three students and another three teachers were gunned down with the shooter also found dead inside the school, say officials.

Dechrapee Kongdee, chief of the Nonthaburi provincial police, told the bbc.co.uk/news/live/cvgjnz67ymzt” rel=”nofollow”>BBC the suspect was in the ninth grade which would likely make him 14 years old.



Police found another 34 rounds of ammunition inside a black bag at the scene along with the gun.

The boy was reportedly wearing a purple sports kit at the time of the shooting as he barricaded himself inside a room.

Footage shows a classroom on lockdown during the rampage as brave students and teachers hid under desks.

Other terrified youngsters managed to climb out of windows at the school as the sounds of bullets rang out.

Dozens fled onto the streets as police rushed inside the building to find the downed suspect and secure the school.



Students and staff trapped inside were evacuated from the campus immediately.

Several of the wounded students were injured when trying to flee, Deputy Interior Minister Polapee Suwunchwee said.

Suwunchwee added that the two grandparents of the teenage suspect were found dead at their home.



Their time of death is believed to have been just a short time before the school shooting with initial investigations pointing to the teen also killing them.

The gun found at the school reportedly belonged to the grandad.

Police Colonel Phatsakorn Chaitaweewong, superintendent of Plai Bang Police Station, said: “The public and parents should avoid the area and follow official updates.”



Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul paid tribute to the victims.

He said: “This is really bad, it shouldn’t have happened. I don’t just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened.

“How can this happen in our country. This is why the government do not allow [citizens] to possess firearms.”



Firearms are available in Thailand in shops and can be easily purchased on the black market.

The country has a tragic past with multiple school shootings.

Back in February, a gunman opened fire with a machine gun and took hostages inside a school in Songkhla Province, southern Thailand.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One teacher was killed.

In 2022, gunman Panya Khamrab killed 37 people, including 24 children, during a rampage at a nursery school in Bua Lamphu province.

News.title: Heartbroken family of British woman found dead in suitcase after being ‘killed by Afghan migrant’ break their silence
News.content:
THE devastated family of the British woman found dead in a suitcase after allegedly being killed by an Afghan migrant have broken their silence.

Afghan boxer Sharif Ahmadzai is currently being held in connection with the death of Elisabeth Jane Ross, 38, having refused to enter a plea on Thursday.



Ross was a regular visitor to Greece as she volunteered with NGOs assisting refugees, homeless people and other vulnerable people, focusing on Afghanistan and Iran.

The Brit, from Edinburgh, had initially been staying with Greek friends in the Keratsini district, having arrived in Athens on June 26.



She moved to Rethymnou Street in the centre of the capital on July 2, police have confirmed, where she was volunteering with a Christian-based NGO, working with refugees.

Her body was discovered in an abandoned building two weeks later.



Ross’ family issued a statement on Thursday, which said: “Lisa will always be remembered by us as kind, principled and selfless.

“Her integrity was absolute, and she dedicated her life to helping others in need.



“We are in deep pain, and we ask for time and privacy as we come to terms with our loss.”

Ahmadzai, 26, is accused of manslaughter, robbery and illegal gun possession.

He did not respond to the charges and the authorities are waiting toxicological test results.



Ahmadzai’s US-born wife Alaina Hall allegedly reported her husband to cops after she became suspicious he was involved in Elisabeth’s death.

She told cops that she had met Elisabeth through volunteer work in Athens and had last seen her on July 12, after a Bible study meeting, according to Greek news outlet Protothema.

Days later, she heard reports of a body being found stuffed in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens.

Later that night, Alaina recalled waking up with a “terrible” feeling.

In the morning she then texted Elisabeth and got two replies which made her suspicious.



Alaina said: “These messages were not in Lisa’s style, both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used.”

When she tried calling Elisabeth she didn’t get a reply.

Alaina also told police she had grown suspicious of her husband after she woke to find him missing on the evening of July 15.

When she checked his shared location, she saw he was in Elisabeth’s flat.



Having later confronted him, he told her he had been watching a football match but had gone to Elisabeth’s apartment to use the toilet.

She told police: “I don’t know what to tell you, but all of the above made me feel strange.

“Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband’s behaviour, I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable.”

Investigating officers also found CCTV footage which allegedly shows him leaving Elizabeth’s apartment with a suitcase and dropping it where her remains were discovered on July 16.

News outlet Protothema reported earlier this week that Ahmadzai had told police in a statement on Saturday that he did not kill Elisabeth, saying her found her dead before panicking.



In his testimony he reportedly said: “I never did harm to anyone. I want you to understand me and believe me. I was just in a panic.”

He is said to have claimed he had visited the house where she was staying and found her lying on the bathroom floor.

Ahmadzai said: “[She] was spitting something like water out of her mouth. I spoke to her two or three times, but she didn’t respond. I froze. My legs went numb.”

The 26-year-old then claimed he panicked and fled and then encountered an elderly man near a bus stop.

He reportedly asked the man what he should do after finding a dead body.



Ahmadzai said: “[The old man] told me that he worked with hospitals and he knows about them and what I should do is remove it from the house, or I will get into trouble.

“I sat and thought about what he told me for a few hours.”

He then said he had returned to the apartment the following day and placed Elisabeth’s body in a black suitcase, before placing it in the boot of the red Peugeot he drove.

Ahmadzai said: “I started in the Peugeot, arrived near my house and parked it.

“I got out of the car, took the suitcase out of the trunk and walked to an abandoned building across from the Panhellenic University.



“There I found the old man I told you about who gave me the advice. He told me to leave the suitcase with him, and he would take care of it.”

He also admitted to the cops he had taken Elisabeth’s phone and bank cards.

Ahmadzai added: “In addition to Lisa’s cards, I also took her mobile phone. From that, I sent some messages to people close to her to reassure them that she was okay.

“I don’t know what I was thinking. I wasn’t thinking clearly.

“I gave all the money I took out of Lisa’s cards to the old man because he was blackmailing me that he would tell everything to the police.

“As far as I know, this old man’s name is Nikos, and he frequents the place where I left the suitcase.”

Along with “intentional homicide” he has also been charged with robbery and weapons offences.

News.title: Russian general is buried following Moscow restaurant blast that also hurt his goddaughter as commander survives
News.content:
MOSCOW BLAST Russian general is buried following Moscow restaurant blast that also hurt his goddaughter as commander survives

A TOP Putin general has been secretly buried after he was killed in a blast that ripped through a restaurant packed with Kremlin Elite.

Major-General Valeri Plokhotnyuk, a high ranking Russian officer, was one of five people killed in an attack at the lavish birthday party of the notorious Col-Gen Alexander Chayko on August 1.



Despite attempts by Russian authorities to suppress news of his death, Plokhotnyuk was covertly buried in Moscow’s Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, in a section reserved for elite military and security officials.

The bomb at the Moscow restaurant was assumed to have been intended for Colonel-General Col-Gen Alexander Chayko, who managed to escape the blast “unharmed”.



The blast was caused by the detonation of a “birthday gift” carried by an unidentified female bomber.

It is understood Plokhotnyuk was the godfather of Chayko’s daughter Maria, 25, who was seriously wounded in the blast.



A report from Astra media revelaved Maria suffered a “traumatic brain injury” as a well as “multiple shrapnel wounds” to her to her neck, abdomen and leg and is in a top Moscow hospital.

Her businessman husband Daniil Peredriy, 27, was killed.



It was previously reported that Lt-Gen Igor Yerusalimov had died but in a shock turn of events Russian media now say he is alive.

Strangely, his name had appeared on a large wreath – yet it is believed he in fact did not die in the blast.

He reportedly answered his phone on Thursday and demanded: “Don’t write anything about me.”

He has recently worked for a secret military institute developing “automated control systems” for Putin’s armed forces.

Plokhotnyuk was burred on Wednesday and Peredriy on Thursday – both had guards of honour.



Plokhotnyuk, believed to be around 50, was a ground forces general who had been deputy commander of the 49th Army of Russia’s Southern Military District.

The explosion took place outside the entrance to the exclusive Balzi Rossi restaurant in central Moscow.

A total of five people died and 19 were wounded.

Among the dead were the female bomber and a security officer who was checking her “gift” when it exploded.

One other of those killed has not been identified.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Kyiv is suspected to be behind the attack because Chayko – a decorated Russian war hero whom Ukraine formally listed as a war criminal in June – is behind a string of ruthless aerial bombings across the war.

In 2022, Chayko commanded Russian forces on the Kyiv front.

News.title: Three quarters of Brits in a ‘friendship recession’ as how people keep pals close is revealed
News.content:
HOLDING ON Three quarters of Brits in a ‘friendship recession’ as how people keep pals close is revealed

THREE quarters of Brits are in a “friendship recession,” as how people keep their pals close is revealed.

People say they have fewer friends than they did fives years ago, research shows.



However, a new poll has unearthed a definitive list of ways to keep the bond going, with giving a friend a hug when they need one (52 per cent) topping the list, followed by sending a thoughtful message (51 per cent) and remembering their birthday (45 per cent).

Checking in when they go quiet (44 per cent), looking after them when they’re ill (44per cent) and listening to their relationship problems (41 per cent) also ranked among the nation’s most valued acts of friendship.



The study, commissioned by The Camping and Caravanning Club as it celebrates its 125th anniversary, found that despite Brits’ reputation for having a stiff upper lip, it is often the smallest gestures that matter most.

But the research also highlighted growing concerns about the state of modern friendships.

Almost three-quarters (73 per cent) admitted it’s tough to maintain relationships as an adult, with 76 per cent spending less quality time with friends in person than they used to.

And we’re blaming busy work lives (68 per cent), family commitments (53 per cent) and living far apart (47 per cent) as the main reasons we’re losing friends.

Lack of free time (46per cent), money worries (36 per cent) and different life stages (32 per cent) also play a major part.

Encouragingly, the survey found that holidays remain one of the best places to form lasting friendships, with two in three Brits (65 per cent) revealing they have made a close friend while away from home.



Camping was identified as one of the best environments for nurturing relationships, with more than half (53 per cent) saying they’d made a mate whilst doing this, and they’d stayed in touch for up to four years.

A surprising 5 per cent said they’d even met their other half on a camping trip.

Sabina Voysey, Director General of The Camping and Caravanning Club said: “Our research suggests that friendships are increasingly being squeezed by the pressures of modern life, yet people are craving more meaningful connections than ever.

“As we celebrate our 125th anniversary, it’s particularly fitting that friendship is at the heart of these findings.

“The Camping and Caravanning Club itself was founded by a group of friends back in 1901 who shared a love of the outdoors and adventure.



“More than a century later, we’re still seeing how camping helps bring people together, whether that’s old friends strengthening their bonds or complete strangers striking up new friendships on a campsite.”

According to the findings, the average Brit has 11 friends, with just three of them described as ‘close’ whilst nearly half of us (49 per cent) have ‘friend’ connections on social media we’d actively avoid in real life.

Top 20 signs of true modern friendship Giving them a hug when they need one – 52 per cent Sending a thoughtful text message – 51 per cent Remembering their birthday – 45 per cent Checking in when they go quiet – 44 per cent Looking after them when they are ill – 44 per cent Listening to their relationship problems – 41 per cent Making them a cup of tea when they are upset – 37 per cent Making them laugh when they are down – 37 per cent Remembering small details about their life – 35 per cent Being honest when they need advice – 34 per cent Being comfortable in silence together – 30 per cent Letting them rant without judgement – 29 per cent Defending them when they are not there – 29 per cent Turning up in a crisis – 28 per cent Making time even when busy – 25 per cent Forgiving them when they make a mistake – 25 per cent Celebrating their wins – 23 per cent Feeling like we can be the truest version of ourselves together – 23 per cent Calling rather than just texting – 22 per cent Offering them a place to stay – 22 per cent

Interestingly, men (13) have more friends than women (10), and it’s the people of Truro who have the most mates (18), ahead of Plymouth (13) and Oxford (13).

Psychologist Dr Sophie, who was involved in the study, said: “Strong friendships are built through shared experiences rather than perfectly curated moments.

“While social media allows us to stay in touch, it doesn’t always provide the face-to-face interactions that help relationships deepen and flourish.



“And sometimes it actively gets in the way of connection.

“What’s really behind a lot of struggling friendships isn’t a lack of time so much as a lack of undivided attention.

“Camping strips away the usual distractions – there’s no laptop open on the sofa, no phone buzzing mid-conversation – so the small acts that actually sustain friendships, like noticing when someone’s gone quiet or simply listening properly, get room to happen again.

“It’s telling that so many people who make a friend while camping stay in touch for years afterwards.

“Friendships formed with that kind of full attention tend to be sturdier, because they were built on real presence rather than the kind of low-effort contact social media makes so easy.”

News.title: Russia provoking Britain with hostile warships & hackers is just ‘tip of the iceberg’, reveals Wes Streeting
News.content:
RUSSIA provokes Britain every single day. That is the lesson Wes Streeting has learned in less than three weeks as Defence Secretary.

But the goading goes mostly unseen by the public.



Hinting at the secret briefings he receives in his new job, Streeting said what is in the public domain is “only the tip of the iceberg”.

On his first day as Defence Secretary a Russian warship opened fire as it steamed towards the Channel.



The frigate Neustrashimy spent 30 minutes blasting shells as big as traffic bollards into waters off the coast of Plymouth.

It was a brazen provocation — disguised as routine training and timed to coincide with the first day of Andy Burnham’s government.

In one sense it was extraordinary. It was the first time a hostile ­warship had fired its main gun in the waters off Plymouth since the end of World War Two.

But Streeting insists it was also routine. It fitted a pattern of rogue behaviour that ranges from bombers buzzing Nato air space to hackers targeting NHS infrastructure or threatening the deep-sea cables that connect Britain to the rest of the world.

The shell-firing was also bizarrely helpful, Streeting said.

Speaking to The Sun on a visit to Ukraine — where he came face to face with the devastation caused by a Russian missile bombardment — he said: “Incidents like buzzing air space or the shooting in the Channel are performative, irresponsible and designed to provoke.



“It does at least provide the ­British with a visible manifestation of the day-to-day provocations that we see from Russia every day.”

He warned the events in the public domain were “just the tip of the iceberg” and the Government has promised a “national conversation” to raise awareness of the threats.

But Streeting refused to say what else Russia was doing, beneath the visible tip of that iceberg.



Several incidents are already known.

As Streeting was speaking to The Sun in Ukraine, German police were revealing that a DHL cargo plane had crashed into a ­suspected Russian drone at Leipzig-Halle Airport.

A second drone packed with explosives was discovered next to the runway. Berlin called it a “hybrid” attack without naming ­Russia as a culprit.

It follows an 18-month “Kremlin campaign” of drone flights over RAF bases, nuclear sites and command posts across Europe.

he London-based IISS think tank said military- grade Russian spy drones were most likely launched from shadow fleet tankers.



The researchers suggested the Russian drones had mapped out ­targets that Moscow would strike in the event of World War Three.

Previous attacks — which police and Western spies pinned on ­Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency — involved sex toys packed with incendiaries which caught fire on planes and in warehouses in Birmingham, Warsaw and Leipzig.

Poland warned the attacks in 2024 were dry runs to bring down a cargo plane over the Atlantic.

It was the same year that Russia hired thugs in London to firebomb Sir Keir Starmer’s old home.



When the arsonists were convicted this year the BBC unmasked their handler as a young Russian ­diplomat called Evgeny Lyukshin.

In April, previous Defence Secretary John Healey accused Russian submarines of conducting a month-long mission to map undersea cables north of Scotland.

In November 2024 he had ordered a Royal Navy Astute-class nuclear submarine to surface yards from the spy ship Yantar, which was caught lurking over cables in the Irish Sea.

In both cases, Healey told Putin: “We see you,” to try to deter future activity.



But it did not appear to have worked, because in 2025 he said there had been a 30 per cent rise in Russian vessels threatening UK waters.

In the skies, the RAF has reported the highest rate of Russian flights in the High North in six years.

In May it revealed that Russian pilots had been split-seconds from disaster by flying six metres in front of an RAF jet.

A pair of Russian fighters “repeatedly and dangerously” harassed an unarmed RAF Rivet Joint spy plane over the Black Sea.

Russia is also active in space and cyberspace. The MoD said it battles 90,000 attacks a year, including many by “Russian-speaking actors”.



Last month the UK’s cyber defence force, the National Cyber Security Centre, issued two specific Russia alerts.

First it warned about Russia’s FSB spy agency targeting “communications, defence, energy, financial services, government and healthcare”.

Days later it warned that a Kremlin-backed cyber espionage group known as Laundry Bear had launched a “zero click” phishing campaign to steal emails.

The UK sanctioned 24 Russian hackers, including several linked to an attack on Poland’s national grid.

In space, the provocations happen “weekly”. Maj Gen Paul Tedman, former head of UK Space ­Command, said Russia routinely uses ground-based systems to jam British satellites.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Wes Streeting insisted the only response was to stand up to Russian aggression.

Reflecting on Ukraine’s experience, he said: “With tyrants like Putin — if you compromise, they come back for more.”

News.title: 'My son had stomach ache and now they've given him less than a year to live'
News.content:
'My son had stomach ache and now they've given him less than a year to live'

Nickodemus Dacres went through months of tests before the devastating diagnosis was confirmed

View 3 Images Nickodemus Dacres has been given less than a year to live (Image: Donna Dacres/SWNS)

A 22-year-old man has been given less than a year to live after having stomach ache.

‌



Nickodemus Dacres has been diagnosed with stage four medullary renal cell carcinoma (RMC) - one of the rarest and most aggressive forms of kidney cancer. He started getting extreme stomach pain two years ago and was urinating blood.

‌



The poker dealer, from Croydon, south London, then went through months of tests while his condition continued to get worse. Nickodemus was eventually diagnosed with RMC on February 6 last year.

‌



He has been in and out of hospital ever since with mum Donna Dacres, 59, at his side. She said she had been told his cancer was only shared by nine other people in the UK. According to the Ricky Casey Trust, the true prevalence of RMC around the world is not known.

The literature is based on small case series and individual case reports, which amount to fewer than 400 reported cases worldwide to date, the charity said.

Donna said: “As a mum, nothing prepares you for watching your child suffer, knowing there is so little you can do to take the pain away. I cry every single day. When I look at my son I just can’t believe it.

‌



“He was such a bubbly young man. He lights up everywhere. It is just hard for me to even go to the hospital and look at him.”

View 3 Images Nickodemus Dacres in hospital (Image: Donna Dacres/SWNS)

Nickodemus started getting extreme stomach pain while on shift in July 2024, but did not think much of it. However, when he went to the bathroom and tried to urinate, blood came out instead, and he was rushed to A&E by a colleague.

‌



After five days in hospital, he was released and sent back to work. For months he went through lots of tests until eventually a scan uncovered a small tumour in his right kidney, but the family still were not informed that this was cancer.

The lump continued growing along with the pain and in December 2024 surgeons decided to remove the kidney and several lymph nodes to do some tests. In February, Donna said she received a call saying that she had to bring her son to the hospital as soon as possible, where he was given the devastating cancer diagnosis.

The single mum, who is originally from Jamaica, said: “He was at work and he started having really bad tummy pain. They sent us to the oncology department and I didn’t even know what that was. No one in our family is ever sick.

‌



“When I asked the doctor why we were going down there he said it was stage four cancer. I was really stunned.

“I am from Caribbean people and it is very rare that we deal with such a disease. I was so shocked.”

By the time it was discovered, the cancer had already spread beyond his kidney to his lymph nodes and lungs. Nickodemus was sent straight into chemotherapy and doctors said that if this treatment didn’t work he would have less than a year to live.

‌



The cancer has continued to progress despite every treatment that has been offered and has since spread to his liver and bones. He has been in hospital for two months straight and is living with constant pain, severe abdominal discomfort and relentless vomiting - being unable to eat properly for weeks. Due to this, Nickodemus has dropped from 74kg to less than 55kg.

View 3 Images Donna Dacres (Image: Donna Dacres/SWNS)

Donna said: “At just 22 years old, Nickodemus should be building his future, chasing his dreams and making memories with his friends and family. Watching that energetic, independent young man become so poorly has been absolutely heartbreaking.”

‌



Nickodemus’ cancer is so rare that the targeted chemotherapy, which could help to shrink his tumours, isn't routinely funded by the NHS. Donna said they had started it as of last week, but it costs £8,000 every 28 days, adding up to a total of more than £50,000. The family has started a GoFundMe page to help him with his last hope, which has now raised more than £11,000.

Donna added: “Asking for help is one of the hardest things we have ever had to do. We have always tried to face life's challenges together as a family, but this is something we simply cannot do alone.

“There are only ten people in the whole of the UK who have the same cancer my son has. Less than a thousand people in the world have it. "

Article continues below

Donations can be made via GoFundMe.

News.title: UK trains cancelled LIVE: Commuters braced for Friday delays after power outage
News.content:
Travel chaos is expected today on trains in northern England and the Midlands today after a major power outage in Manchester ground the network to a halt

Rail passengers are bracing for another day of travel chaos with a power outage bringing trains to a standstill across the Midlands and northwest of England.

Electricity cut out in the main control hub for north-west England’s railways, the Manchester Rail Operating Centre yesterday causing widespread cancellations and delays to services.

Trains are back running but they are "now in the wrong locations for the start of service today", said National Rail.

A statement from National Rail continued: "This means that some trains are still expected to be affected this morning. Trains across the Greater Manchester area and North West of England may still be cancelled in full or revised to only run for part of their normal journey until service is able to fully recover."

News.title: 'I was suddenly left on floor babbling and unable to move as my kids watched'
News.content:
'I was suddenly left on floor babbling and unable to move as my kids watched'

'My children had been asking me questions and I thought I was answering, but no words were coming out'

View 3 Images Anthony Ojo with one of his children (Image: Cover Images)

A dad-of-four has told of the terrifying moment he was left dribbling, babbling and unable to move his arms at home in front of his children. Anthony Ojo thought he was answering his frightened youngsters as they tried to speak to him, but no words were coming out.

‌



The 41-year-old support worker, from Ashford, in Kent, said: “I will never forget it. My children had been asking me questions and I thought I was answering, but no words were coming out. It was just babbling and I was dribbling from one side of my mouth.”

‌



Fortunately, Anthony’s wife was working from home when he suddenly collapsed and was able to dial 999. Paramedics contacted stroke consultant Dr Saidu Abubakar by video call so he could assess Anthony before he had even reached hospital.

‌



“Dr Abubakar was asking me to do simple tasks like raising my hands and I just couldn’t do it,” he said. He was then taken directly to the Kent and Canterbury (K&C) Hospital, where a CT scan revealed a blood clot was blocking an artery in his brain.

Anthony said: “I don’t really remember any of it, just waking up in hospital and my wife and the doctors telling me I had suffered a major stroke.”

View 3 Images From left to right: Deputy Medical Director Nic Goodger, acting Chief Executive Dr Des Holden, National Medical Director Prof Frankie Swords, National Clinical Director for Stroke, Dr David Hargroves, Chief Medical Officer Sir Chris Whitty, Dr Robert Kaikini, lead for Stroke Thrombectomy (Image: Cover Images)

‌



An interventional radiology team carried out a mechanical thrombectomy, using suction to remove the clot and fibrous tissue. Specialist live imaging allowed doctors to pinpoint the blockage and showed blood flow to Anthony’s brain being restored immediately after it was removed, preventing permanent damage.

Anthony spent four days in hospital and is now recovering at home with his family. He was among the first patients treated at what East Kent Hospitals said was the country’s first standalone mechanical thrombectomy service.

The dedicated suite opened at K&C earlier this year as the final phase of the £4.5 million Kent Interventional Radiology Centre. Mechanical thrombectomy is a time-critical procedure used to treat some of the most severe strokes, where a major artery carrying blood to the brain has been blocked.

‌



Until the Canterbury service opened, patients from Kent and Medway who needed the treatment had to be taken by ambulance to London. More than 1,200 people suffer strokes in east Kent each year, with hospital bosses estimating more than 100 could benefit from thrombectomy.

Dr Robert Kaikini, consultant vascular and interventional radiologist, said Anthony’s recovery demonstrated the importance of providing the procedure locally. “When he arrived at hospital he was unable to communicate, but just a few days later he was able to go home, walking and talking normally,” he said.

“Without the procedure, there would be no blood flow to part of his brain and the tissue would have died, leaving him with permanent effects. Thanks to the team here, he is now able to carry on life with his family.”

‌



The new centre uses advanced imaging equipment to allow clinicians to treat not only blood clots, but severe internal bleeding, ruptured aneurysms, fibroids and cancer. Dr David Hargroves, the trust’s clinical lead for stroke, said bringing thrombectomy to east Kent had halved the time taken to provide the treatment.

“Improving the number of patients able to receive this innovative, life-changing intervention is as important as how quickly it can be delivered,” he said. “A local service in east Kent has been able to halve the time taken and significantly improve the outcome for local patients.”

Chief Medical Officer Professor Sir Chris Whitty and NHS England’s National Medical Director Professor Frankie Swords have since visited the Canterbury unit alongside representatives from other Kent and Medway NHS trusts. Professor Swords described thrombectomy as one of the most significant advances in modern stroke medicine.

‌



She said it could reduce life-changing disability and give eligible patients the chance of a much faster recovery, greater independence and an improved quality of life. But the new service has opened against an uncertain backdrop for wider stroke care at K&C.

View 3 Images Protesters outside the Kent & Canterbury Hospital rally against a new planning application to close its top-performing unit and move a new hyper-acute stroke unit to the William Harvey Hospital in Ashford (Image: Cover Images)

The hospital’s existing stroke unit, which was created as a temporary arrangement during the Covid pandemic, is still due to be moved to a new 54-bed hyperacute stroke unit at the William Harvey Hospital in Ashford. Thousands of people have backed a campaign calling for the highly rated Canterbury unit to be retained.

‌



The Ashford unit is currently expected to open in late 2027 or early 2028. Under the planned system, however, stroke patients who need a mechanical thrombectomy would be transferred from William Harvey back to K&C for the procedure.

Anthony, meanwhile, said his experience had completely changed his attitude towards his health. He had previously been diagnosed with high blood pressure, but admitted he did not always take his medication because he exercised and believed he was otherwise fit.

“It was a wake-up call for me,” he said. “I had been told I had high blood pressure, but I didn’t think it was a big deal, so I didn’t always take the medication.

Article continues below

“When I went back to church and spoke to people, a lot of other people were the same, but now they all take it seriously. I’m so thankful my wife was at home because my children didn’t know what to do, so now we have given them step-by-step instructions in case anything happens in the future. The team were top-notch. I cannot fault them at all.”

News.title: Chrissie Hynde left 'heartbroken' and issues urgent plea as dog goes missing in London
News.content:
Chrissie Hynde left 'heartbroken' and issues urgent plea as dog goes missing in London

Chrissie Hynde has revealed she's been left 'absolutely heartbroken', after her beloved dog, Jack Russell cross Nico, was last seen near a park in London over two weeks ago

View 3 Images Chrissie Hynde has issued a plea to her followers to help find her dog, Nico (Image: PA)

Singer Chrissie Hynde said she was “absolutely heartbroken” as she searched for her “very dear” dog, who went missing over two weeks ago.

‌



The Pretenders frontwoman, 74, has issued multiple appeals to social media for the safe return of her five-year-old Jack Russell cross, Nico, who was last seen in a park in London.

‌



Hynde shared a photo of her beloved dog on Instagram on Thursday as she made her latest plea, and wrote: "Can anyone in Great Britain tell me of the whereabouts of my little dog Nico?

‌



"I don't know if someone has fallen in love with her and is harbouring her in their home? Or maybe someone has grabbed her and using her for some malicious purpose…? Or maybe she's been knocked over by a car and is lying in a bush, dying.

3 View 3 Images Chrissie issued a plea to her followers 3 View 3 Images Nico was last seen two weeks ago

‌



"Please, please, please if anyone has seen her at all, can you let me know? Last seen: Silkstream Park in Colindale, London. NW7/NW9." Her online fans were quick to offer their support, with one writing: "Praying or Nico's return!!"

"Feeling and knowing the anguish and desperately hoping Nico is found," a fan said, while another went on to write: "She so gorgeous please universe bring Nico home to her mummy."

A follower penned: "Oh I do hope you find her Chrissie! There are several volunteer organisations in the UK who can help you find a lost dog. Friends here in Edinburgh managed to found their family dog with lots of support from lovely volunteers. I'll be keeping you and your beautiful dog in my thoughts!"

‌



"Chrissie devastated for you. Praying for his safe return. I saw him in one of your paintings in Edinburgh just yesterday and felt very. connected to it. Little did I know what had transpired. Praying for his safe return," an Instagram user added.

Hynde previously shared an appeal on Wednesday, in which she described her dog as "very dear to me" and said she is "absolutely heartbroken".

She said Nico was last seen near the entrance to Silkstream Park in Colindale just over two weeks ago, and urged her followers not to chase the dog if they spot her “as she might be very nervous”.

‌



The singer also described the dog as having a “tan coat with white markings” and “wearing a black collar with a silver tag” in a previous plea to “help us bring her home”.

Hynde is best known for founding rock band Pretenders in 1978, and is the lead vocalist, guitarist and primary songwriter of the chart-topping group. She leads the current line-up alongside drummers Martin Chambers and Kris Sonne, and guitarist James Walbourne.

The group are famed for hits such as Brass In Pocket, Talk Of The Town and Don’t Get Me Wrong, and have achieved multiple Grammy nominations, one UK number one single and a chart-topping album.

Article continues below

The Pretenders were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005.

News.title: NHS deadline as patients urged to act quickly by Monday
News.content:
NHS deadline as patients urged to act quickly by Monday

Patients are being urged not to miss the deadline

View 3 Images The NHSBT chief executive promised the results would be transparent (Image: Maskot via Getty Images)

The NHS has urged patients to act quickly and avoid an upcoming deadline if they want to be heard.

‌



Blood donors, transplant patients and donor families have just days left to influence how NHS services are run before a key consultation closes. NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) is urging people to complete an online survey before Monday, August 10, as it draws up a new policy on how it listens to patients, donors and their families. The organisation says the findings will help shape future services and will be presented directly to the NHSBT board before being published.

‌



Anyone who has received treatment through NHS Blood and Transplant, donated blood, organs, tissues or stem cells, or is part of a donor family, can take part. The surveys take around five to 10 minutes to complete and people do not need to have previously been involved in NHS consultations.

‌



View 3 Images The findings will help shape future services (Image: Me 3645 Studio via Getty Images)

Frances O'Callaghan, Chief Executive of NHS Blood and Transplant, said: "I have commissioned this work because NHSBT wants to improve how we listen, involve, and work with patients and their families."

She acknowledged there was room for improvement, adding: "Across NHSBT, there are many good examples of colleagues who are working hard to listen to patients and donors, but we have not always done this as well or as consistently as we should. People have not always been able to see how their views have shaped decisions or led to change."

‌



She said there was "a commitment from the very top of this organisation to make this better", with patients, donors and families helping to develop recommendations for a new engagement policy.

Urging people not to miss the deadline, Ms O'Callaghan said: "The survey is an important part of this work. It will help us understand what is working, what needs to change, and what would make the biggest difference to the people and communities we serve."

View 3 Images The consultation is being overseen by two independent external co-chairs (Image: MoMo Productions via Getty Images)

‌



She added: "Please complete the survey and tell us what you think. Your voice matters. If you do not tell us, we may not know or fully understand what needs to change."

The NHSBT chief executive also promised the results would be transparent, saying: "The findings will go directly to the NHSBT board, and they will be made public, so you can see what we heard, what we are proposing, and how your voice has influenced our work."

NHS Blood and Transplant says stronger engagement with patients and donors will help build trust in its services, improve the experience of patients, donors and their families, and ensure decisions are informed by people's lived experiences.

Article continues below

The consultation is being overseen by two independent external co-chairs working alongside patients, donors, donor families and NHSBT staff from across the organisation. The surveys close on Monday, August 10. More information here.

News.title: DVLA '01' rule for drivers wearing glasses - when ignoring it could cost £1,000
News.content:
DVLA '01' rule for drivers wearing glasses - when ignoring it could cost £1,000

Millions of people wear glasses to drive but there are rules in place that must be followed

View 3 Images Millions of drivers wear glasses but there are rules to follow (Image: Getty)

Figures show that approximately one in five motorists should wear glasses to drive to ensure they are safe on the road. Many of these will have only begun to have reduced vision after they passed their driving test as many people's eyesight deteriorates as they grow older.

‌



There is a code on a driving licence which shows if people must wear glasses to drive - 01 on the licence means the holder must use eyesight correction such as glasses or contact lenses. However, most people do not have this section ticked even if they do need help to see when they are behind the wheel.

‌



View 3 Images People can find their eyesight deteriorates as they get older

‌



According to the government there are some times you must notify the DVLA if you need to wear spectacles and others when you do not need to. It advises: "You must wear glasses or contact lenses every time you drive if you need them to meet the ‘standards of vision for driving’."

When to tell the DVLA

There are a number of health conditions which motorists must notify the DVSA of, including several affecting vision.

"You must tell DVLA if you’ve got any problem with your eyesight that affects both of your eyes, or the remaining eye if you only have one eye. This does not include being short or long sighted or colour blind. You also do not need to say if you’ve had surgery to correct short sightedness and can meet the eyesight standards."

‌



Eye conditions that mean you must notify DVLA

GOV.CO.UK says: "You must tell DVLA if you have certain eye conditions." It adds the eye conditions you must tell DVLA about are:

blepharospasm

diabetic retinopathy (with laser treatment)

diplopia (double vision)

glaucoma

nyctalopia (night blindness)

retinitis pigmentosa

View 3 Images There are minimum vision standards to drive (Image: Getty Images)

‌



You must tell DVLA if any of the following apply:

your eye condition affects both eyes

your eye condition affects one eye - but you only have vision in that eye

you have retinitis pigmentosa that affects one or both eyes

a GP, optician or eye specialist has said you should not drive

you do not meet the visual standards for driving

Vision standards

Drivers must also meet other standards when it comes to driving a car or van with impaired vision. According to GOV.CO.UK: "You must be able to read a number plate from 20 meters away (about the length of 5 parked cars). You can wear your glasses or contact lenses if you use them for driving.

‌



"You must also meet the minimum eyesight standard for driving by having a visual acuity of at least decimal 0.5 (6/12) measured on the Snellen scale (with glasses or contact lenses, if necessary) using both eyes together or, if you have sight in one eye only, in that eye.

"You must also have an adequate field of vision - your optician can tell you about this and do a test."

How to tell DVLA

If you have one of these conditions, you should report your eye condition online. If you have a condition in one eye and another condition affecting your other eye, you need to fill in and send form V1 to DVLA.

Article continues below

The address is on the form. You can also use form V1 if you cannot use the online service.

News.title: Prof Tim Spector issues leftover bread warning as he says 'don't throw it away'
News.content:
Prof Tim Spector issues leftover bread warning as he says 'don't throw it away'

The co-founder of Zoe, a renowned epidemiologist and noted TV science expert, says you should never throw it out

View 2 Images Professor Tim Spector says people should not throw away leftover bread - file image (Image: https://www.instagram.com/tim.spector/)

UK households have been told not to throw away leftover bread by a prominent British scientific expert. Tim Spector, the co-founder of the Zoe app and Professor of Genetic Epidemiology at King's College London, issued the guidance in a new post on Instagram.

‌



In it, he told people that they should not be throwing away leftover bread. Instead, he offered a solution that is good for your health - and it can also be applied to potatoes and pasta.

‌



He told his 775,000 followers: "I've got a hack for you. You've got to start freezing your bread. Next time you have a bit of leftover bread, don't just throw it away.

‌



"Stick it in the freezer because it will be healthier when it comes out. And the reason is because the starch in the bread gets converted by that cold into resistant starch."

He said doing this tweaks that chemical into something that does not get absorbed early on in the gut. Instead, he said it goes further on to the lower part of the colon.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Once there, it meets our gut microbes and can help our gut microbes. "And it's treated like fibre," he said. "So the same thing applies to potatoes and pasta, and you can improve both of those just by keeping them in the fridge or the freezer and reheating them afterwards. So if you want to fiber max your bread, store it in the freezer."

The text accompanying the post notes: "When bread is freshly baked, most of its starch is easy for your body to break down into glucose. Freeze it, though, and a portion of that starch changes its structure through a process called retrogradation, becoming what’s known as resistant starch."

It says that resistant starch resists digestion in your small intestine. Rather than turn it into sugar, it goes into your colon where your gut microbes ferment it, producing beneficial compounds that help support the gut lining. The post states: "Because less total starch is converted into immediate glucose, freezing bread can also lead to a smaller blood sugar rise than eating the same slice fresh." Yet it advises: "The quality of the bread still matters, try to choose a wholegrain or authentic sourdough where possible. But if you regularly eat bread, freezing it, and even better, toasting it straight from frozen, is a simple habit that can give your gut microbes a little more to feed on."

‌



View 2 Images Professor Tim Spector talks about his bread method in his Instagram post (Image: Instagram/https://www.instagram.com/tim.spector/)

One follower said simply: "Love love love this one." Another added: "As a person who loves bread but can't eat one by myself before it goes bad (prefer to get the big ones for financial reasons lol), I've been doing this for years."

Professor Spector is far from the only one to offer this advice. The Good in Bread website says that a scientific study from 2007 suggested that freezing white bread could lower its Glycaemic index, especially when the bread is toasted after being defrosted. Another study in 2017 showed similar results, it said - along with a more recent study from 2023.

Article continues below

The Conway Medical Center in America also says on its website: "Instead of being digested in your small intestine like regular starch, resistant starch travels to your large intestine, where it ferments and produces short-chain fatty acids. These support gut health, help reduce inflammation, and may even benefit your immune system.

"So freezing your bread before eating it gives you two benefits: better blood sugar control and a healthier gut microbiome."

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
In a statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Stuart Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
More arrests have been made in Thetford as disorder linked to anti-immigration protests continued for a third night in the Norfolk market town.

A further two men in their 40s were arrested on Thursday evening, Norfolk Police said, taking the total number of people arrested in relation to the disorder to five.

One of the pair was arrested on suspicion of racial hatred, relating to offences on Wednesday, the force said. The other man was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and failing to give his details to police when asked.

Policing powers were stepped up in Thetford on Thursday evening following the disorder earlier in the week.

It came after police officers were "subjected to significant aggression" on Wednesday, including a female police officer who was "seriously bitten".

Crowds also attempted to storm homes linked to alleged asylum seekers on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings.

Police removed some people from inside a property on Thursday evening.

When responding to claims the evacuated homes were housing asylum seekers, Norfolk's chief constable Paul Sanford told the BBC: "On some of the occasions that absolutely was the case.

"We did have people protesting in the Thetford area who were targeting addresses they believed housed asylum seekers and on a couple of occasions that required us to escort the residents of those properties away for their safety."

Amid the disorder, pictures appeared to show a heavy police presence in the residential area of Canterbury Way on Thursday night.

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

Norfolk Police has imposed public safety measures in the town, including requiring people to remove face coverings if asked to do so or face arrest.

They will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or who they suspect may commit, anti-social behaviour, to leave the area.

The measures were put in place from 18:00 BST on Thursday and remain until 07:00 on Friday.

Sanford refuted any suggestions of excessive force by officers.

News.title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
News.content:
Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cellsâ¦ this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

News.title: Village sees record 50 days without rain during summer heatwave
News.content:
As the extremely dry spell continues across much of England and Wales, a small village in Surrey has notched up 50 consecutive days without rain this summer.

Wisley, most famous for being the site of the 240-acre garden owned by the Royal Horticultural Society, saw 36 continuous dry days back in the hot summer of 1976 - but has comfortably exceeded that number so far this year, with no rainfall since mid-June.

It comes after the driest July for England and Wales since Met Office records began 190 years ago, external.

Meanwhile, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued further yellow heat health alerts, external for most of England this weekend as the temperatures start to build again. The alerts cover the Humber, West and East Midlands, east of England, London, and the South East and South West from 09:00 BST on Saturday until 21:00 on Tuesday 11 August.

News.title: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
News.content:
The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigned amid allegations of copying other academics' research.

Jason Arday's appointment in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment. Now, Cambridge says it has launched an investigation after "new information" emerged about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments.

There are two fundamental questions for the university.

Did it fail to adequately check Arday's credentials when appointing him, and did it defend that decision because of an institutional push to position itself as more diverse?

For one of the world's leading universities known for academic excellence and globally significant research, this is about its institutional culture and decision-making at the highest level.

The biggest reputational risk surrounds the accusations of academic plagiarism now under investigation - and denied by Arday - because they get to the heart of what a university is about.

The University of Cambridge uses the common definition of plagiarism as "passing off someone else's work as if it were your own without appropriate acknowledgement".

There is no allegation more serious that can be levelled at an academic.

One of the fundamental purposes of a research-led university is the creation of knowledge through original thinking, insights and inquiry.

The quality of this is the foundation of Cambridge's reputation, and a source of significant funding.

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
News.content:
Do you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?

The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.

But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.

Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago.

But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?

News.title: How a diary entry solved the murder of a missing man
News.content:
When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had disappeared six years earlier.

Richard Dyson vanished without trace in November 2019. He was last seen alive on 17 November that year and was reported missing eight days later when he failed to meet his daughter, Bethany.

"He was by all accounts a very good father, and he was regularly in contact with his daughter Bethany who was, I believe, 19 at the time of his disappearance. It was totally out of character," Ryan recalled.

"It was clear that he had disappeared off the face of the Earth."

Richard, who was 55 at the time, had been living in his car at Parkside Cottage on Christopher Wright's farm on Sheffield Road in Barnsley, helping with small jobs around the farm.

The farm was searched, but other than a collection of illegal weapons belonging to Wright, nothing more unusual was found and there was no sign of Richard.

His phone, however, showed it had never left the farm.

Police believed from the outset that Richard had been killed and that Wright and his childhood friend, Karl Schwalbe, were responsible, according to Ryan.

"We very much suspected their involvement, but without a body it's very difficult to prove murder," he said.

On 28 July, Wright, 73, and Schwalbe, 72, were convicted for their roles in Richard's disappearance and murder, ending a six-year wait for answers for Richard's family.

At a sentencing hearing at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday, Wright was jailed for 35 years for murder and Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

But how did police finally catch them?

News.title: Boxer charged with killing aid worker in Athens after his wife gave police 'key' details
News.content:
Appearing in court earlier, Ahmadzai asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.

His lawyer, Christos Erdas, said his client had exercised his right to remain silent, and that his rights had been "violated" through leaks of evidence and documents from the case file - including his right to the presumption of innocence.

The lawyer said that when Ross was found, she had no injuries and any apparent cause of death was "entirely absent".

He said his client wanted the forensic medical report and the "toxicological and histological examinations of the deceased" to be included in the case file.

Erdas added: "His [Ahmadzai's] stance towards the prosecuting and investigating authorities did not constitute a stance of denial but, on the contrary, one of reservation, so that he may present his defence in full once the case file has been completed with the above essential documents â which were not sought by the preliminary investigating authorities â with the sole aim of establishing the substantive truth for both sides."

Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months.

News.title: Amanda Knox defends Fringe comedy show after claims it will 'trivialise violence'
News.content:
Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has defended her solo comedy show following calls for it to be cancelled.

The sold-out show called Cartwheel, which Knox will perform at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, discusses motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter.

Knox told the BBC she is not the first person to use comedy to talk about traumatic events and said her material focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women".

But Stephanie Kercher, the victim's sister, said she is concerned it will "normalise and trivialise" violence against women, and Meredith, in particular.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Stephanie Kercher, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Responding to the comments, Knox said: "The interesting irony of that is that my daughter is a huge motivation for me doing this show.

"It's about how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women and what it means to raise a daughter in that world, knowing how bad it can be.

"If they [Kercher's family] saw my show, they would recognise that."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by nearly 5,000 people.

It states the show disrespects her memory and risks making light of such a harrowing event.

News.title: Police to end review into siblings who died in farmhouse 'bloodbath'
News.content:
A forensic review into the deaths of a brother and sister 50 years ago will end almost four years after it began, despite not delivering any new conclusions.

The bodies of Martha and Griff Thomas were found at a farmhouse in Llangolman, Pembrokeshire in 1976, originally prompting a double murder investigation.

Family member Huw Gibby, 79, said he was left "shell-shocked" that the investigation had failed to find any new answers, and described crime scene photos as a "bloodbath".

Dyfed-Powys Police said a "significant amount of complex work" had been undertaken, and "the family has been updated on the limitations faced in reviewing an incident that took place 50 years ago".

On a chilly Saturday morning in December 1976, postman Nigel Rossiter pulled up outside the isolated Ffynon Samson farmhouse in west Wales.

It was his first week in the job, and he spotted a couple of letters still lying on the floor of the porch where he had delivered them days before.

Smelling burning inside, he raised the alarm. This led to the discovery of two bodies â Griff, 73, who was badly burnt, and Martha, 70, who had severe injuries.

Police were called and found Martha - known as Patti - lying slumped on a magazine rack in the corner of the living room, with severe head injuries.

Chairs had been knocked over, and an overturned television lay at her feet. It was still switched on, with the sound of static filling the room.

News.title: Wildfire damage could take hundreds of years to recover from, experts say
News.content:
It could be hundreds of years before habitats destroyed by wildfires in Wales recover, an environment watchdog has said.

Nick Thomas, from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), said if soil had been incinerated in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at about a millimetre a year, it could take centuries for the vegetation to come back.

He called 2026 the worst year Wales had ever experienced.

As well as damage to natural habitats and animal life, Thomas warned loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.

Wales has witnessed huge wildfires this summer, including one major incident and the evacuation of a village in Conwy county.

In the Rhinogydd mountain range in Gwynedd, which is home to a National Nature Reserve and a Special Area of Conservation, a blaze burned for nearly two weeks and affected over 2,000 acres.

Both fires were visible from space.

Meanwhile, a fire in Blaenavon, Torfaen, could be smelt as far away as Cardiff.

Although fewer wildfires were reported in the second half of July in England and Wales compared with 2025, Thomas said: "This year seems to have been worse, I would say, than any of the ones I can remember.

"I would expect this to probably be the worst year for wildfires perhaps we've ever had."

While some areas will recover quite quickly - potentially within a couple of years - he said: "It all depends on how deep the fire goes.

"If a fire burns into the soil and incinerates the soil... then you've lost hundreds of years worth of soil.

"So it's going to take hundreds of years really for that vegetation to come back in a similar way to what it was."

News.title: Veteran camps in woods for months waiting for home
News.content:
An Army veteran has spent the last 15 weeks camping in woods while waiting for his social housing application to be processed.

Blair Murray, 44, served more than a decade in the Royal Logistics Corps up to 2010, but was made homeless by a landlord last year and spent months staying with friends before setting up camp in woodland near Crook in County Durham.

Murray said he had lined up a job and arranged to start counselling sessions, but both were being held up by his lack of a home.

Since the BBC got in touch with Durham County Council, homeless prevention manager Christopher Hepworth said the authority had worked with the Armed Forces Outreach Service and booked him into a Travelodge.

Hepworth said: "We will continue to work with him to secure suitable, stable, long-term accommodation."

In the most recent survey carried out by the Office for Veterans' Affairs, one in 400 ex-service personnel reported they were homeless or sleeping rough.

News.title: Four men arrested after violent disorder near Pontypool, police say
News.content:
Four men have been arrested and two are in critical condition in hospital after violent disorder in south Wales.

The arrests were made following a disturbance involving a group of men in Pontnewynydd, near Pontypool, at about 19:15 on Thursday evening, Gwent Police said.

Two of the men arrested are in police custody. In total, three men were taken to hospital for treatment.

Specially trained firearms officers and the National Police Air Service attended the scene, alongside paramedics, the force said.

Det Ch Supt Anne-Marie Salwey said: "Violence in any form is completely unacceptable and anyone who is found to be involved in this disorder will be dealt as we will not accept this behaviour in our communities.

"We recognise that reports of this nature will prompt concern from our residents and it is likely that you will see officers in and around the area conducting enquiries as part of this investigation," she added.

Police are asking for anyone with information, CCTV or dashcam footage from the area around Hospital Road and Mill Road between 19:00 and 19:30 on Thursday to contact them.

The road between Mill Road and Hospital Road is currently closed in both directions, with motorists urged to seek alternative routes.

News.title: Man wrongly jailed for murdering man wants to restore his 'forgotten' grave
News.content:
A man who was wrongly jailed for 11 years for murder is raising money to restore the grave of the man he was accused of killing.

Michael O'Brien was one of three men wrongly convicted of the 1987 murder of Cardiff newsagent Philip Saunders.

O'Brien, along with Darren Hall and Ellis Sherwood, became known as the Cardiff Newsagent Three. They were eventually cleared in 1999, in what became one of Wales' worst miscarriages of justice.

He said he recently visited Saunders' grave and was "sad" to see there was no longer a headstone there and the area was "unkempt."

"It just sort of hit home that one, the killer was still at large, and two, this man has largely been forgotten about," O'Brien said.

Saunders was killed with a shovel in his backyard. It seemed the ambush and brutal attack was an attempt to steal his day's takings.

In June, nearly 40 years on from the original crime, South Wales Police said they were launching a review of the evidence in the case, "in the hope advances in forensic science will provide the breakthrough needed".

News.title: All schools in England to get pupil attendance targets, government says
News.content:
Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve pupil attendance, the government has confirmed.

Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

It comes as official attendance data, published on Thursday, suggested school absence rates in England remained above pre-pandemic levels, with nearly one in five pupils missing at least 10% of school in the 2025/26 academic year.

Education minister Paul Waugh said the new attendance targets would take each school's local challenges into account, but that "every school has a role to play to improve attendance".

Before the Covid pandemic, when many schools closed to pupils for significant periods of time, attendance rates at English mainstream state schools regularly stayed above 95%, but schools have struggled to get back to those rates in the years since.

Thursday's figures, external suggested an overall attendance rate of 93% for 2025/26, a slight decrease on the previous year. That includes both authorised absences, such as illness, and unauthorised absences, which is when pupils miss school without permission or a valid reason.

The rates of persistent absence have doubled since the pandemic. A pupil is described as persistently absent if they miss at least 10% of school sessions.

In 2018/19, persistent absence rates for England state schools were around 10%, while the most recent data showed it was at 19% in 2025/26.

Pupils on free school meals and those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) were also still more likely to be absent from school than their peers.

After the rush and expense of the summer holidays, it’s natural to feel a bit anxious about money.

It’s easy for spending to creep up during this time, with holidays, days out, social events and treats all adding to the bill. Along with that, it’s common to save less and rely more heavily on credit cards during this busy period.

We spoke to Jennifer Crichton, associate planning director at Killik & Co, about why the end of summer is the ideal time for a financial reset, and the practical steps you can take to get your money back on track.

open image in gallery Jennifer Crichton Headshot (Killik & Co/PA)

Address any short-term debt

open image in gallery (Alamy/PA)

Make tackling any short-term high-interest debt an immediate priority.

“When looking at your finances after the summer holidays, I would recommend thinking about any short-term debt that has built up first,” advises Crichton.

She notes that lots of people put big purchases like flights on credit cards during the summer break which can lead to high-interest charges if you do not pay the balance off right away.

“Think about how to either get rid of that debt or get a plan in place to get it down as quickly as possible,” recommends Crichton.

Sort out your emergency reserve

open image in gallery (Alamy/PA)

“Once you have looked at your debt position, make sure that you’ve sorted your emergency cash reserve,” advises Crichton. “For this, we would recommend a minimum of three months of essential expenditure, if that’s possible.”

Having that emergency cash fund will help lower stress as knowing you have money saved for sudden bills prevents panic.

“When you’ve got that emergency fund as a back-up, it’s nice to know that you wouldn’t be living month to month if something did unfortunately happen to your more stable income,” says Crichton.

Review any spending

Looking back at your summer spending can sometimes be helpful.

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.
