World.title: South Korea recovers landmines believed to have washed from North by monsoon floods
World.content:
South Korean authorities have collected 15 landmines believed to have washed over into their coastal territory from the inter-Korean border on monsoon deluges, officials said on Friday.

 

The Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), splitting the Koreas since their 1950-53 war ended with an armistice, is one of the most heavily mined places on Earth.

Some 800,000 are estimated to be buried around the area, according to military data cited by the Yonhap news agency, many from the war but mine-laying has continued in recent years.

Choi Young-ran, head of civil defence for South Korea's northwestern border country of Gwangwha, said 15 "suspected North Korean landmines" were "discovered along coastal areas."

She told the AFP news agency the mines "believed to have been washed away during the monsoon season and recent torrential rains" had been found between 23 July-3 August.

Smoke rises after a blast to remove landmines as South Korean soldiers work to reconnect the inter-Korean railway at the DMZ in Paju, 9 October, 2002 YUN JAI-HYOUNG/AP

"We have recovered all 15," she said.

Gwangwha, an archipelago county, sits at the mouth of the Han River estuary which is bisected by the border between North and South Korea.

Seoul's military warned last month about the risk of heavy rainfall washing explosives into rivers crossing the border and causing "serious damage" if they explode downstream.

In 2015, two South Korean soldiers patrolling the western DMZ lost limbs when they were severely wounded by a North Korean mine, the military said.

In late July, Gwangwha county sent out alerts to residents warning them of the danger of North Korean mines along coastal areas.

County officials said Wednesday they had "not ruled out the possibility that more could arrive."

Barricades near the Unification Bridge which leads to the Panmunjom in the Demilitarised Zone in Paju, 15 October, 2024 AP Photo

Park Heung-yeol, a Gwanghwa resident, said tourist numbers fell for a time after the 2015 landmine incident and locals fear that could happen again.

Despite the heat, "there are still around 300 people who dig for clams by hand," he told AFP.

"It seems like a dangerous activity for them" given the risk from mines, he said.

Natural disasters tend to have an outsized impact on North Korea due to its weak infrastructure. Deforestation has left it vulnerable to flooding.

Specialist outlet NK Pro said on Thursday hundreds of homes at a large North Korean border military base were washed away by heavy rains in late July after an apparent dam collapse.

Citing satellite imagery, it said "at least 380 single-story row houses were completely swept away, while the site is reportedly a key artillery command."

South Koreans living along the high-security border face frequent disruptions and danger.

Pyongyang has sent trash-filled balloons and also broadcast bizarre, unsettling noises over the border.

The broadcasts became a major nuisance under President Lee Jae Myung's hawkish predecessor, Yoon Suk Yeol.

World.title: Australia grants citizenship to two Iranian women footballers who sought asylum
World.content:
Two members of the Iranian women’s football team who claimed asylum in Australia in March have been granted citizenship.

 

Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh said in a statement on Thursday that Immigration Minister Tony Burke swore them in the day before at a citizenship ceremony in their adopted home city Brisbane.

Friends and supporters from the local Iranian community attended the ceremony.

“Yesterday was a truly special and unforgettable day for me. I feel proud and deeply grateful to become an Australian citizen. Australia has given me the opportunity to build my life and my future, and I feel, more than ever, that I belong here,” Ramezanisadeh said in the statement.

Ramezanisadeh said her Iranian roots and memories would always be part of her.

Pasandideh said Wednesday had been “one of the happiest days of my life.”

“I’m incredibly proud and grateful to officially become an Australian citizen. After everything we’ve been through and all the challenges we faced, this moment means more than words can express,” Pasandideh said.

Iran players pose for a team photo ahead of the Women's Asian Cup soccer match between Iran and the Philippines in Robina, 8 March, 2026 AP Photo

When the Associated Press news agency asked Burke's office why the women’s citizenship was fast-tracked, his department said it could not comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.

The Refugee Council of Australia, a nonprofit umbrella organisation representing asylum-seekers, said refugees usually must live in Australia on a valid visa for four years before they can apply for citizenship.

Their citizenship could potentially have been fast-tracked under Australian law to make them eligible to play football for Australia.

The Iranians joined Brisbane Roar, a football team which plays in Australia’s elite A-League Women’s domestic competition, after they were granted asylum when Iran dropped out of the Women’s Asia Cup that Australia hosted.

They were among seven Iranian women who initially accepted asylum but five changed their minds within days and returned to the team for undisclosed reasons.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks during a press conference in Melbourne, 9 July, 2026 AP Photo

The team had arrived in Australia before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Concerns for the team’s welfare at home were raised when players decided against singing the Iranian national anthem before their first match of the tournament.

Protesters demanding asylum for the team widely cited Iranian sports commentator Mohammad Reza Shahbazi calling the women “wartime traitors” in a television broadcast.

US President Donald Trump used social media to call for the team to be granted asylum and telephoned Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the issue.

World.title: More than 160 styles and a tasting for all the senses: Beer's Old and New Worlds
World.content:
With more than 10,000 years of history, beer today is much more than a drink associated with informal moments. Its cultural richness, the more than 160 styles that exist and its potential for gastronomic pairings have been gaining recognition, albeit slowly, in markets traditionally dominated by wine, such as Portugal.

 

This International Beer Day, always celebrated on the first Friday in August, thus serves as an invitation to discover a vast, constantly evolving universe.

The date was created in 2007 in the city of Santa Cruz, California (United States), by a group of friends who decided to establish a day to bring people together around one of the most widely consumed drinks in the world. The initiative took on an international dimension and is now marked in more than 50 countries.

According to Sagres beer sommelier and brand manager Filipa Santos, interest in beer often stems from discovering its complexity. From the ingredients to the different brewing schools, the drink offers a diversity that ranges from classic European beers to contemporary interpretations from the so‑called "New World".

Filipa, who has worked in marketing for 20 years and has been involved in the beer sector since 2011, has worked with several beer brands, both national and international, and took a beer sommelier course because she "felt the need to really know the product she worked with". Along the way, what fascinated her most was "the diversity and richness of the beer world".

Beer is traditionally made from four natural ingredients: water, malt, hops and yeast. However, the way these elements are combined and handled gives rise to an enormous variety of styles.

The difference lies in the role that each ingredient then takes on, depending on the brewing tradition and the style Filipa Santos Beer Sommelier

Water, for example, can directly influence the flavour, depending on its mineral composition.

"Around 93% of a beer is water, so if we want a pilsner, which is a low‑bitterness, versatile beer, very easy to drink, we use soft water. Here the water is not going to dominate and we will have a beer in which the malt can provide good balance. If we want a more intense, more complex beer, such as a Guinness, a stout, then we should use hard water, because we need the minerals to help the malt take on a bigger role, to really stand out," the specialist explains to Euronews.

Every day, more than 10 million glasses of Guinness stout are consumed worldwide AP Photo

Malt — usually barley, but also wheat or other cereals — is responsible for the colour and the cereal notes, which can range from fresh bread to toasted bread.

In the case of hops, bitterness predominates, along with aromatic notes of tropical or citrus fruits. "They can range from herbal and floral to fruity, including tropical and citrus notes, rose and so on."

Yeast, in turn, is the invisible ingredient that transforms sugar into alcohol and gas, and is also decisive in the final profile. "There are beers in which yeast is the protagonist, for example Belgian beers. In those we can find notes of clove, spicy notes, and banana notes as well."

A world of more than 160 options, far beyond the standard lager

From these four elements, more than 160 recognised beer styles emerge.

Even so, Portugal remains a market dominated by one particular style. "We are a country of pilsner beer – light, easy‑drinking and refreshing," notes Filipa. But that is only a small part of the beer universe.

Among the best‑known styles are IPA (India Pale Ale), marked by the intense hop aroma; stout, dark beers with notes of coffee or chocolate; and weissbier, wheat beers with softer, more fruity characteristics.

The diversity also reflects different geographical traditions – the so‑called brewing schools, which are divided between the "Old World" and the "New World".

In the Old World, the most classic styles can be found – "the true archetypes of beer", says Filipa. In Germany, Austria and Czechia, where tradition places particular value on working with malt and wheat beers, styles often appear that are more cloudy and smooth, with slightly sweet notes and characteristic aromas such as banana.

Typical of Germany are witbier, which have a straw‑yellow to pale golden colour, and Weissbier, which have a somewhat stronger colour, ranging from gold to amber. Both have a cloudy appearance because they are unfiltered.

Pilsner, now dominant in many markets, was born precisely in the city of Pilsen, in present‑day Czechia.

Another group includes England, Scotland and Ireland, where beer is also strongly linked to malt, "but also because historically they are whisky‑producing countries," Filipa explains.

The hops used in these countries also take on their own identity. "The English have very earthy hops and I think that has a lot to do with their history in terms of tea."

Then, the Belgians and the French "are very given to irreverence, originality and make bold blends". Here, production includes techniques such as spontaneous fermentation, in which tanks are left open and micro‑organisms present in the air take part in the process. The result is more unpredictable and complex beers, often with marked acidity or with added fermented fruit, as in kriek, made with cherry, the sour cherry.

In Belgium, there are more than 1,500 different types of beer, each with its own characteristics of flavour, aroma and production method GEERT VANDEN WIJNGAERT/AP

In contrast with these traditions, the so‑called New World, notably countries such as the United States, Brazil and Japan, has brought a new approach to beer, reinterpreting classic styles. One of the clearest examples is India Pale Ale (IPA), originally British but profoundly transformed by North American brewers, who introduced hops with more tropical, intense profiles.

That difference is also linked to territory. As with wine, hops reflect the place where they are grown. In the United States, regions such as Yakima Valley have become central to production, giving rise to more fruity, exuberant aromas, in line with the preferences of new consumers.

Tasting with all five senses

Understanding beer is not just about knowing styles or origins; it is also about how it is tasted. "To taste a beer, I always advocate, first of all, not having a glass filled to the top. We can even use the so‑called universal tasting glass, which is very similar to a white wine glass," reveals the beer sommelier.

The choice of glass can be important when it is necessary to capture the aroma better, so that it is easy to put the nose inside the glass and smell the beer.

This is because beer tasting uses all the senses. The first contact is visual, to assess aspects such as the colour of the beer, its clarity or cloudiness and the head it produces. Touch then allows us to feel whether a beer is at the right temperature.

Hearing also plays a part in this process. "We can even listen to the beer – whether the gas is very expressive or not, whether we can hear the little bubbles of gas."

The glass, the temperature and the way it is served are important to guarantee beer quality AP Photo

Next comes the aroma, to identify which aromatic notes stand out. Depending on the style, it is possible to pick up citrus, tropical, toasted, spicy or even sour notes.

Only then does flavour enter into it, confirming or not what the aroma suggested, because the nose does not always match the taste. At this stage, a beer sommelier will assess the balance between the sweetness of the malt and the bitterness of the hops, the lightness or body, the freshness or intensity. "We taste in small sips and try to understand which flavour prevails and what happens on our tongue.

In the end, unlike wine tastings, no spittoon is used, "because it is important to assess the retronasal effect, what aroma comes back through the nose at the end". Beer specialists also swirl the glass and that gesture, as well as helping to release the beer's aromas, brings back the head.

According to Filipa Santos, "a rigorous beer tasting can take 20 minutes or more".

New habits and new consumers

The interplay between tradition and innovation has been crucial for the evolution of the global market, increasing diversity in the beer world, driven both by craft beers and by more demanding, better‑informed consumers.

Although it retains a central role as a social element, beer has been gaining space in new contexts, including at the table.

"Beer is a bit of a social glue, because it also works as a disinhibitor. It is always associated with an early‑evening moment, with socialising, with drinking, with or without food. It may simply be a meeting of friends. But I feel that, over time, beer is gaining more space in different consumption occasions," observes the beer specialist, pointing to a growing openness to food pairings.

There are still those who associate beer only with informal moments of socialising, such as meeting up with friends AP Photo

That versatility translates into unexpected combinations. "There is a huge range of possible pairings," she explains, citing examples that range from light beers with seafood to more daring proposals such as dark beer with pastel de nata.

Another decisive factor is the change in habits. "We have consumers who are more concerned about a healthy lifestyle, more diligent about what they consume," says Filipa Santos, pointing to the growth of the alcohol‑free segment and to a new generation that "drinks less alcohol" and makes more conscious choices.

All this means the market has to adjust and provide a different response. And we can see that in other categories. More alcoholic drinks, such as white spirits, already have 0.0% options on the market. Wines also have 0.0% options. Filipa Santos Beer Sommelier

In the sector, the challenge also lies in valuing service and the overall experience. "We may have good beers, but if the beer is not served in the right way, in the right glass at the right temperature, we cannot move forward. So the question of service is very important," she warns, stressing the importance of the so‑called "perfect serve" to guarantee beer quality.

Despite the progress, some prejudices persist. "There is a stigma, but it makes no sense," she says, referring to the idea that beer is less sophisticated than wine. For the specialist, it is above all a question of lack of knowledge: "Beer has great richness, not only in its history but also in its diversity, which is barely recognised."

World.title: The beetle that hears fire: why it is so valuable to science
World.content:
For weeks now, devastating wildfires have been raging across large parts of Europe. Entire regions have to be evacuated, people are losing their homes and, time and again, lives are being lost. The persistent heat is making the situation even worse. According to many researchers, climate change is increasing both the frequency and intensity of forest fires.

 

However, science has long since been looking not only at how fires can be extinguished . It is also investigating what happens afterwards and which solutions nature itself has in store. A key role here is played by a rather inconspicuous inhabitant of our forests: the black pine jewel beetle.

A beetle that seeks out fire

The black pine jewel beetle (Melanophila acuminata) is one of the few animals that actively respond to forest fires. As soon as a fire has gone out, it flies to the burnt areas to lay its eggs there. Biologist Lydia Schübel, head of the animal welfare inspection unit at the Munich Animal Welfare Association, explains to Euronews why this is.

"The beetle flies towards the flames because its larvae can only develop in freshly burnt trees. Healthy trees have defence mechanisms that the small white larvae cannot overcome."

What is remarkable, Schübel says, is that the animals can detect a fire "from distances of at least 80 kilometres".

How exactly the beetle finds fires has fascinated researchers for decades. Scientists at the University of Bonn have now been able to show that the insect can literally "hear" fire.

The beetle has special sensory organs on both sides of its body. They consist of tiny cavities filled with fluid. When the heat radiation from a fire hits these structures, the fluid expands and deforms fine sensory hairs. The nervous system registers these pressure changes in much the same way as sound waves.

A model for new fire detectors

This very mechanism is now set to help people as well.

Since the early 2000s, researchers at the University of Bonn have been working on replicating the beetle's sensory organ in technical form. The field of research is known as bionics, in which solutions found in nature are transferred to technical applications.

The scientists developed a simple infrared sensor inspired by the beetle. Instead of the natural sensory organ, they use a thin plastic plate that expands slightly when exposed to heat radiation and passes this movement on to a sensor.

Project leader Helmut Schmitz explained in a report on the project's current status that forest fires cause damage running into billions of euros in the European Union alone. Detecting them as early as possible could help prevent devastating mega-fires. In the long term, bionic infrared sensors could therefore contribute to early detection of fires.

According to the researchers, the first prototypes cost only a few euros and were therefore significantly cheaper than conventional infrared sensors. Although they initially did not match their performance, the researchers see them as a promising approach.

After the fire, the forest starts again

The question of what happens after a fire is also on many people's minds.

The black pine jewel beetle is one of the so-called pyrophilous species, animals that benefit from fire. Its larvae burrow through the dead wood, speeding up its decomposition.

According to Lydia Schübel, this returns nutrients to the forest soil more quickly. The loose deadwood at the same time creates favourable conditions for new plants.

The black pine jewel beetle is not alone in this. "Other pyrophilous animal species in Germany include the four-spotted ground beetle, the pit ground beetle, the pine bark bug and the smoke fly," Schübel tells Euronews.

Worldwide, they are considered important helpers in the regeneration of forests.

Some plants too are adapted to fire, Schübel says. Some possess particularly fire-resistant properties, while others only open their seed pods after being exposed to intense heat, helping forests to grow back quickly.

Even certain bird species benefit temporarily from the altered habitats. Species such as the wryneck, tree pipit or common redstart use dead trees as nesting sites and find food particularly easily in the open areas.

Forest fires remain natural disasters with usually devastating consequences. At the same time, though, they also show how resilient ecosystems can be and how much there is to learn from nature. Ironically, a beetle that goes looking for fire could in future help to detect blazes earlier and limit their impact.

World.title: How Europe’s drought exposes ‘weakness of fossil fuels’ as Poland forced to shut down coal plants
World.content:
Poland has been urged to double down on clean energy after Europe’s drought wreaked havoc on its coal industry.

 

Earlier this week (4 August) utility giant Enea was forced to reduce generation at the Kozienice and Połaniec coal-fired power plants after critically low water levels in the Vistula River limited cooling water supplies.

The move is said to have removed 1.3 GW from Poland’s power system, enough to power more than one million average households. This is around two per cent of the country’s current energy capacity.

River flow near the Kozienice Power Plant fell to just 135 cubic metres per second on 5 August, reflecting severe drought conditions.

The plant’s cooling system withdraws approximately 80–100 m³/s of water from the river – more than half of the remaining flow under such conditions.

Despite growing evidence that the plant is killing millions of fish larvae, including from six protected species, Enea is cracking on with plans to build a near 1.3GW gas-fired power plant at the Kozienice site. Experts warn that such a move will increase pressure on the Vistula River ecosystem through continued high cooling water demand.

‘The paradox of the climate crisis’

“This is the paradox of the climate crisis: power plants driving climate change are increasingly becoming its victims,” says Paweł Pomian, Vice-President of Polish environmental organisation EKO-UNIA.

“As the Vistula River dries up, an energy system built around large thermal power plants loses its resilience. Kozienice isn’t unique. There are many plants with similar cooling systems across Poland and there will be more if the government continues to expand fossil gas.”

Pomian argues that Europe’s latest drought should be a “wake-up call” for Poland and the rest of the continent to transition towards technologies like solar and wind power that require the least amount of water to generate electricity.

Poland urged to ditch coal

Despite witnessing some of the most rapid growth in solar power in Europe – adding more than 20 GW of solar capacity between 2020 and 2025 – Poland’s combined share of wind and solar remains five per cent lower than the EU average.

According to energy think tank Ember, Poland relies on coal for more than half (51 per cent) of its electricity – while wind and solar only make 25 per cent of the mix.

Poland aims for 51 per cent of renewable electricity generation and 64 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, but its coal addiction is proving difficult to shake.

“Coal plants are paying the price for the problems they created,” says Kasia Szeniawska, a campaigner at Beyond Fossil Fuels.

“As heatwaves and droughts become more severe, it has exposed the weakness of fossil fuel-based energy systems. While most EU countries cut down their coal use, Poland is not only failing a timely phase-out, it’s also proposing new gas plants that will only aggravate environmental issues.”

Europe’s drought hits renewables

Europe’s hot and dry summer, which climate scientists say would be “virtually impossible” if it wasn’t for the burning of fossil fuels, has also impacted the renewable energy sector.

According to energy intelligence firm Montel, inflows to reservoirs and run-of-river hydropower plants in Austria and Switzerland were nearly 50 per cent below average in July.

Total hydro production for Austria in July was only 51 per cent of normal levels (compared against the last 15 years) due to low rainfall, Montel adds. Similarly, Switzerland saw 48 per cent of normal production, while Germany (63 per cent) and France (68 per cent) also suffered.

While significant drops in hydro output can push countries back onto polluting sources like coal, solar and wind can often compensate for the drop in electricity generation.

For example, Ember says weather conditions caused a 12 per cent drop in annual hydropower production last year, contributing to gas generation in the EU rising by eight per cent (compared to 2024).

However, the same weather conditions (which also caused wind power to fall by two per cent) boosted solar generation.

This meant that in 2025, solar generated more EU power than ever before, growing by more than 20 per cent. It highlights the importance of diversifying the renewable energy mix in an era of climate-fuelled extreme weather.

World.title: Stunning new hotels set to open on Europe’s islands in 2026 and beyond
World.content:
Are you dreaming of an island escape? You don’t have to venture beyond Europe.

 

From Sardinia’s turquoise coves to Greece’s whitewashed villages, Europe is home to some of the world’s most spectacular island retreats. And with the island hotel scene only gaining momentum, there’s never been a better time to visit.

In recent months, a wave of new openings have already welcomed guests including Zannier Hotels' Zannier Île de Bendor in France, Mykonos’ first Four Seasons hotel, and the Mamula Island by Banyan Tree in Montenegro's Bay of Kotor.

This momentum is showing no sign of slowing down with more highly anticipated openings on the horizon set to debut this year and beyond.

Whether you’re looking to add a wellness escape getaway or seeking an upscale waterfront retreat, here are the island stays to keep on your radar.

New island hotels in Europe

Luura Paros Cliff, Greece

Nestled in the heart of the Cyclades and perched above the bay of Agia Irini on the island’s western coast, this property welcomes guests 12 years and above and marks Luura Hotels’ first entry into Paros.

Having opened on 1 August 2026, an array of 39 suites offer uninterrupted sea views from its expansive gardens and terraces. Guests are also spoilt for choice for where to take a dip as there are 19 private pools which sit alongside a private chapel, a vast wellness area and two restaurants.

Contemporary Japanese dining concept, Mimi Kakushi, plates the dynamic energy of 1920s Osaka, while Lenea serves contemporary Mediterranean cuisine with every dish highlighting seasonal ingredients.

Luura Paros Cliff, Greece Luura Hotels

Luura Paros Cliff invites guests to immerse themselves in local experiences with curated programmes from in-house ceramics workshops hosted by local artisanal ceramic artist Maria Economides. Guests can also board a private boat for fishing tours to remote islets.

A second Luura hotel on Paros is set to open by 2028 at New Golden Beach.

Eha Retreat, Estonia

Located on Estonia’s Hiiumaa Island in the Baltic Sea, Eha Retreat is earmarked to open in September 2026.

The property will feature eight suites and three forest cabins that can accommodate a total of 22 guests.

With an emphasis on wellness, each stay begins with a consultation to create a personalised programme for individualised wellbeing, while in-room elements include guided sleep meditations.

Lobby and fireplace Eha Retreat

Guests can choose between spending either three, five or seven nights, shaped around Estonia’s so-called “five seasons” and designed to support deep rest and regenerative wellbeing.

A five-night retreat starts at £5,500 (€6,417.81) per person, based on double occupancy. This covers dining experiences, curated programmes of treatments, wellness sessions and activities.

Eha’s culinary offerings are led by Michelin green star-awarded chef Peeter Pihel and champions local produce. The retreat collaborates with fishermen, grain growers and herbalists local to Hiiumaa to serve up fresh dishes. Guests also have the chance to explore Estonian food conservation techniques.

Costa Smeralda, Sardinia, Italy

Located just north of Porto Cervo and centred around stunning sea views, this Sardinian resort by Rocco Forte will open its doors in 2027.

Set to be an intimate retreat of 64 rooms and suites, each with its own private terrace overlooking the shortline, the opening of Costa Smeralda will mark the Rocco Forte brand’s debut property on the Italian island.

It promises three dining concepts serving guests fresh and local ingredients, as well as a state-of-the-art spa.

The two-acre seafront resort will also feature lush, palm-filled gardens.

Six Senses Comino, Malta

This Six Senses retreat is set to be nestled across the bays of San Niklaw and San Marija on the lesser-known Maltese island of Comino, which boasts rugged cliffs, bright turquoise waters including the Blue Lagoon, as well as wild herbs and flowers.

Six Senses Comino will feature 71 low-rise suites overlooking the bay, each with their own private decks.

A further collection of 19 standalone two- and four bedroom retreats will have large gardens, private pools and a secluded central courtyard. The retreats will also have a separate clubhouse with a restaurant and piazza with sweeping views of Santa Marija bay.

The 1,000 square metre Six Senses Spa will offer treatments, longevity therapies and personalised wellness programmes inspired by local Maltese culture.

Mandarin Oriental Porto Cervo, Sardinia, Italy

Alongside Rocco Forte’s new property, Sardinia’s Costa Smeralda is also set to have a luxury opening from Mandarin Oriental.

Near the sought-after seaside resort of Porto Cervo, the five-star Mandarin Oriental property will have 83 rooms and suites. Guests will have no shortage of eateries to choose from, with five dining concepts promising a variety of culinary offerings.

Mandarin Oriental Porto Cervo, Italy Mandarin Oriental

At the retreat, guests can take advantage of the Spa at Mandarin Oriental, as well as a fitness centre and large indoor and outdoor pools, with the latter featuring lush garden surroundings.

On the Porto Paglia beach, the property’s new beach club will be the place for waterfront rest, relaxation and rejuvenation.

World.title: Thailand: Several killed in school shooting north of Bangkok
World.content:
The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. At least six people were killed in the attack.

Several people were killed and others injured in a shooting at a high school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, just north of the capital city of Bangkok, local authorities said.

Students, teachers and other workers were evacuated from school as authorities deployed police officers, rescue workers and emergency doctors to the scene.

According to the police, the gunman, who is a student at the school, first fatally shot his grandparents with his grandfather's handgun. Then, he went to his school, located north of Bangkok, and killed three teachers and three students before killing himself.

Earlier, Thai national police spokesperson Trairong Phiwphan said that 15 people were wounded.

In a statement, police said the gunman fired 26 rounds, and an additional 34 rounds of ammunition were found at the scene.

Students, teachers and other staff members were evacuated from the school Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

Meanwhile, Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul expressed his condolences and stated that he had instructed relevant officials to assist those affected.

School shootings in Thailand

The incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi.

According to district authorities, the Debsirin Nonthaburi School had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers in the 2025 academic year.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. It is estimated that around 10 million firearms are in circulation, or about one for every seven people.

In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from the police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand. The two-hour attack resulted in one death and two injuries.

World.title: US judge orders Meta to pay $567 million over harm to children
World.content:
A New Mexico judge ruled Meta created a "public nuisance" that harmed children's mental health, ordering the company to pay over half a billion dollars in damages and overhaul safety features on Facebook and Instagram.

A judge in the US state of New Mexico has ordered Meta on Thursday to pay $567 million (€492 million) and overhaul how Facebook and Instagram operate for young users in the state.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid's ruling, issued in Santa Fe, states the company created a "public nuisance" that harmed children's mental health. It also comes on top of $375 million in damages a jury ordered against Meta in March, bringing the company's total New Mexico liability to $942 million. That March verdict found Meta violated the state's consumer protection law by misleading the public about the safety of its platforms for children.

Why smart glasses threaten privacy of women and children To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

State Attorney General Raul Torrez sued Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, in 2023. On Thursday, he said the ruling holds the company accountable for design choices that put children at risk.

"Today's decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online," he said.

What does the verdict entail?

Roughly three-quarters of the $567 million, to be paid out over five years, will fund mental health treatment for young people. The rest will go toward prevention programs, screening, and related services.

US jury fines Meta in landmark child‑safety case To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The judge also ordered Meta to make direct changes to Facebook and Instagram, including monthly limits on teen usage, tighter notification controls, stronger safeguards on adult contact with minors, oversight of AI chatbots, and improved handling of child sexual abuse reports.

The company must also work with schools to build a reporting system for flagging underage users, and must also delete data it holds on children under 13. Federal privacy law bars Meta from collecting personal data to verify children's ages, so the court instead ordered the company to keep improving its AI-based age-estimation tools.

How has Meta responded?

Meta has pledged to appeal the latest New Mexico verdict.

"We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content," the company said in a statement, adding: "We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts."

The new penalty, ableit massive, is still a small fraction of Meta's roughly $60 billion in annual profit. Investors have largely shrugged it off, with shares dipping less than half a percent in after-hours trading. However, the company still faces a wave of related lawsuits, including a trial set for later this month in Oakland, California, involving 29 states, and separate suits already underway or filed in several other states.

Australia's under-16s forced offline by social media ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moreover, several countries are contemplating social media bans on children under the ages of 15 or 16 to limit the harm caused by being online, Australia — citing mental health, cyber bullying and concerns over lack of physical activity, among others — became the first nation to introduce such a ban for kids under 16 back in December.

Britain, Canada, Indonesia, Malaysia, Turkey and several European countries have also cracked down on teen use of social media.

World.title: Middle East: Houthi attack wounds 11 in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
08/07/2026 August 7, 2026 Houthi militia attack wounds 11 in Saudi Arabia

An attack by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis late on Thursday wounded 11 civilians in southern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, a military official said.

The attack injured seven Saudis, two Egyptians, a Yemeni and a Pakistani, according to General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Shiite Houthi rebels.

He accused the rebels of "using indiscriminate shelling against civilian objects."

Neither the militia or Iran immediately responded to the coalition's statement.

Tehran has targeted Saudi Arabia since the US-Iran war started this February, as its regional archrival hosts US military facilities. Less then three weeks ago, the Houthi militants in Yemen declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, signaling that Riyadh's long-running conflict with the Houthis in Yemen is becoming increasingly intertwined with the wider Middle East war.

World.title: Argentina: Milei's property bill triggers protests, anger
World.content:
Police clashed with protesters in Buenos Aires after thousands rallied against President Javier Milei's private property bill. The government had already dropped a provision on foreigners buying land in Argentina.

Security forces used tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannons against demonstrators in downtown Buenos Aires on Thursday, eventually dispersing the crowd which was protesting a new law pushed by the government of President Javier Milei.

Several thousand demonstrators, mobilized by left-wing groups and labor unions, rallied outside the Argentine Senate against the "Inviolability of Private Property" bill, which is currently under debate.

Opponents of the property bill see the danger of 'colonization' Image: Luis Robayo/AFP

According to EFE news agency, the protest had been peaceful before police intervened. AFP news agency, however, reported that some protesters threw stones and other projectiles at officers.

Why are Argentinians opposing Milei's private property bill?

The new bill aims to streamline eviction procedures, change the rules on rural land use and install new limits on government seizing private property.

The proposal would have also raised the limit of land that could be owned by foreign buyers from 15% to 25%. Amid growing backlash, however, the ruling party removed the chapter on foreigners buying land.

Milei's government hopes the reform would help the country attract investment, but rivals of the libertarian leader warn against "colonization, fragmentation, fracture and balkanization" of Argentina.

On Thursday, protesters carried placards reading: "The homeland is not for sale."

"Defending our territory is crucial … We must take to the streets to protest. It is our Argentina that we must defend; it is not for sale," Marcela Arin, who traveled from the southern province of Neuquen to join the protest in Buenos Aires, told EFE.

Nearly 5% of Argentina's territory — an area similar in size to England — is already foreign- owned, according to a 2025 study by researchers from the University of Buenos Aires and other academic institutions.

The study said that in some districts the percentage of foreign owners already exceeds the current 15% cap.

World.title: Trump signs new orders restricting birthright citizenship
World.content:
The US president's move comes just two months after the Supreme Court ruled that his first executive order on citizenship was unconstitutional.

US President Donald Trump dismissed a previous Supreme Court decision on citizenship as "very unfortunate" while signing two new executive orders restricting birthright citizenship on Thursday.

"It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision," Trump said of the 6-3 vote top court ruling two months ago.

The ruling rebuked Trump's previous attempt to challenge the constitutional provision that allows individuals born on US soil automatic citizenship.

Birthright citizenship is enshrined in the 14th ​Amendment of the US Constitution. The rule guarantees citizenship for babies born in the US with only narrow exceptions, such as the children of foreign diplomats or members of an enemy occupying force.

"This was done for a different reason. This ​was done right after the Civil War. This ‌was for the babies of slaves, and what's happening now?" Trump said on Thursday.

What are the new executive orders?

Trump's close advisor and the architect of his immigration policy, Stephen Miller, said one of the orders signed Thursday seeks to deny birthright citizenship to children of members of "foreign terrorist organizations" as well as "large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments."

Miller added that the order "ensures that large numbers of people who wrongly (would) be getting birthright citizenship will no longer be eligible for those benefits."

ICE targets South Asians for removal from United States To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The second executive order targets what Trump called "birth tourism." The expression refers to visitors securing visas and traveling to the US so they would give birth while in the country, so their children are entitled to US citizenship.

"That practice of birth tourism is, as of ​the signing of this order, hereby banned. What that means is that no one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a ​visa for this ‌fraudulent purpose," Miller added.

Currently, there are no official figures depicting the number of foreigners who come to the US for the explicit purpose of giving birth to obtain citizenship. But the Trump-aligned Center for Immigration Studies claims that between 20,000-25,000 mothers did so 2016-2017.

Trump: 'Our country suffers'

The White House has argued that the new executive orders do not fall within the limits of the Supreme Court ruling.

Still, the orders are expected to be challenged in court.

"I thought we were going to win it at the Supreme Court," Trump said on Thursday. "Unfortunately, we had a bad decision, very unfair decision. Our country suffers because of it and we’re ending it a different way," Trump said.

Currently, no US law bans so-called birth tourism, but a federal regulation implemented in 2020 during Trump’s first term prohibits using temporary tourist and business visas for the primary purpose of obtaining US citizenship for a newborn.

World.title: Ebola: Africa CDC plans to use vaccine for different strain as outbreak spreads
World.content:
The head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control pledged to deploy a vaccine for a previous Ebola strain in the current DRC outbreak, with test cases indicating a potentially live-saving level of protection.

African health authorities say they would start using a vaccine for the prior Zaire ebolavirus strain to treat the current outbreak involving a different, fast spreading strain known as Bundibugyo. The ongoing outbreak is centered in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The director general of the African Centres for Disease Control, or Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, told reporters in a videoconference on Thursday that there was evidence of the vaccine eliminating deaths, if not symptoms, in the test cases conducted so far.

The Africa CDC and the World Health Organization also plan to launch research checking for a possible mutation or some other abnormality in the current outbreak, as the virus spreads at a rate six to eight times faster than any past outbreak on record.

The warnings come amid continued strikes and protests in the hardest-hit regions by some medical staff complaining either of non-payment or of inadequate pay and conditions.

Medics trying to contain the virus are noting an unusually high rate of infection Image: Dirole Lotsima Dieudonne/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What did Kaseya say about the speed of the spread?

Kaseya was speaking from Brazzaville in the neighboring Republic of Congo,after meeting with World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus in Kinshasa the previous day.

The Africa CDC chief said authorities estimated 4,000 cases have been confirmed by now, given that 3,973 had been confirmed as of Tuesday in the latest available data. That data also pointed to 1,801 confirmed Ebola deaths. The current oubreak was only declared in mid-May and is already the second-largest on record.

Compared to the West Africa outbreak, which took place from 2014 to 2016 and is considered the largest ever, the current strain was causing deaths 6 times faster.

"As Dr. Tedros shared with me yesterday, it's time for the WHO and Africa CDC to conduct studies to check that there is no issue, additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating, because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented," Kaseya said.

"This outbreak is just expanding."

Everyone in Ituri at risk

Kaseya said cases had now been logged in 51 health zones, compared to nine in May.

He also drew attention to the numbers of cases identified as a share of the contact tracing program's size. During the most virulent and deadly outbreak on record, the Zaire strain outbreak in DRC between 2018 and 2020, one patient was identified from every 57 contacts identified as being at risk.

Across the border in Uganda, which says it has eradicated the small number of cases it experienced this year, it had an average of one confirmed case from every 41 contacts in the list.

In DRC this year, meanwhile, there was one confirmed case for every 10 people in the contact list. Kaseya said that in his estimation, a point had been reached where anybody in the hardest-hit city of Bunia or the worst-affected region of Ituri should be considered potential contacts.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Kaseya say about the Zaire strain vaccine?

Doctors have had only limited chances to treat or test against the Bundibugyo Ebola strain as it had been considered rare. There are also no recognized vaccines or treatments. However, medical experts have already started working on a new jab.

During the Thursday conference, Kaseya said that the Africa CDC planned to start dispensing an existing Ebola vaccine for the Zaire strain in the current outbreak. During limited testing, while people vaccinated against the Zaire strain did experience some symptoms, "we saw zero deaths among people who are vaccinated."

He said that this "means there is a level of protection" provided by the vaccine.

Kaseya said authorities also planned to expand the use of the antiviral drug remdesivir in affected areas.

Neighboring Uganda had reported successes treating its limited number of cases with redemsivir. It recorded 20 cases and said that only two of the patients died.

It wasn't immediately clear how many supplies of the vaccines or treatment were ready and available to dispense in a fairly remote region of the DRC that's close to active insurgencies and other forms of conflict. Africa CDC's Professor Placide Mbala said any initial rollout would be a relatively small trial.

What's the latest on the stranded barge in Maluku near Kinshasa?

Meanwhile, authorities near the DRC capital of Kinshasa continued screening more than 300 people traveling on a river boat after the death of a passenger reported to have Ebola-like symptoms.

Health teams deployed a mobile laboratory to the vessel to conduct precautionary tests in Maluku where it was intercepted, northeast of the capital.

The ship was intercepted and halted in Maluku on Thursday, and authorities have started screening the passengers as a precaution Image: Wendy Bashi/DW

The city has so far avoided being exposed to the Ebola outbreak.

Kaseya on Thursday told reporters that the boat had come from Mongala province, where no Ebola cases have been reported. Prior reports had said the vessel hailed from Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province, which is an affected area. Kaseya said that initially even the government had received this erroneous information.

He said health authorities and the government nevertheless decided to screen all passengers to try to minimize risk, with results still pending.

World.title: How drought threatens electricity supplies in Europe
World.content:
Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are better prepared.

Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure.

In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube.

Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria, Slovakia, Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania.

DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others.

Hungary: Most severe energy crisis in decades

No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest, and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country.

Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely.

Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity.

In Prahovo (eastern Serbia), the Danube's low water level has revealed the remains of a German WW II warship Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy.

Romania: Blasting rocks to redirect water

Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week.

Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch.

Romania's navy carried out a controlled blast of submerged rocks to allow more water to flow into the eastern branch of the Danube Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one.

Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production.

Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry — and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics.

Serbia: An unfavorable energy mix

Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower.

The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade, which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production.

In Hungary, dropping water levels of the Danube threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO

Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production.

Slovakia, Austria less affected

In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought.

In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages.

Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities.

Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts.

In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources.

Bulgaria: Large battery storage capacity

Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria.

The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity.

At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity.

The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world.

These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Ceuta leader says 100 migrants died in border rush
World.content:
With over 3,000 migrants still in Ceuta after rushing the border last week, Ceuta leader Juan Jesus Vivas warns the situation in the Spanish exclave is "unsustainable." Hundreds of those migrants are minors.

Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas told EU lawmakers at the European Parliament on Thursday that some 100 people had died during last week's border surge.

He also said the city was still reeling from the event and now dealing with unaccompanied migrant minors who remain in Ceuta.

Vivas called the situation "unsustainable," and pleaded for government help.

His visit to Brussels comes a week after some 72,000 migrants rushed through the border between Morocco and Spain's North African territory of Ceuta.

The incident caused a spat between several EU countries and Madrid, with Italy suspending the Schengen free-travel pact with Spain.

On Wednesday, Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras said some 141 people had died on July 30, with 63 bodies found in Morocco and 78 in Ceuta.

Vivas said the large number of unaccompanied migrant children poses 'a high risk for order and public security' as reception centers were overwhelmed Image: Javier Fernández/Europa Press/IMAGO

Ceuta asks for more security resources

The Spanish government said that nearly all of the migrants had returned to Morocco, but Vivas noted that between 3,000 and ‌5,000 migrants were ⁠still in Ceuta.

Vivas also said Ceuta lacked the security resources necessary to deal with the situation.

"Security forces have not been deployed with the intensity required by the situation ⁠we are still facing," he told a European Parliament committee.

"Immigration services have not ⁠been sufficiently reinforced to ⁠handle the border rejections," he added.

Right groups warn some children living on the streets had been beaten and assaulted Image: Violeta Santos Moura/REUTERS

Large number of migrant children in Ceuta

Morocco said it is ready "to work towards identifying unaccompanied ‌minors with a view to their return ‌to ​their homeland," state ​news agency MAP reported on Thursday evening, citing a diplomatic source.

It is estimated that hundreds of unaccompanied minors are currently facing limited access to food, water, shelter and sanitation in Ceuta.

Some children have been beaten and assaulted, says Jose Miguel Morales, head of Federacion Sur Acoge, a migrant rights and assistance group from southern Spain.

"Every day that passes without a solution and without safe accommodation means leaving these children — especially these girls — exposed to all kinds of abuse," he told Spanish public television.

"We are talking about real children — 10 years old or younger in some cases. Many are under 14."

Another charity, Save the Children, urged for all minors to be registered. It also warned that girls face "heightened risks of violence, trafficking and exploitation."

Minors likely to be distributed to ther parts of Spain

In 2025, after a surge of migration overwhelmed reception centers in the Canary Islands, Spain passed an immigration law reform. The new law mandated the redistribution of unaccompanied minors from overstretched territories within 15 days of their case file being completed.

However, the redistribution of the children to the rest of Spain is expected to meet resistance from regions governed by the center-right Popular Party (PP) and the anti-immigration, far-right Vox party.

But Spain's socialist government already has warned against the pushback, with Deputy Prime Minister Carlos Cuerpo saying that PP and its regional governments "must comply with the law just like everyone else."
