World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018849/Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.title: Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018849/Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.content:
China has discontinued the blue exterior lights common to its vehicles equipped with autonomous driving features.

The ban, leaked by a car industry blogger on microblogging platform Weibo on July 29, was outlined in an official notice from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. According to the notice, the ban took effect as of July 27 for new vehicles, while existing vehicles are apparently not affected at this time.

The same day, the state-affiliated China Automotive Standardization Research Institute, while not directly confirming the ban, said on its public account on messaging app WeChat that the blue lights have been used excessively and improperly, and that a new national standard is under revision.

The blue lights, or advanced driver assistance system indicator lights, are usually found on the wing mirrors or lower front and back fenders of vehicles with advanced driver assistance systems. Introduced in 2022 by domestic car brand Li Auto, automakers began adopting them to indicate to other road users that intelligent driving systems were in use.

However, China’s current vehicle lighting standard does not include specific provisions for blue lights and permits only white, red, yellow, and amber for vehicle signal lights.

In its July 29 post, the China Automotive Standardization Research Institute said blue lights can cause glare for other road users at night, distracting them or interfering with their judgment of road conditions. It also noted that vehicles equipped with the lights are more likely to be cut off or followed closely by other drivers, increasing the risk of accidents.

In addition, many vehicles’ blue lights are installed in the car’s preexisting turn lamps, meaning that turn signals can sometimes glow blue.

An insider at Geely Automobile, China’s leading car manufacturer, confirmed to domestic media that they had indeed received notice of the ban but declined to disclose specific details. “We are aware of the news and will strictly comply with national regulations, awaiting further instructions from the government,” the insider said.

Zeng Qinglin, general manager of domestic car brand Yijing, listed what he sees as the reasons for the ban on his Weibo account. “First,” he said, “the brightness and flickering of various blue lights lack unified standards, affecting traffic safety and causing light pollution.”

“Second, other drivers, seeing blue lights on the car ahead, know it’s using an intelligent driving system and deliberately cut in, assuming the system will brake automatically,” he wrote. “As a result, drivers using the intelligent driving system are often startled by sudden braking. A device intended to signal safety has instead become a new source of risk.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Blue lights on a car indicating self-driving mode. VCG)

World.title: At least 7 killed, 15 hurt in Thailand school shooting, police say
World.content:
SCHOOL VIOLENCE. A student reacts with a relative after being evacuated from Debsirin Nonthaburi School, following a shooting incident at the school, in Bang Kruai district in Nonthaburi province on the outskirts of Bangkok, Thailand, August 7, 2026.

Initial reports say a student opened fire at a school in Thailand before killing himself

BANGKOK, Thailand – Seven people were killed in a school shooting in Thailand on Friday, August 7, including the gunman, and 15 people were wounded, Thai national police spokesperson Trairong Phiwphan said.

One of those reportedly killed was a teacher.

Initial reports said a student opened fire at a school in Thailand before killing himself, authorities said.

Lieutenant Colonel Dechrapee Kongdee, Nonthaburi Provincial Police commander, earlier confirmed the casualties to Reuters and said the suspected gunman had committed suicide.

The incident took place in the Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province north of Bangkok.

One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought there were firecrackers going off or someone banging an object.

“I didn’t think it was a gun at first,” he said. “There were many shots: bang, bang, bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again.”

In photos circulated by emergency workers, students streamed out of the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, on the northwestern outskirts of Bangkok, as ambulances operated. In one photo, one person is seen lying on a stretcher outside an ambulance, while another is attended to by a medic.

In the 2025 academic year, the school had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers, according to district authorities.

In February a teacher died and a student was injured in southern Thailand’s Hat Yai district after a gunman opened fire at a school. – Rappler.com

World.title: Loren Legarda, Leandro Leviste out of the country – immigration bureau
World.content:
WINNER. Businessman Leandro Leviste is proclaimed winner of the congressional race in Batangas 1st District on May 13, 2025.

Legarda and Leviste left the country days after the Ombudsman announced the plunder and graft complaints against them

MANILA, Philippines – The Bureau of Immigration confirmed on Friday, August 7, that Senator Loren Legarda and her son Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste have left the country on August 2, days after the Office of the Ombudsman announced the plunder and graft complaints against them.

“The office confirms the departure of [Senator] Loren Legarda and [Representative] Leandro Leviste in separate flights last August 2. Both had no derogatory records at the time of departure,” BI spokesperson Dana Sandoval told Rappler.

On July 31, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla announced that plunder and graft complaints are currently pending against Legarda and Leviste over the latter’s solar energy projects.

The Ombudsman also included Duterte-time energy secretary Alfonso Cusi in the pending complaints over the alleged conspiracy “to secure exclusive government rights over the country’s solar energy resources through legislative and regulatory actions.”

According to the Ombudsman, investigation also revealed that some service contracts were transferred to Leviste’s affiliated corporations that only exist on paper, but had not started operations.

“All indicators point to the fact that they had no intention to fulfill contracts that they had garnered. The terminated contracts resulted in more than ₱10.44 billion in unpaid financial obligations to the government,” the Ombudsman said.

Complaints are not enough to bar Legarda and Leviste from leaving the country.

The Ombudsman, however, could ask for a precautionary hold-departure order (PHDO) against the two since the complaints are already at the preliminary investigation level or one step before becoming actual cases. The investigator may file this with a court and the latter will issue a PHDO as needed.

On Friday, the Senate confirmed that Legarda is currently on medical leave.

“Last August 3, the [chief of staff] of the Office of Senator Legarda sent a letter informing the Office of the Secretary that ‘Senator Loren Legarda will be on medical leave from 3 to 5 August 2026’,” Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. told Rappler on Friday, August 7.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Senator Erwin Tulfo also confirmed that Legarda filed for a medical leave, adding that this was the reason for her absence during the Senate impeachment hearings.

“Wala naman ho binanggit kung ano’ng klase. Basta sinabi lang ho, medical need (It was not specified which type of medical leave. She just said it’s for medical need,” Tulfo said.

Legarda has skipped the impeachment trial from August 3 to 5. – With a report from Patrick Cruz/Rappler.com

World.title: How Maria de Leon’s guilty plea strengthened US case vs Quiboloy
World.content:
CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – Who is Maria de Leon, the septuagenarian who was sentenced for her role in an immigration fraud scheme that helped members of doomsday preacher Apollo Quiboloy‘s group remain in the United States?

On Tuesday, August 4, a US federal judge sentenced the 77-year-old Los Angeles-based paralegal to time she already served, crediting the roughly four months she spent in custody after her 2021 arrest. She posted bail after her arrest.

It was her guilty plea that gave US prosecutors a vital insider’s account of how followers of Quiboloy allegedly manipulated the American immigration system.

For years, De Leon’s work unfolded not from the pulpit of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) but through paperwork.

A former Quiboloy follower told Rappler on Friday, August 7, that De Leon was an “outsider” to the KOJC and that her dealings with the detained preacher’s group were limited to handling its immigration paperwork. She is known in the KOJC as “Liberty,” the name of her firm.

Through her firm, Liberty Legal Document Services, prosecutors said she prepared immigration filings that helped KOJC members stay in the US, allowing them to continue soliciting donations for what authorities described as a bogus charity.

Her admissions would later substantiate one of the central mechanisms of the US government’s case against Quiboloy.

In 2022, De Leon agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy, admitting she knowingly prepared and filed immigration petitions based on sham marriages, arranged solely to obtain legal status for KOJC members.

According to court records, the paralegal participated in an eight-year conspiracy with Quiboloy’s subordinates to secure permanent residency and, ultimately, US citizenship for church workers who otherwise could not lawfully remain in the country.

In her plea agreement, she acknowledged that the immigration applications were “based upon false representations of the bona fides of the underlying marriages.”

Federal prosecutors said the immigration scheme supported a wider trafficking operation detailed in a 74-page indictment unsealed in November 2021. Weeks later, Quiboloy and two other of his associates were placed in the US Federal Bureau of Investigation’s list of wanted people.

The Quiboloy church workers brought to the US on fraudulently obtained visas were allegedly dispatched across the country to solicit donations for the Children’s Joy Foundation, which authorities described as a bogus charity used to finance KOJC operations and the lavish lifestyles of its leaders.

The same indictment charged Quiboloy and seven associates in an alleged sex trafficking conspiracy, accusing KOJC leaders of coercing girls and young women into sexual relationships with the Davao-based religious leader through threats of “eternal damnation” and other forms of psychological coercion.

De Leon was not accused of participating in the alleged sexual abuse but was charged as part of the broader conspiracy.

Quiboloy and several of his associates have been detained in the Philippines due of a trafficking case before a Pasig City court and child sexual abuse cases before a Quezon City court.

The US has sought Quiboloy’s extradition, and the Philippine foreign affairs department said it endorsed the request to the justice department.

Quiboloy is closely associated with detained former president Rodrigo Duterte — they are known to be close friends and the preacher served as presidential adviser during the previous administration. – Rappler.com

World.title: SC latest ruling: Bad news for Duterte’s impeachment battle
World.content:
ARRIVED. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Senate on July 7, 2026, to meet with her lawyers but did not attend the impeachment trial.

The Supreme Court recently junked Duterte's petition questioning the initial process of her impeachment at the House level

Vice President Sara Duterte suffered a defeat at the Supreme Court (SC) filled by appointees of her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Via a unanimous decision on Wednesday, August 5, the High Court junked the two petitions — including the one filed by the Vice President herself — questioning her impeachment proceedings.

The petition questioned the validity of the hearings on the impeachment complaints conducted by the House committee on justice. In other words, the Vice President was challenging the early stages of her impeachment proceedings that are currently in full-blown trial at the Senate impeachment court.

Should the petitions have been granted, they might have had an adverse effect on the ongoing trial.

The SC dismissed the consolidated petitions GR No. E-05546 (filed by lawyer Israelito Torreon, et al.) and GR No. E-05667 (filed by Duterte) for being moot, or no longer being in need of resolution. It explained that this was so because the House already approved and transmitted the articles of impeachment to the Senate.

The impeachment articles — in this case, four — refer to the list of impeachable allegations against Duterte. They include Duterte’s alleged misuse of her confidential funds and threats to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

By constitutional design, it’s the House of Representatives that has the mandate to assess if an impeachment complaint against an impeachable official is substantial. The House committee on justice is supposed to hold hearings, and the House plenary could later decide whether or not to approve the articles of impeachment.

On May 11, a total of 257 lawmakers voted to approve the articles, impeaching Duterte for a second time.

After the approval, the articles are now with the Senate which is in the middle of the impeachment trial.

At the trial’s end, the senator-judges will vote to either convict or acquit Duterte. If convicted, the Vice President will be removed from her position and will be barred from holding government office perpetually. She can no longer run for president in 2028.

In its briefer, the SC explained that the House’s transmittal of the articles marked the end of the lower chamber’s role in the impeachment process, and the initiation of an impeachment case. The actions Duterte and Torreon wanted to stop had already been completed, said the High Court.

“The SC further held that the impeachment process had already moved to the Senate, which had convened as an impeachment court and had begun proceedings…. Any ruling on the validity of the actions taken by the House and its Committee on Justice would no longer affect the controversy,” said the High Court.

Settle the debate?

Duterte’s 2025 impeachment was stopped by an SC decision that found that the articles of impeachment were unconstitutional, therefore voiding them, and stopping the trial at the Senate before it could even go full-blown.

The decision penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen said the 2025 impeachment proceedings violated Duterte’s right to due process and the one-year bar rule. This rule prohibits the initiation of more than one impeachment proceeding against an impeachable official within a year.

For 2026, Duterte wanted to replicate the same feat.

She argued before the SC that the 2026 impeachment complaints violated the one-year bar rule and that their referral was invalid. The Vice President also questioned the public hearing held by the committee on justice which evaluated the evidence and witnesses against her.

Some called the committee hearings a “mini-trial,” but Duterte called it a “fishing expedition.” University of the Philippines College of Law associate dean and constitutional law professor Paolo Tamase explained that a fishing expedition means that a party is using an existing legal proceeding to dig deeper into another offense.

Its purpose is to look for things against a person using evidence that can be found only through another legal proceeding, he added.

For the House prosecution, the latest SC ruling settled the debate on this so-called fishing expedition.

Play Video

“This means that all the talks about the mini-trial fishing expedition that we saw earlier, repeated by the defense, are now coming to an end. This means that the launch of the fight is no longer at the Supreme Court, but here in the Senate Impeachment Court. And we have high confidence that at the end of this process, the truth will prevail,” House prosecutor Terry Ridon said in Filipino.

“They’re questioning the proceedings at the House, including the decision to transmit to the Senate. And therefore, they hope that if the House is junked, this process will also be junked. That will not happen because the petition has already been trashed,” he added.

Senate: Independent, jurisdiction absolute

The Senate impeachment court, speaking through its spokesperson Reginald Tongol, said the SC ruling confirmed that the job of the House in initiating the impeachment had already been accomplished.

According to Tongol, the ruling also affirmed that the Senate, as the impeachment court, has exclusive jurisdiction over the impeachment trial as stated in Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution.

“Like what’s stated in the Supreme Court resolution, the transmittal of the articles of impeachment activated the Senate’s power to convene into an impeachment court. The jurisdiction of the Impeachment Court is now absolute,” the spokesperson said in Filipino.

Tongol explained that the Senate was never a party to the SC petitions and is operating “entirely distinct” from the House prosecutors. That being said, the spokesperson said that the procedural history, evidentiary gathering, as well as the House’s internal findings prior to the transmittal of the articles are within the House’s jurisdiction.

“The Impeachment Court does not inherit their legal disputes, nor will the Court litigate them in the adjudicatory phase of the process,” Tongol said.

“Because the impeachment court is fully insulated from whatever happened at the House of Representatives, the impeachment court begins with a blank slate in this adjudicatory phase,” he added.

This exclusive jurisdiction of the Senate could have been put to a test if the SC ruled the other way.

When the SC decided that the 2025 impeachment against Duterte was unconstitutional, the Senate archived the articles of impeachment. But that was a different instance — a full-blown trial had yet to commence at the time.

“Had the petitions been granted, the trial could have been put in doubt and a constitutional stand-off created. The Senate is quite protective of its prerogatives in impeachment, and unlike last year, this trial is well under way. So as in the last time the Supreme Court stopped an active trial (2011-2012), the Senate would have taken a vote,” Tamase told Rappler.

As of writing, there is a pending third petition against the proceedings of the House committee on justice, filed on April 20 by lawyer Hue Jyro Go and companions. The SC has yet to act on this, but it’s likely that this will be declared moot too, given the ruling in the first two petitions.

Meanwhile, impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero’s position is still under question at the SC after Torreon and companions filed a petition on July 7 with the High Court. But for Tamase, this legal question should not affect the trial and its validity.

“The power to try is vested by the Constitution on the Senate, not the presiding officer or any single officer. The presiding officer’s rulings are impliedly supported by the rest of the Senate — otherwise they would have called a vote and overturned the call. So any defect in his election by his colleagues will not change the legal bottomline that the Senate is running the show, according to and aided by its own rules,” the UP law associate dean explained. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala, Venus Williams reunion ends in early Canadian Open exit
World.content:
PARTNERS. Alex Eala and Venus Williams in action in the 2026 Bad Homburg Open in Germany.

Filipino star Alex Eala and American icon Venus Williams absorb a straight-sets loss in the opening round of doubles action in the Canadian Open

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala’s keenly awaited reunion with tennis icon Venus Williams ended quickly.

The Filipino and American duo dropped their opening match in the Canadian Open in Toronto as they absorbed a 6-4, 6-3 loss to Japan’s Miyu Kato and Russia’s Liudmila Samsonova in the round of 32 of women’s doubles action on Thursday, August 6 (Friday, August 7, Manila time).

Eala and Williams suffered their second straight defeat as partners after their first team-up in the Bad Homburg Open in Germany in June culminated in a quarterfinal exit.

After pulling level at 4-4 in the opening set, Eala and Williams lost the next six games as their chances of winning slowly slipped away, with Kato and Samsonova wrapping up the match in 1 hour and 15 minutes.

Eala and Williams fought back from a 0-4 hole in the second set, clinching three of the next four games to close the gap to 3-5. However, their comeback ultimately fell short after they were broken in the ensuing game.

The loss marked Williams’ exit from Toronto as she also lost her first match in singles play, falling to Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova in straight sets in the round of 128.

In contrast, Eala — who received a first-round bye as the 25th seed — advanced to the third round after a 6-1, 4-6, 6-2 victory over the USA’s Alycia Parks in the round of 64.

After Bad Homburg, Eala, 21, and Williams, 46, were supposed to link up again in the Washington Open, but the Filipina dropped out at the last minute and the American found another partner in Russia’s Diana Shnaider.

That turned out for the better as Eala went on to capture her first-ever WTA Tour singles title in Washington, where she beat the top three seeds, including American world No. 30 Jessica Pegula in the final.

Now that her doubles stint in Toronto has concluded, Eala can focus on her singles bid as she battles a third consecutive American in Caty McNally in the round of 32 on Friday (Saturday, August 8, Manila time). – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Japan orders evacuations as Typhoon Dolphin approaches, cancels 500 flights
World.content:
Authorities issue evacuation orders for nearly 260,000 residents in Kagoshima and Okinawa prefectures, while Toyota suspends work at nine factories

TOKYO, Japan – Hundreds of thousands of people in southwestern Japan were ordered to evacuate and more than 500 flights canceled on Friday, August 7, as slow-moving Typhoon Dolphin approached the region to bring violent winds, heavy rain and high waves.

The Category 1 typhoon had maximum sustained winds of 144 kph (89.5 mph) with gusts reaching 198 kph and was nearing a chain of islands between the Kyushu region and Okinawa prefecture, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.

Authorities issued evacuation orders for nearly 260,000 residents in Kagoshima and Okinawa prefectures, while Toyota suspended work at nine factories on Friday.

Dolphin was expected to maintain its strength as it approached Okinawa prefecture, raising the risk of winds that could damage or collapse some structures, authorities warned. A linear rain band — or a narrow band of intense precipitation and thunderstorms — could also develop, possibly triggering flooding, the weather agency said.

The large storm was also enveloping much of the southernmost main island of Kyushu with strong winds, including Kumamoto prefecture, still reeling from last week’s magnitude 7.1 earthquake.

Some 6,700 Kumamoto residents remain in evacuation centres after many houses collapsed. The weather agency has also warned of heatstroke risks with temperatures expected to reach 36 degrees Celsius (97 degrees Fahrenheit) in some areas. – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippine economy slows to 2.3% in Q2 2026, weakest since 2009
World.content:
HAZARDOUS AIR. Haze blankets the skyline of Metro Cebu and nearby areas before sunset on April 19, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) Public construction plunges as officials remain hesitant following the flood control scandal, and household spending posts its weakest non-pandemic growth in nearly 16 years

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine economy grew by only 2.3% in the second quarter of 2026, slowing further as weak investment and elevated prices weighed on economic activity, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported on Friday, August 7.

The latest figure was lower than the 2.8% growth recorded in the first quarter of 2026 and the revised 5.4% expansion in the second quarter of 2025. It brought economic growth in the first half of 2026 to 2.6%.

The 2.3% expansion in Q2 2026 was the weakest since Q4 2009, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic, when the economy grew by 1.8%.

Economy, Planning, and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said domestic demand remained subdued as total investment continued to decline, while household consumption slowed down amid higher prices, job losses, and weaker remittance receipts linked to the conflict in the Middle East.

Gross capital formation, a broad measure of investment, contracted by 9.2%. Its largest component, gross fixed capital formation, fell by an even steeper 13.7%, its worst non-pandemic performance since the second quarter of 2011.

The biggest drag was general government construction, which plunged by 32.4% year-on-year. The broader industry sector consequently contracted by 2.4%, even as manufacturing continued to grow.

“Although public construction is a small part of the economy, the amount of that contraction, 32%, brought a significant impact on the economy,” Balisacan said.

He added that the economy could have grown by at least one percentage point more had public construction simply recorded zero growth instead of contracting. He said that reports on the ground showed that officials and employees were more reluctant to approve or take responsibility for projects given the heightened scrunity following the flood control scandals of 2025.

The country’s chief economist also said that there are reasons to believe that hesitancy will ease.

“The Department of Budget and Management began releasing mobilization funds for 2026 infrastructure projects to the Department of Public Works and Highways toward the end of June. The DPWH in turn started awarding contracts in June and July. We therefore expect public construction and infrastructure spending to begin picking up in the third quarter and gain further momentum in the months ahead, ” he added in his opening statement.

The government expects construction spending to pick up in the third quarter and accelerate further toward the end of the year, as agencies implement catch-up plans and spend funds left unused during the first half.

Household spending, traditionally the Philippine economy’s main growth engine, expanded by just 2.8%. Excluding the pandemic, this was its weakest growth since the third quarter of 2010, when consumption rose by 2.6%.

Balisacan attributed the slowdown partly to high inflation and weaker consumer confidence. He said the government must convince households that elevated prices are not permanent and that economic conditions will improve.

The government has already slashed its growth target range to 3.5% to 4.5% for the full year, amid weaker investment, elevated inflation, and domestic and external uncertainties. The World Bank expects the Philippine economy to grow by 3.7% in 2026.

To reach at least the 3.5% lower end of that target, Balisacan said the economy would have to grow by no less than 4.4% in the second half. He acknowledged that this would be “demanding,” but maintained that it remained possible if infrastructure spending rebounds and inflation continues to ease.

Despite the combination of slower growth, high inflation, and rising unemployment, Balisacan rejected concerns that the Philippines was heading toward stagflation, a prolonged period of weak economic activity accompanied by persistently high prices.

There were also bright spots in exports, agriculture, and manufacturing. Agricultural output grew by 2.7%, while exports of goods surged by 17% and exports of services rose by 6.9%. Net exports contributed 1.2 percentage points to gross domestic product (GDP) growth.

Balisacan said stronger exports, particularly semiconductors and electronics used in artificial intelligence systems, electric vehicles, and other advanced technologies, were helping diversify the economy beyond consumption. Exports of consumer electronics grew by 230.3% year-on-year in the second quarter, while exports of components/devices, or semiconductors, rose by 13.4%.

Balisacan said this was related to the “boom” in AI and related sectors, which require these electronics and semiconductor components.

“We have been exporting electronics and semiconductors for a while. But we now have to expand and move into higher level of manufacturing, semiconductor and electronics manufacturing, especially those that make use of advanced or supporting advanced technologies like AI,” he added.

The World Bank had earlier warned that investment was slowing amid heightened scrutiny of infrastructure spending following alleged corruption in flood control projects, as well as a surge in global energy prices that compounded the country’s already high power costs. (READ: Cheaper PH electricity? Go beyond system loss; fix costly power contracts)

Ahead of the announcement, Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. forecast second-quarter growth at 1.9%. He cited another steep contraction in public infrastructure spending, softer private investment, and slower household consumption as high transport and electricity costs eroded purchasing power. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Sustainable Aviation Fuel Industry With Alatau Pilot Project
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan took a step toward entering the emerging market for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) after signing a memorandum with Hong Kong-based Full Vision Capital to explore building an integrated production ecosystem in Alatau, a project that could position the country within the global aviation industry’s decarbonization efforts.

The memorandum, signed on Aug.4 following a meeting between Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Full Vision Capital founder Dr. Peter Lee, outlines plans to study the creation of a complete SAF value chain from cultivating agricultural feedstock to processing and producing aviation fuel. The partners will also assess opportunities to deploy smart energy technologies and nickel-hydrogen energy storage systems to support renewable energy integration.

The agreement brings together the Alatau City Authority, Kazakhstan’s Ministries of Energy, Agriculture and Transport, and Full Vision Capital under the Green Kazakhstan initiative.

Speaking during the meeting, Bektenov said Alatau’s special legal regime creates favorable conditions for international investors.

“The Constitutional Law on the Special Legal Regime of Alatau City provides legal certainty, stable tax conditions and a one-stop-shop mechanism for investors. Alatau can become a pilot platform for localizing technologies and your development expertise,” he said.

Lee described the initiative as the beginning of a long-term partnership focused on sustainable urban development.

“We hope to introduce innovative technologies that will help Alatau and Kazakhstan more broadly establish a new international benchmark for sustainable urban development,” he said.

Why sustainable aviation fuel matters

The project reflects a broader global shift as aviation seeks to reduce carbon emissions. Unlike electric aircraft, which remain impractical for most commercial flights, sustainable aviation fuel is widely viewed as one of the few near-term solutions capable of significantly lowering emissions from existing aircraft without requiring major changes to airport infrastructure or airline fleets.

International airlines are also facing growing regulatory pressure to increase SAF use, particularly in Europe, where blending mandates are gradually taking effect. Those requirements are expected to drive long-term demand for new fuel suppliers outside traditional markets.

For Kazakhstan, which possesses extensive agricultural resources and is seeking to diversify its economy beyond conventional energy exports, SAF represents an opportunity to move further up the value chain by producing higher-value, low-carbon fuels rather than exporting raw materials alone.

Alatau as a testbed for green technologies

The project also reinforces Alatau’s role as Kazakhstan’s flagship innovation city. Established under a special legal framework offering tax incentives and simplified administrative procedures, Alatau has been positioned as a testing ground for advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and clean energy solutions.

Rather than focusing solely on fuel production, the memorandum envisions a broader ecosystem combining renewable energy, energy storage and industrial processing, suggesting Kazakhstan aims to integrate green manufacturing with wider urban development.

The memorandum does not commit the parties to immediate construction, but it signals Kazakhstan’s intention to explore participation in a sector expected to expand rapidly over the coming decades. It also reflects a broader shift in the country’s investment strategy from attracting capital for traditional energy projects toward developing industries linked to the global energy transition.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Launches New World Tour
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen has announced a new world tour titled DiMENSIONS, presenting the project as his most personal stage production to date and the latest step in an international career that has steadily expanded beyond music.

According to the artist’s official website, the new program is designed not as a journey through time and space, but as an exploration of the person behind the performer, revealing the different dimensions of Qudaibergen as a singer, composer, producer and individual.

“The world has long known him for his unique voice. This concert is intended to reveal the person behind that voice, presenting a deeper and more complete portrait of the artist,” reads the statement.

Organizers describe the production as a narrative built around emotions, memories and defining moments in Qudaibergen’s life. Rather than presenting isolated episodes, the performance seeks to unite them into a single story shaped by his connection to Kazakhstan, personal values, artistic ambitions and ongoing search for self-understanding.

The announcement comes as Qudaibergen continues to expand his international presence through performances and cultural initiatives. Last October, he performed to a sold-out audience of 15,000 at Mexico City’s Palacio de los Deportes following his first solo concert at the Auditorio Nacional, further strengthening his popularity across Latin America.

His international recognition has also extended beyond the stage. In December, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) appointed Qudaibergen as a Global Goodwill Ambassador in recognition of his humanitarian engagement. Earlier this year, he received the Ambassador of Turkic World Culture order, TURKSOY’s highest distinction, honoring his contribution to promoting Turkic cultural heritage. He was also named Cultural Figure of the Year at Kazakhstan’s People’s Favorite awards.

The announcement also reflects Qudaibergen’s evolving position in Kazakhstan’s cultural diplomacy. While his vocal performances first brought him international recognition, recent years have seen his role expand through humanitarian initiatives, international cultural awards and appearances across new markets. As his audience continues to grow across Asia, Europe and Latin America, Qudaibergen has become one of Kazakhstan’s most visible cultural representatives abroad.
