World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Men to be offered prostate screening from age 45 under new guidelines
World.content:
New guidelines for prostate cancer detection mean men under 50 and over 70 will be offered testing by their GP in an effort to improve early diagnosis.

Prostate cancer is estimated to be the most diagnosed cancer in Australia and last year there were an estimated 4,000 deaths, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

The new guidelines, developed by the Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia, replace those from 2016 and aim to open testing eligibility while also preventing over-diagnosis.

The guidelines put the onus on GPs to offer prostate specific antigen (PSA) blood testing from age 45 instead of the previous recommendation of age 50.

This applies to men who are at high risk due to factors such as a family history, but also men not at high risk but simply interested in their prostate health.

MRIs are recommended in the first instance if a doctor suspects prostate cancer. (Supplied: QIMR Berghofer)

The guidelines stress that doctors must discuss the possible benefits and harms of PSA testing and patient choice is key.

"Previously it was recommended that you talk to your doctor but now we're recommending that GPs initiate that discussion — that's an enormous change," said Peter Heathcote, chair of the guideline expert advisory panel.

Lowering the starting age for testing to 45 was important, he said, as new research had shown those at high risk were more likely to have an aggressive form of the cancer at a younger age.

Further to that, PSA testing is more accurate in younger men because the prostate naturally grows larger with age and pushes up a man's PSA levels.

The guidelines still recommend routine testing every two years for those 50 to 69 but the new guidelines remove the cut-off that previously excluded those over 70.

Now men over 70 could be tested every two years if they have a life expectancy over seven years.

"We did this because the average survival rate for prostate cancer for a 70-year-old is about 14 to 15 years, so they're going to benefit [from continued screening]," Professor Heathcote said.

Prostate cancer support groups Michael Platts panicked when he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. Now he wants to help others break through the stigma around the condition.

The new guidelines also establish that those with Black sub-Saharan ancestry and the BRCA2 gene mutation are considered high-risk, so should be tested every two years from age 45 to over 70.

If someone has elevated PSA levels, the guidelines stress the importance of using a special kind of MRI to see the prostate gland before considering the need for a more invasive biopsy of the gland.

"By doing the next test as an MRI rather than biopsy, we're eliminating 50 per cent of cases who don't need biopsy … the MRI can show it's just a non-cancerous enlargement," Professor Heathcote said.

The guidelines have also moved away from the digital rectal examination, advising it did not need to be offered by GPs as a routine addition to a PSA test.

Recent evidence has shown the rectal test can be inaccurate and fear of a rectal exam is the biggest barrier for men talking to their GP about prostate health.

Aims to reduce over-diagnosis

Screening for prostate cancer has been contentious in recent years because of the risk of over-diagnosis and unnecessary treatments.

"It would be fair to say that in the past, prostate cancer was over-treated when it was found at low-grade, low-volume, non-aggressive cancer level," president of the Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand, Professor Damien Bolton, said.

It meant some men had surgical intervention, which could lead to erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence, when they did not need to.

PSA testing is recommended every two years for those deemed high-risk. (Flickr: Phillip Jeffrey)

But Professor Bolton, who was not involved in writing the new guidelines, said they went a long way to winding that back.

"In many ways now, the guidelines lean towards more individualised therapy and significantly reduce the risk of over-treatment," he said.

"They prioritise active surveillance instead of interventional treatment. The MRI triage [recommendation] will avoid unnecessary biopsies and be an excellent way to reduce over-diagnosis."

The guidelines have been approved by the National Health and Medical Research Council.

The federal government is providing $320,000 to the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners to roll out an awareness program for doctors about the new changes.

In coming months, the Prostate Cancer Foundation will apply for Medicare subsidisation of the expanded PSA testing and MRIs.

World.title: Devastated family of young Cairns crash victim thank community for support
World.content:
The family of Savannah Spence Paige, who was killed in a car crash in Far North Queensland on Wednesday, say they are "beyond devastated by her passing".

The 25-year-old Kewarra Beach resident died at the scene of the crash on the Smithfield Bypass in northern Cairns.

On Friday afternoon, Ms Spence Paige's family issued a statement thanking the community for supporting them "during the horrific loss of our beautiful Savannah".

"We are beyond devastated by her passing," the statement said.

"Savannah was beautiful inside and out, with a smile that lit up every room.

"She had an incredible sense of humour, a kind and caring heart, and was loved by everyone who had the privilege of knowing her.

" She has left a hole in our hearts that can never be filled. "

Loved ones 'struggle to comprehend'

Ms Spence Paige and her husband, Lachie Paige, relocated to Cairns in 2024.

The family said the couple, who previously lived on the Gold Coast, was "only just beginning the next chapter of their lives together".

"They had built a new home and community in Cairns and were excited about the future they were creating," the family's statement said.

"To have that future taken away so suddenly is something our family is struggling to comprehend.

Savannah Spence Paige's family remember her for her smile and infectious humour. (Supplied: Facebook)

"During this unimaginable time, we have been surrounded by extraordinary kindness, compassion and support.

"We would like to express our heartfelt gratitude to the detectives from Queensland Police Service and the many emergency and support services who have treated our family with such professionalism, care and respect throughout the investigation.

"Their compassion has meant more to us than words can express."

An online fundraiser has been organised to support Mr Paige, a self-employed carpenter.

He and Ms Spence Paige had been together since 2017 and were approaching their second wedding anniversary.

Family 'not facing heartbreak alone'

The family also thanked the communities of Cairns and the Gold Coast for "the overwhelming outpouring of love, kindness and support".

"Every message, phone call, gesture of compassion has reminded us that we are not facing this heartbreak alone," the family said.

A candlelight vigil has been organised to honour Ms Spence Paige's life in Cairns on Sunday evening.

A floral tribute at the scene of the crash. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

"We are deeply touched by this beautiful tribute and the love that has been shown to our family," the statement said.

"As we try to come to terms with the loss of our precious Savannah, we ask for privacy as we grieve and support one another through the days and weeks ahead.

"Thank you for keeping Savannah, Lachie and our entire family in your thoughts.

"Your kindness has given us strength when we have needed it most, and we will be forever grateful.

"Savannah will be loved always, remembered forever, and never forgotten."

It is alleged that Jake Edward Warn, 36, was under the influence of an intoxicating substance when he crashed a stolen ute into two cars, including Ms Spence Paige's SUV.

He has been charged with several offences, including manslaughter.

Mr Warn has been remanded in custody and his case is next due to be heard at the Cairns Magistrates Court on October 27.

World.title: Live: Coaching great Bellamy says he will coach Storm in 2027
World.content:
— reporting by AAP

Craig Bellamy has confirmed he will coach on at the Melbourne Storm in 2027 in what is set to be his final hurrah to a glittering career at the NRL club.

(Getty)

And the legendary coach says while he would love Cameron Munster to see out his NRL career at the Storm, he gives the superstar five-eighth his blessing to finish elsewhere.

Bellamy's future has been up in the air since he revealed in April he had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder.

Although contracted until the end of 2028, there were fears Bellamy might step aside at the end of this season so he could focus on family and his health.

But the 66-year-old, who led the Storm to five premierships, of which two were later stripped due to salary cap breaches, confirmed in Perth on Thursday that he was keen to coach on for a 25th season

"I'll be coaching next year, but I think that might be the end," Bellamy said ahead of Saturday's clash with Manly in Perth.

"But anyway, we'll see what happens."

Melbourne (8-12) sit in 12th spot and, barring a mathematical miracle, will miss the finals for the first time since 2010.

They received a huge boost this week when Munster was given the green light to face Manly after recovering from knee surgery.

Loading Instagram content

The Queensland captain is contracted to the Storm until the end of 2027, but his future beyond that remains up in the air.

The 31-year-old says he will stay in Melbourne if Bellamy stays.

But with his mentor set to depart at the end of next year, it opens the door for Munster to explore his options elsewhere, with expansion club PNG one of the most enticing prospects given the tax-free salary on offer.

Bellamy would "love" Munster to stay at the Storm, but would also support his star player if he chose to leave.

"If he thought there was another club or another way that he'd like to finish his career, I'd back him up all the way," Bellamy said.

"He's been super invested in our club the whole time he's been here, and whatever he wants to do in the last couple of years of his career, I'll back it up."

Munster wasn't set to return until next week at the earliest, but he made a special effort to get back sooner to bolster the under-manned outfit.

Last week, Bellamy declared he was feeling "pissed off" after his team's finals hopes all but evaporated in a 36-22 loss to the Bulldogs.

The frustration was still bubbling for Bellamy on Friday when he spoke about his team no longer being in the finals mix.

"It's been tough, I won't bullshit there," Bellamy said before catching up with Perth Bears coach Mal Meninga during the Storm's light training run.

"We've had a few injuries, but there's a lot of other clubs that had that as well.

"At the end of the day, we're just not where we would have liked to have been."

Manly (9-10) are still in the finals hunt, but they need a strong showing in their last five games to secure a top-eight berth, and they will be without Kobe Hetherington (pectoral tear) for the rest of the season.

World.title: Visa overstayers to have work rights revoked if asylum claim rejected
World.content:
Temporary migrants applying for protection would have their work rights revoked once their claim has been rejected, as part of a planned overhaul of Australia's immigration system being considered by cabinet.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is finalising a suite of measures to clamp down on temporary visas and reduce the number of overseas arrivals, with the government under attack from One Nation and the Coalition for consistently overshooting its own migration forecasts.

Mr Burke was due to unveil the plan at the National Press Club this week but cancelled his appearance on Tuesday, a day after it was considered by both the Expenditure Review Committee and cabinet, which identified questions in need of resolution.

There were also concerns the measures were not tough enough to actually reduce migrant numbers.

The discussion in cabinet, according to sources, was heavily focused on the dealing with so-called "visa over-stayers", people who come to Australia on a temporary visa and stay for years longer than expected, often on a bridging visa.

Burke delays speech The ABC understands the cuts to migration numbers are contentious within Labor, but no reason for the delay is given.

The ABC has been told the migration package had already been taken to cabinet "several times", pointing to internal disagreement over proposals including a crackdown on backpacker visas, tightening the rules for family reunion visas and restricting the work and appeal rights for asylum seekers whose initial claims had been rejected.

The measures, first reported by the ABC, have prompted pushback from the business and mining sectors, which rely on skilled migrants, and caused some angst within Labor ranks about the prospect of changes to the family reunion or humanitarian program.

While the prime minister has been on leave for most of the week, ministers have been publicly defending Mr Burke after what has been an unusually public airing of cabinet grievances.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said today Mr Burke would be speaking at the Press Club "shortly" and that it was "not unusual for dates to be moved around in people's diaries".

"I don't think anyone's unhappy. Where we're working through what is a complex policy, but a policy where we're making significant progress," Mr Marles told News24 (formerly Sky News).

Richard Marles repeatedly rejected suggestions Mr Burke had to cancel his address to the press club. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

There is no suggestion Labor is pursuing deep cuts to migration levels. Rather, the party is seeking to meet its own forecast, or what Mr Marles described as a "guiding star", of reducing net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.

The figure, which represents the number of people coming to live in Australia minus those departing to live overseas, reached a peak of 558,000 after COVID.

According to multiple sources, the biggest challenge confronting the government is the number of temporary visa-holders who make claims for protection to remain in Australia for as long as possible.

Assistant Immigration Minister Julian Hill recently highlighted the issue, telling a Law Council conference the "policy settings that drive long-term temporary stays must continue to be reviewed".

"The core proposition is that when people come to Australia for a temporary purpose and they complete that purpose, then the default expectation must be that if there is no pathway to permanency, then they leave promptly."

Visa-holders 'gaming the system'

Figures from the Home Affairs department reveal an average of 1,580 claims for protection are being lodged onshore every month (a figure that has fallen in recent years), mostly by people from China, India and Malaysia who have come to Australia on a student or visitor visa.

About 90 per cent of those claims for asylum are rejected, according to department figures, but applicants have the right to appeal the rulings through the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) and the Federal Court, a process that regularly takes up to eight years.

During that time, a person is placed on a bridging visa allowing them to stay in the community and work, prompting government concerns some are simply "gaming the system".

As at June, the ART was reviewing nearly 37,000 claims for protection which had been rejected, with most claims taking up to three years to resolve.

Sources have told the ABC that as well as speeding up the ART reviews, cabinet was considering revoking the work rights of visa-holders once their claims for protection had been rejected, to encourage them to leave the country.

Between 2017 and 2026, the number of people in Australia on a bridging visa more than tripled from 130,450 to 413,000, while the number of backpacker visas had doubled in the same period from 146,340 to 225,650.

Student visas too have nearly doubled from 383,910 in 2017 to 528,000 in 2026. The three temporary visa categories, along with skilled migrants and New Zealanders, account for the majority of Australia's net overseas migration figure, which Labor is determined to lower.

Any tweaks to the notoriously complex system are contentious, and carry legal and economic risks, as demonstrated by the public statements made by business and mining groups this week.

In a veiled reference to One Nation, Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar warned the government not to "shoot ourselves in the foot" by "rushing changes" in response to "shallow political imperatives".

The Minerals Council similarly cautioned Labor against restrictions on skilled migrants, who made up a small but "critical" portion of the sector's workforce. The lobby group took issue this week with a directive issued by Mr Burke to prioritise skilled workers, already in Australia, for permanent visas.

"Without faster access to skilled migrants, labour shortages especially in critical and hard to fill specialised roles would put project timelines, export earnings, and the broader national economy at risk," chief executive Tania Constable said in a statement.

World.title: Woman who torched funeral chapel to impress friends jailed
World.content:
A woman who set fire to a chapel in Perth's main cemetery, causing more than $3 million damage and widespread disruption to mourning families, has been sentenced to five years in prison.

Tianna Addison Diodato-Day, 30, set the Norfolk Chapel at Karrakatta Cemetery alight in October 2024.

Diodato-Day concealed her face and smashed her way through the glass door before pouring fuel from a jerry can onto the floor and furniture.

The arson attack caused extensive damage to the chapel and led to hundreds of funerals being disrupted. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

After she set the fuel alight, she sent a video to someone named 'Bunter' — though it was not explained who that was.

"I hope I did you proud," she messaged.

"I want to be part of this friend group still."

The District Court heard the chapel was closed for 12 months and the cost of repairs exceeded $3.4 million.

Parts of the Norfolk Chapel at Karrakatta Cemetery was destroyed by fire in October 2024. (Supplied: Metropolitan Cemeteries Board)

Judge Carmel Barbagallo said families were unable to farewell loved ones in a place they had chosen, and there was pressure on facilities and staff.

She said the cemetery was where 40 per cent of all funerals in WA took place, describing it as a place of "mourning, remembrance and cultural significance".

Trail of destruction

The Karrakatta blaze was the most destructive in a series of fires Diodato-Day was involved in over the course of several days.

She also accompanied a man named Dennis Dear as he lit fires at Mandurah's Lakes Lawn Cemetery causing $412,000 damage.

Diodato-Day also used accelerant to set fire to a grave at another cemetery in Mandurah.

She then sent a video via Snapchat to 'Bunter'.

"She's burning this one," she messaged.

There was no attempt by Diodato-Day or Dear to extinguish any of the fires and they did not alert authorities.

Judge Barbagallo said Diodato-Day wanted to prove her worth to a friend group by lighting the fires.

The chapel is one of Perth's major venues for funerals, with hundreds of services held there every year. (Supplied: Metropolitan Cemeteries Board)

Dear, 28, was sentenced to three years and four months in prison after pleading guilty to two Lakes Lawn arsons and breaching a conditional imprisonment order. He will be eligible for parole in February.

Judge Barbagallo refused the City of Mandurah's application for $133,000 in compensation from Dear after his lawyer told the court he had no capacity to pay.

The judge said that while the $3.4 million cost of the Norfolk Chapel fire was covered by an insurance policy, the community would ultimately pay through higher insurance premiums.

The Norfolk Chapel has since been renovated. (Supplied: Metropolitan Cemeteries Board)

The CEO of the Metropolitan Cemeteries Board Kathlene Oliver, said on Friday said the crime had caused significant distress to many families.

"The arson attack on Norfolk Chapel was not just an attack on a cemetery building, it was an attack on the community," she said.

"The Norfolk Chapel holds deep significance for generations of Western Australian families who have come together there to honour and remember loved ones."

World.title: Man killed in suspected dog attack may have been an intruder, police say
World.content:
Police are investigating whether a man suspected of being mauled to death by dogs at a property in Sydney's south-west was an intruder.

The body of a 23-year-old man was found at a rural property on Badgally Road at Eschol Park near Campbelltown, about 12am on Wednesday.

He was found with significant injuries which appeared to be the result of a dog attack.

"Initial inquiries indicate the man may have been attacked by animals prior to his death," police said earlier on Friday.

The incident occurred at a rural property on Badgally Road at Eschol Park. (ABC News)

The circumstances behind why the male was at the property remained unclear to detectives and was under investigation, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said.

"It's a terrible set of circumstances," Commissioner Lanyon said.

" He certainly doesn't appear to be a resident of that location. "

Commissioner Lanyon said a "very key line of inquiry" would be whether the dead man was an intruder.

"We need to understand why that male was at the location," he said.

Dogs seized from property

Police and Campbelltown City Council officers attended the scene on Friday.

Vision showed a number of dogs being removed from the property in a series of vans and being taken to a council animal care facility.

A spokesperson for Campbelltown City Council said it was assisting police with its investigation.

"Council is supporting police inquiries and will continue to assist as required, in accordance with its legislative responsibilities, including determining the registration and ownership status of the dogs," the spokesperson said.

The ABC understands that if an investigation finds the animals caused the man's fatal injuries, they would be euthanased.

The property is known as Saturn's Rings. (ABC News)

The suspected attack happened at Saturn's Rings property, which features conjoined circular buildings based on the rings of the planet and comprised three concentric units.

According to a Campbelltown City Library blog, it was built by late Polish immigrant Stefan Dzwonnik in the late 1970s and into the 80s and features "one of the most spectacular in New South Wales with a limitless, panoramic view of the surrounding countryside" but was never completed.

It was designed to be the centre point of a worldwide movement directed toward a better life on Earth, the blog said, with the largest top level being the family living quarters and the two lower levels "for the society".

It is unclear if anyone was living at the property at the time of the incident.

A crime scene has since been established, and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Drug trafficker takes fight to freeze eggs while in prison to High Court
World.content:
The country's highest court will decide whether a Queensland prisoner can freeze her eggs while serving time for drug trafficking.

Rachel Smith is currently completing a 10-year jail sentence after pleading guilty to the single charge in 2021.

Partway through her term, when she was 33 years old, Smith applied to the Queensland Corrective Services (QCS) for approval to undergo a privately funded Oocyte cryopreservation procedure.

The application was automatically refused based on QCS legislation which states that prisoners are prohibited from accessing the medical treatment, as it is considered "assisted reproductive technology".

In 2024, Smith sought a judicial review in the Supreme Court, with her lawyers submitting at that time that egg freezing was a "preparatory" step.

Smith's original application was dismissed automatically based on a legislative ban on "assisted reproductive technology" while incarcerated. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

It was argued because there was only a possibility it could lead to other future processes which could involve conception, it did not amount to "assisted reproductive technology'."

This challenge was dismissed, and last year Smith launched an appeal against that decision.

During a hearing in Brisbane, her lawyers again submitted the procedure did not fall under the "ordinary meaning" of the phrase "assisted reproductive technology" because it alone cannot cause reproduction.

The appeal also heard evidence about age-related infertility, as well as associated medical risks to pregnant women and babies, and how egg freezing at a younger age could reduce this.

Smith, who will be eligible for parole in 2029 when she will be age 39, wanted to try and fall pregnant after being released from prison, the appeal heard.

Smith has been given leave to appeal the decision in the High Court of Australia. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Earlier this year the Court of Appeal also ruled against her, finding the meaning of the phrase within the Act was "broad" and was "not confined to excluding a prisoner from steps which pertain to fertilisation itself".

"It is not limited to the act which begins reproduction, but any step which would be participating in assisted reproductive technology by engaging in the preparatory steps to enable assisted reproduction to occur," the COA said in its judgment.

Smith subsequently applied for special leave to the High Court of Australia, which was granted this week.

The High Court hearing to appeal the COA decision will be heard at a later date.

World.title: Federal inquiry hears of entrenched racism towards First Nations people
World.content:
The federal racism inquiry has heard evidence of First Nations children being bullied for their culture, community events for Stolen Generations survivors coming under attack and the needs of domestic violence survivors being ignored by police.

The final day of hearings in Naarm/Melbourne heard the current climate of racism had left children fearful of publicly identifying as Aboriginal.

"We are seeing rising racism in sport and at the grassroots level," Aunty Muriel Bamblett from the Victorian Aboriginal Child and Community Agency told the Senate inquiry.

"Racism and stereotyping permeates social media and television. It turns children and young people away from our culture.

"They don't want to identify. They don't want to acknowledge that they're Aboriginal because of the racism that's out there as society."

Aunty Muriel Bamblett says the Voice referendum caused "untold harm" to First Nations communities. (Supplied: naidoc.org.au)

Amid a rising tide of social media abuse, Ms Bamblett said her organisation had been reluctant to publicly identify a victim of family violence as Aboriginal because of the response it would receive from "haters online".

"We were concerned that people would move away from sympathising with her and start to vilify her as an Aboriginal woman," she said.

"Now isn't that sad? We can't celebrate the fact that she had children, she had a life, she contributed so much."

Aunty Muriel said the 2023 Voice referendum had caused "untold harm" to First Nations people.

She said public attacks such as the booing of Welcomes to Country on Anzac Day had been widely publicised, but the attacks at local community events went unseen.

The inquiry has heard about the traumatic experiences of Indigenous children in the child protection system. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We had a Stolen Generations Return to Country where we saw our mob being attacked on these visits and it was really shameful," she said.

"Our children are being bullied because of their culture … They get it in the school grounds, our workplaces …

"Aboriginal people can't run businesses and be public without attracting suspicion, disdain, discrimination, hate and violence."

The inquiry has received nearly 1,000 submissions, with many detailing "very personal and traumatic experiences of racism", committee member Senator Kerrynne Liddle said.

Catherine Liddle says media and political narratives are stoking racism. (ABC News)

That racism was being "reinforced" by the messages people heard in public life, Catherine Liddle from the national peak body for Indigenous children SNAICC told the hearing.

"It is … stoked by narratives of politicians and the media, which continuously misrepresent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, narratives that say we are problems to be solved or negated, or culprits to be blamed."

Child protection, policing impacted by racism

Nerita Waight from the peak body for Aboriginal legal services NATSILS said she has seen first-hand the impact of racism in the child protection system.

Narita Waight says child protection decisions are undermined by racial bias. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

"You would have many instances where notifications were made … referring to family violence that occurred some 10 years ago and at times not even with the current partner, and that was enough for them to decide to remove an Aboriginal child from their family," she said.

"We often have Aboriginal mums who are having babies ripped away at the moment of birth …

"Stories that we hear each and every day about children whose only home is a garbage bag because there is no stability, there is no family, there is no community.

"That is being taken from them because of the racial bias that exists in the system."

Aunty Muriel Bamblett said schools needs to play a greater role in stamping out racism. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

She called on the Commonwealth to nationally enshrine the Aboriginal child placement principle, which aims to keep children in care with Aboriginal communities and maintain their cultural identity and connection to family.

" You have a thing called the constitution. It gives you power. It is time to use it. "

Recent child protection changes by the Northern Territory government have been widely criticised by Aboriginal groups as weakening the principle.

Ms Liddle said taking First Nations children away from their community and culture had devastating impacts.

"A little one was removed and taken up to Darwin … the little one could not speak English and there was no-one … in the foster care environment that could speak the language," she told the hearing.

"The baby cried consistently for two months and would not let anyone cuddle them and got sicker and sicker.

"This is the impact of not being able to respond to systemic racism."

She said poverty, overcrowded homes and limited access to healthcare in remote areas were often perceived as neglect, and these were areas in which governments could step in and do more to keep families together.

"The department will make an assessment that says, 'You're not able to access a healthcare provider or a specialist, therefore your child will be removed,'" she said.

The inquiry heard about the challenges First Nations women have dealing with police. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The inquiry heard racism also impacted Aboriginal women's treatment by police.

Darlene Thomas from Aboriginal family violence service Djirra said many acts of violence against First Nations women were "ignored" by law enforcement.

"Our women tell you that police often refuse to take their statements or properly investigate family violence or breaches of intervention orders," she said.

"Aboriginal women are often not believed because they don't present as the perfect victim, and police regularly believe male perpetrators over Aboriginal women.

"These men are most often non-Aboriginal. We don't call this misidentification. We call this racial targeting."

Closing the Gap a framework to 'eliminate' racism

Coalition of Peaks lead convenor Donnella Mills said there was no "silver bullet" to combat racism but there was a framework in the National Closing the Gap Agreement.

Donnella Mills says community-controlled organisations need long-term funding. (Supplied)

"[The agreement] provides the architecture needed to address racism by strengthening self-determination through shared decision-making, building the community-controlled sector, transforming government organisations and improving data and accountability," she said.

Coalition of Peaks represents more than 80 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community-controlled peak organisations and is a partner to the agreement.

With four out of 19 targets worsening nationally, and only three on track and one met, committee member Senator Lidia Thorpe described the targets as "an absolute joke" which people at the grassroots had "no faith in".

"I predominantly only work with people that are experiencing deaths in custody, child removals, suicides, homelessness, you know, the hard end of the stick," she said.

"Why are [the targets] failing? And what's the point of pointing out Closing the Gap targets when they mean absolutely nothing to those families?"

Ms Mills said Closing the Gap would only work if First Nations people shared in decision-making and community-controlled services received long-term funding.

She also said the agreement also required governments to tackle systemic racism within public sector agencies, including hospitals and police.

"Addressing racism requires more than responding to individual incidents. It requires structural reform, genuine partnership and accountability," she said.

Witnesses expressed disappointment many state and territory agencies did not front the inquiry. (ABC News: Michael Black)

"The public service itself needs reform to be both … safe for our people but also to ensure that institutions that are developing policies involving government are not reinforcing structural racism."

Ms Mills said she felt 'deep disappointment' that state and territory government representatives, except Tasmania, had declined to participate in the public hearings.

Aunty Muriel Bamblett reminded the inquiry that fighting racism should not be the "burden" of First Nations people.

"Government did a lot to turn white Australia against us. It's now time to turn the tide back and to take responsibility and accountability to address the racism that's in our country,' she said.

"What assurance can you give us as Aboriginal people that this inquiry will deliver meaningful change?

"How does the Commonwealth intend to turn the harmful community impacts of the No vote around?"

The final report to parliament is due by the end of the year.

World.title: AFL demands Geelong ‘please explain’ secret concussion agreement
World.content:
SportAFLConcussion crisis AFL demands Geelong ‘please explain’ secret concussion agreement Bridget McArthur August 7, 2026 — 5:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL has written to Geelong demanding a “please explain” as to why it did not seek the league’s approval before allowing a player to sign a waiver that saw him assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries. It comes less than 24 hours after the league issued a statement saying it was “satisfied” the Cats had not used the letter to allow a medically unfit player to return to the field, and that the club had advised it would remove the waiver in question. Steve Hocking held a short media conference on Friday afternoon. Eddie Jim The response included no mention of a sanction, sparking widespread condemnation, and calls of double standards in light of recent penalties imposed on Carlton for its mishandling of Elijah Hollands’ on-field mental health episode. Speaking to media on Friday, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had only just learned of the “please explain” prior to the press conference. He described the secret player agreement as a “process misstep” that the club was now looking at.



As for Chris Scott, he said the senior coach was always kept “at arm’s length” from discussions on player health and had no knowledge of the contract in question. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age “I’m CEO of the Geelong Football Club. We’ll work through it over the coming week as we have been over the last couple of days,” he said, adding he had not put any thought to his future at the club as he had been “busy working through this”. Hocking evaded a question around whether there had been any fallout within the club, and defended the “extensive process” the club and player went through two years ago, emphasising the legal and family representation he had before signing the deal, and reiterating that he was not coerced into doing so. “I’ve spoken to that player today and he still feels that care from the club is as strong as ever,” he said.



Hocking avoided giving straight answers to questions about what penalty the Cats expect to cop, how this issue might be perceived by others, including rival clubs, or the involvement of AFL chairman Craig Drummond, who was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision. Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player “Whatever the AFL decides to do from here is up to them … what I can reinforce is what an excellent chairman Craig’s been down here,” he said. Drummond was also a director of the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health – a brain research centre – from 2009 to 2017. The institute led a much-criticised past-player project from 2014 to 2019 investigating the brain health of former footballers.



More to come Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Ambitious Scottish expat taking Missile shot for growing new stable
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Ambitious Scottish expat taking Missile shot for growing new stable Craig Kerry August 7, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rookie Scone trainer Liam Ruddy has already shown he’s not afraid to have a crack, whatever the odds, on or off the track, as he tries to build his stable. And while Ruddy did not expect Saturday’s group 2 Missile Stakes at Randwick to come up as strong as it has, the 26-year-old is not shying away from the challenge with $151 shot Aviatress. Aviatress, centre, winning the Doveton Stakes at Caulfield on November 29 last year. Racing Photos via Getty Images “She’s found probably the deepest Missile in probably the last 10 years,” Ruddy said. “I think off the last few years, a 102-rater like her would be about the top rater, and she’s found one that isn’t the case.



“She will run because the next week you’ve got a benchmark 94 and she’s a group 3 winner, so there’s no point going back to benchmarks. The week after there’s the Show County over 1200m, but she’s going to get some weight. There’s a 1100 mares race as well, but I don’t want to go back to 1100. “Three weeks between runs is the Mona Lisa Stakes at Wyong, which is probably the perfect race for her, over 1350m. The week after there’s the group 2 Sheraco over 1200. Liam Ruddy. Ruddy Racing “I think she’s got to run and if she gets beat four or five lengths by this lot, she’s probably the right horse for one of those mares races. I think she’ll hold her own.” Ruddy paid $360,000 for the mare, now six, at the Magic Millions National Broodmare Sale in May after she won more than $575,000 across 23 starts for Richard and Chantelle Jolly. On debut for Ruddy, she was six and half lengths off the pace in the July Sprint (1100m) three weeks ago on a heavy Rosehill track.



He said Aviatress’s “wheels spun” on the surface after tracking well into the race and he expected a better performance at Randwick, which was a soft 5 on Friday. Aviatress has been among many several horses, tried or yearlings, Ruddy has bought to kick-start his new stable, which had its first runner last December. That became possible when Ruddy, and Cade Hunter from Hunter Lodge, bought subsequent JJ Atkins winner Tron Bolt for $250,000 as a yearling then sold him for $900,000 to Hermitage. It was the major boost the former Ciaron Maher racing manager needed to go out on his own with partner Emily Kelly, an ex-assistant trainer to Annabel Archibald at Scone. But for the ambitious Ruddy, a former jumps jockey who came to Australia from Scotland seven years ago, it is only the beginning. “He was a good result and we had a few other little bits on the way, but when you try to set up training, if you want to get upscale, it takes a shit-ton of money to get on your way, so it’s all back in,” Ruddy said. “We bought some yearlings this year and probably 10 tried horses this last six months, so we’re chips in buying horses. It’s not sat in a bank, I can tell you. Hopefully we can find a good one the next few years and we’ll be away.



“I worked 48 horses this morning. I’ve got a farm and 10 boxes at the track, and I’m about to get another 30 at the track, so I’ll be up to 65 boxes. “It’s going to take a year or two, but hopefully we can be in the position where we’ve got 60-80 horses out there and be a decent force in the country.” Ruddy has had eight wins overall so far but six city runners without a placing, including $350,000 buy Melody Again running 10th in the group 1 Tatt’s Tiara. “It’s chewed me up and spat me out, to be honest, but that’s all right,” he said of metro racing. “We’ve had a group 1 runner and come four lengths off them, and finish fourth in a listed race. For me, seven or eight months into training, it’s good to put saddles on horses at that level.”



Apprentice ready to work after Crown Lodge call-up Apprentice Shannen Llewellyn stumbled into racing just five years ago because she wanted a second job. Now the 25-year-old former Woolworths assistant manager is ready to work even harder to make the most of a golden opportunity to ride for three-time Australian premiership-winning trainer Ciaron Maher. Shannen Llewellyn after winning on Lightning Glory at Scone in May. Getty Images Llewellyn is set to start on August 17 at Maher’s newly acquired NSW headquarters, Crown Lodge in Warwick Farm, after being offered a three-month loan stint.



The Wyong-based rider is set to move from Newcastle trainer Nathan Doyle and hopes to turn the chance into a long-term position with Maher. “I was shocked that there was interest because obviously you don’t expect people like that to be watching you and wanting you to come around,” Llewellyn said. “I’m just grateful that they offered it to me and I’m just taking it with a grain of salt. I don’t want to get too ahead of myself. “Going from 50 to 150 horse, it will definitely be a big change, but I like to work, and that’s what I’ll be doing. “I’ve had a pretty good stint with Nathan, but I think the opportunities are drying up with him, so it’s long overdue for a move.



“Ciaron has more numbers and he’s able to spread them around a bit and utilise me more. It’s a bit tougher when you’re with a smaller stable to get those opportunities.” Llewellyn had her first race ride in February 2024 for initial boss Brett Robb and has since racked up 152 winners, including seven at metropolitan level. One of those, Cherish Me, was for Maher last month at Randwick. She now hopes to maximise her two-kilogram provincial claim with Maher before focusing on the city. On Saturday, Llewellyn has the chance on eight-year-old Eliyass ($41) for Maher in the Premiers’ Cup Prelude (1800m). Third in the 2024 group 1 Turnbull Stakes and a two-time group 3 winner at Randwick, Eliyass is second-up from more than a year out with injury. He finished well back in his return in the Civic Stakes in June. “I trialled him on the Beaumont track as he was resuming after a long time off,” Llewellyn said.



“It’s really good to get on a nice horse like that. He was a good horse in his day, so it will good to take him around.” She also reunites with Paul Perry-trained Cosy Corner ($17) in the Midway Handicap. She was a close fourth on the mare two starts ago in a Rosehill Midway. “She’s a lovely little horse and she was very gallant and unlucky in the Midway at Rosehill to run into a horse of Cold Brew’s calibre,” she said. “She was beaten not even a length to him, so there’s some good form there. She tries her guts out.” Her other ride is Beaumista ($18) for Scone trainer Simon Casey in the Highway Handicap.

World.title: ‘The bill should not pass’: Australians with disability escalate fears over NDIS cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDisability ‘The bill should not pass’: Australians with disability escalate fears over NDIS cuts Natassia Chrysanthos August 7, 2026 — 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s biggest disability networks and the national legal aid service have made a private intervention to the health department, sounding the alarm that thousands of disabled Australians will be harmed under Labor’s push to save billions from the ballooning National Disability Insurance Scheme. In the week since their presentation to department officials, other disability groups, advocates and legal services have escalated their campaign against the government’s overhaul by providing evidence to an eight-week Senate inquiry about their fears for participants. Campaigners came to Parliament to protest NDIS cuts during budget week. Dominic Lorrimer The Australian Human Rights Commission added its weight on Wednesday, urging the Albanese government to pull its NDIS bill until “significant human rights concerns around process, accountability and the impact of the reforms are addressed”. A further 100 academics and community organisations – including former disability royal commissioner Alastair McEwin – also signed an open letter on Thursday to reject, specifically, the new powers that will allow Health Minister Mark Butler to make sweeping cuts to funding for participants’ personal social and community support budgets.





The Senate inquiry has heard that about 241,000 people will be removed from the scheme by mid-2031 under eligibility changes that will come in over the next few years. Of that group, 155,000 would be 18 and under – 60 per cent of whom would be autistic. The five peak disability organisations, National Legal Aid and other legal groups made a presentation to the health, disability and ageing department last Thursday to make their case that the bill will cause “significant and foreseeable harm”. They raised concerns about the bill’s drafting, saying it relied on broad and undefined concepts and future rules that would have uncertain impacts. They suggested legal amendments that would strengthen the bill’s language around access and permanency, bolster people’s right to reviews and embed strong protections for carers. “[We] were united in their position that the bill should not pass in its current form,” their communiqué, published on Friday, said.



Related Article Disability ‘Am I disabled enough?’ The question autistic participants are asking after NDIS overhaul The attendees included Disability Advocacy Network Australia, Children and Young People with Disability Australia, Inclusion Australia, People with Disability Australia and Women With Disabilities Australia. The Human Rights Commission, meanwhile, said it recognised the need for NDIS reforms so the scheme met its intended purpose, was sustainable, and market failures were fixed. But it said all seven commissioners as well as the president were jointly urging the government to slow down the process and “take a more considered approach to modifying the scheme in a way that protects and promotes human rights”.
