World.title: Cap Raise Crucible: Canaccord, Petra shine in busy cap raise fortnight
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Cap Raise Crucible: Canaccord, Petra shine in busy cap raise fortnight Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 7, 2026 — 4:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If the final fortnight of July proved anything, it was that Australia’s capital markets are open for business again. The numbers certainly suggest they are. This edition of Cap Raise Crucible highlights $1 billion raised across 60 companies in the last fortnight More than $1 billion flowed into at least 60ASX capital raisings between July 20 and August 4, producing the busiest reporting period of the year and signalling a marked improvement in investor sentiment after months of subdued activity. However, the billion-dollar headline only tells part of the story. The real contest wasn’t necessarily raising the money, it was competing for the available funds.



With dozens of companies approaching the market at the same time, institutional investors had the luxury of being selective. They backed projects moving towards production, acquisitions capable of creating value and management teams that could clearly explain how every new dollar would be spent. Others still found funding, but generally on much tougher terms. The evidence was written into the pricing. Some companies barely needed to discount their stock before institutions reached for the cheque book. Others were forced to offer big concessions simply to complete their books. A select handful even convinced investors to subscribe at, or above, prevailing market prices, one of the strongest endorsements any company can receive. The next three companies illustrate how judgement was dispensed by the market in the last fortnight under very different scenarios. 2. Visible gold in quartz veining at Saturn Metals Apollo Hill project 60 kilometres south east of Leonora in WA. Saturn Metals (ASX: STN)



Raised: $105 million Price: $0.40 Discount: 11.1 per cent to the pre-raise closing price. Post-raise performance +15% Joint lead manager: Petra Capital/Canaccord Genuity



One of the reporting period’s standout resource transactions belonged to Saturn Metals, which secured firm commitments for a $100 million placement before launching a fully underwritten $5 million share purchase plan to accelerate development of its Apollo Hill gold project in Western Australia. Petraand Canaccord assembled one of the strongest institutional books of the fortnight, reinforcing confidence in what is increasingly viewed as one of Australia’s more significant undeveloped heap leach gold projects. The size and quality of the book suggests the brokers had little difficulty finding institutional support despite the nine-figure raise. An 11.1 per cent discount was sufficient to attract strong demand without signalling distress, an important distinction in today’s market. Since the raise, Saturn’s shares have traded 15 per cent above the issue price, suggesting investors have strongly endorsed the company’s strategy. For Saturn, the raising wasn’t simply about strengthening the balance sheet. It was another step towards becoming a mine developer rather than just another explorer. Lotus Resources’ Kayelekera uranium project in Malawi.



Lotus Resources (ASX: LOT) Raised: $138.1 million Price: $0.22 Discount: 66.7 per cent to the pre-raise closing price. Post-raise performance -Steady



Lead Manager: Canaccord Genuity If Saturn Metals demonstrated where institutions were prepared to back quality, Lotus Resources highlighted the price investors still demand for taking on additional risk. The company assembled one of the reporting period’s largest and most sophisticated funding packages, combining fresh equity, convertible notes and inventory-backed finance to support the restart of its Kayelekera uranium mine in Malawi. Canaccord’s clients were basking in the glow of one of the larger discounts to market in the $60 million equity raise portion which went out at 22c, a whopping 66.7 per cent below the previous closing price. On face value it looked brutal. Context, however, matters. Restarting a uranium mine requires significant capital, carries execution risk and demands patient investors prepared to look well beyond the next quarter. The discount reflected those realities just as much as it reflected market conditions.



Despite the pricing, investors still committed more than $138 million to the Lotus raise, underlining continued confidence in uranium’s longer-term outlook. Lotus shares traded as high as 38 cents post raise, giving Canaccord’s nimble punter’s a quick turn for those who took it before the slide back to 22.5 cents. Vysarn (ASX: VYS) Raised: $65.3 million Price: $1.05 Discount: 0.5 per cent to the pre-raise closing price.



Post-raise performance +11% Lead managers: Unified Capital Partners/Morgans/Canaccord Genuity Canaccord also had its hand in the Vysarn raise recently along with Unified Capital Partners and Morgans. The integrated water services company Vysarn tapped the market for a fully underwritten $65.3 million placement to help fund its acquisition of Welltech, a water and sewage management business. The deal was priced at just0.5 per cent below the previous closing price, one of the tightest discounts of the period. In a market where many companies were still offering double-digit discounts simply to complete a book, Vysarn barely needed to sharpen its pencil.



The transaction, jointly managed by sole underwriter Unified Capital Partners, Morgans and Canaccord Genuity, suggested investors were far more interested in securing stock than negotiating a cheaper entry price. Since the raise, Vysarn’s stock has traded as high as $1.19, a nice little earner against the $1.05 entry price. It is currently holding up at$1.16.5. Taken together, Saturn Metals, Lotus Resources and Vysarn probably tell the story of the fortnight better than any market statistic. One attracted more than $100 million at a moderate discount to advance a flagship gold project. Another secured a transformational uranium funding package, but only after investors demanded a substantial margin of safety. The third barely needed to discount its stock at all. Three very different transactions. Three very different prices for capital. One unmistakable message. Investors are writing sizeable cheques again. They’re simply demanding much better reasons to do it and the price has to be spot on to reflect the risk. At the lower end, Euroz Hartleys and Taylor Collison managed to put away a lazy $13 million for Pacgold at 15 cents a pop to accelerate work at its White Dam North gold project.



Priced at a 12 per cent discount, Pacgold’s stock has held at the issue price and is still going out the door at 15c. Petra Capital has seen a busy year with its clients taking a well-timed punt on Kalamazoo Resources nailing some big numbers during infill drilling at its Mt Olympus gold deposit in WA. Petra led an oversubscribed $8 million placement at 12 cents for Kalamazoo on July 20th and by the 3rd of August Kalamazoo had tabled some stellar numbers like 74m at 4.1g/t gold and 10m going a serious 49g/t gold. In fact, it was hard to see a dud number in the latest drill results and not hard to see why the stock is now trading at 17c a share, a handy 41% hike for the Petra faithful. Casting the broking world aside, Western Mines Group quietly secured a modest $2.74 million at 16.3 cents per share, introducing cornerstone insto Lowell Resources Fund to its register. The arrival of a strategic 10.6 per cent shareholder shouts more about confidence in a project than the amount of money raised. Since the placement, Western Mines has traded as high as 19.5 cents, although the longer-term significance of the cornerstone investment may ultimately prove more important than the market’s initial reaction. If one transaction in the last fortnight illustrated the value investors are still prepared to place on conviction, it belonged to Golden Dragon Mining.



While much of the market continued to rely on discounted placements, Chinese player Chengtun Gold filled its boots with Golden Dragon stock at, wait for it.......a 17.65 per cent premium with a$2.2 million hit out. The outcome will see Chengtun sitting purposefully on Golden Dragon’s register with a 19.9 per cent stake. Premium placements are like hen’s teeth however, they generally occur when investors believe the market has materially undervalued the opportunity. Since completing the transaction, Golden Dragon has traded slightly below its 20-cent placement price at 18.5 cents, most likely just chump change for the Chinese. Golden Dragon wasn’t the only company able to command premium pricing though. Jade Gas ($11 million), Cambium Bio ($1 million) and RooLife Group ($1.06 million) also completed raisings above their prevailing market prices. Not every company had the luxury of getting cap raises away at a premium, however. The clients of West Perth mover and shaker Leeuwin Wealth are in the process of picking up a 2 for 1 entitlement offer in mining services firm Babylon Pump and Power at a 35 per cent discount to the last traded price when Babylon slipped off the ASX boards back in April this year.



Leeuwin is looking to plug about $12.7 million into Babylon at 5 cents a pop and will put its money where its mouth is with a $7.27 million underwriting package. The market has not yet been able to deliver its verdict on the raise with Babylon’s stock remaining suspended pending the outcome of the raise. Meanwhile, biotech firm Radiopharm Theranostics put away $12.5 million through Bell Potter and is currently down 20 per cent, Dalaroo Metals slotted $2.5 million via 62 Capital and is currently up 15 per cent, Greenvale Energy placed $3.25 million via Alpine Capital Partners and is down 24 per cent and finally G50 Corp raised $26.25 million through Bell Potter and Morgans Corporate, with Hancock Prospecting tipping in $7.95 million, which is now worth 16 percent less, not that Hancock would notice. Notably, July was also the busiest month for IPO’s so far in 2026 with nine new companies and one AI trust hitting the boards with retail investors continuing to prove they have an important role to play outside of providing sufficient shareholder spread for a company to be able to list. In the final 2 weeks of July, Lux Copper Corp was up 30 per cent after its IPO, Ceretas Limited hiked128 per cent and Gwardar Resources shot the lights out at 187 per cent. It wasn’t all peaches and cream however with Alurion Resources tracking down by about 27 per cent.



UBS Securities and MA Moelis along with Ord Minnett handled the biggest IPO for July which went to construction and infrastructure player FDC Consolidated with $400 million raised and is currently up 20per cent on its $3.00 subscription price. All things considered, it appears as though the IPO market is back in the black. Different sectors. Different commodities. Different strategies. The common thread was easy to spot. Companies that clearly articulated where the money was going generally found stronger support than those asking investors simply to extend the corporate runway. One other truth quietly emerged as the fortnight unfolded; the market doesn’t waste time delivering its verdict. Some companies have already moved comfortably above their issue prices, suggesting punters believe management will deliver exactly what was promised.......well almost. Brokers largely have an unenviable task - on the one hand they need to extract a decent discount to market for their investing clients and on the other hand, they need to keep the listed companies onside to secure a constant flow of business.



It is essentially a soft shoe shuffle and a high wire act that is not for the faint hearted. Convincing your listed client that the discount was appropriate when the market ran the stock hard post the raise is no mean feat. At the end of the day however, a stock that is heading north tends to be the only tonic that matters. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Second Liberal frontbencher called to ICAC
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Second Liberal frontbencher called to ICAC Michael McGowan Updated August 7, 2026 — 4:53pm ,first published 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A second Liberal frontbencher has received a summons to provide evidence to the anti-corruption watchdog’s bombshell investigation into allegations senior Liberal figures took illegal donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for political favours. Eleni Petinos, the shadow minister for jobs and industry, received a summons to appear at the Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry in the coming weeks. Former NSW fair trading minister Eleni Petinos has received a summons to appear at the ICAC inquiry. Rhett Wyman Petinos, who is on maternity leave, would be the second member of NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane’s frontbench to give evidence to the inquiry after shadow attorney-general Damien Tudehope appeared this week. Petinos was not named as a person of interest by the ICAC. However, her involvement in the resignation of former NSW building commissioner David Chandler is likely to be a key focus of the inquiry. She was not included on the list of witnesses to appear at the inquiry next week.



The ICAC has previously heard that Nassif paid significant funds to a group of Liberal Party apparatchiks, in part to seek Chandler’s removal. Related Article Operation Rosny Secret $2m deals, phone taps and ‘filthy money’: Explosive claims aired at ICAC They include one of the then-premier’s brothers, Charles Perrottet, and two other men: Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood. In phone taps played to the commission, Nassif bragged to a developer associate that he had “hands on the state government” and would “step on [the] neck” of Chandler by having “one of my girls” appointed fair trading minister. Two months after the recorded call, Petinos replaced Kevin Anderson as fair trading minister in a reshuffle.



By July 2022, Chandler had resigned as NSW building commissioner after an investigation into his conduct ordered by Petinos’ office. In her opening address to the commission, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, said: “Over the course of this public inquiry the commission will examine whether Mr Nassif’s predictions to his associate were an incidence of wishful thinking that serendipitously came to pass, or whether Mr Chandler’s resignation was, in fact, the result of work Mr Nassif had paid Charles Perrottet, Mr Greenwood and others to do for him.” Dwyer said she anticipated the inquiry would hear evidence Charles Perrottet sought assistance from both Petinos and Christopher Spence, then the chief of staff to planning minister Anthony Roberts, in seeking Chandler’s removal. Neither Petinos nor Spence have been named as persons of interest in the inquiry.



Petinos did not respond to a request for comment. However, senior party sources familiar with the December 2021 reshuffle told The Sydney Morning Herald that Petinos had not requested the fair trading portfolio. Charles Perrottet was involved in internal factional discussions about the reshuffle at the time, two Liberal Party sources said. Sloane has previously said she would not be commenting on Petinos’ potential involvement in the ICAC inquiry. On Friday she confirmed Petinos would be a witness but said she was “assisting the inquiry”. “She’s not a person of interest. I would encourage any of my team or people within the Liberal Party or outside of the Liberal Party to assist the inquiry to help provide support their evidence,” she said.



Related Article Operation Rosny Intercepted calls, leaked reports and cafe meetings: What we learnt from Rosny week two “That doesn’t mean they’ve done anything wrong. It means that they’re doing a very good job of supporting the inquiry. And you know, if anything comes up that isn’t that, then I’ll consider it at the time. But being a witness is being supportive of the inquiry. Nothing else.” Tudehope stood down from the frontbench ahead of his appearance, citing his “close relationships” with several of the people at the centre of the probe. He is not a focus of the inquiry but this week he conceded that he leaked a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a key witness who deliberately avoided giving evidence to a parliamentary inquiry into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council. The commission has previously heard evidence from Dylan Whitelaw, a NSW Reformers member who worked in Roberts’ office, that Spence had wanted to “get rid” of Chandler. Whitelaw told the commission Spence had wanted Petinos to raise a video of Chandler during a budget estimates hearing, with the goal of damaging his career.



The video, Whitelaw said, allegedly included the imputation Chandler was “racist” and included a reference to a list of building certifiers and developers he had given to banks. “I believe his [Spence’s] words were something to the effect of ‘we’ve just got to get rid of this guy’,” Whitelaw said. He told the commission that Spence and Petinos were “close” but did not know why she would want to have Chandler dismissed. Whitelaw said Spence later complained that Petinos had “f---ed it up” by not raising the video in her budget estimates appearance. Further reading Here are some of the highlights of our coverage.

World.title: AFL demands Geelong ‘please explain’ secret concussion agreement
World.content:
SportAFLConcussion crisis AFL demands Geelong ‘please explain’ secret concussion agreement Bridget McArthur August 7, 2026 — 5:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL has written to Geelong demanding a “please explain” as to why it did not seek the league’s approval before allowing a player to sign a waiver that saw him assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries. It comes less than 24 hours after the league issued a statement saying it was “satisfied” the Cats had not used the letter to allow a medically unfit player to return to the field, and that the club had advised it would remove the waiver in question. Steve Hocking held a short media conference on Friday afternoon. Eddie Jim The response included no mention of a sanction, sparking widespread condemnation, and calls of double standards in light of recent penalties imposed on Carlton for its mishandling of Elijah Hollands’ on-field mental health episode. Speaking to media on Friday, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had only just learned of the “please explain” prior to the press conference. He described the secret player agreement as a “process misstep” that the club was now looking at.



As for Chris Scott, he said the senior coach was always kept “at arm’s length” from discussions on player health and had no knowledge of the contract in question. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age “I’m CEO of the Geelong Football Club. We’ll work through it over the coming week as we have been over the last couple of days,” he said, adding he had not put any thought to his future at the club as he had been “busy working through this”. Hocking evaded a question around whether there had been any fallout within the club, and defended the “extensive process” the club and player went through two years ago, emphasising the legal and family representation he had before signing the deal, and reiterating that he was not coerced into doing so. “I’ve spoken to that player today and he still feels that care from the club is as strong as ever,” he said.



Hocking avoided giving straight answers to questions about what penalty the Cats expect to cop, how this issue might be perceived by others, including rival clubs, or the involvement of AFL chairman Craig Drummond, who was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision. Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player “Whatever the AFL decides to do from here is up to them … what I can reinforce is what an excellent chairman Craig’s been down here,” he said. Drummond was also a director of the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health – a brain research centre – from 2009 to 2017. The institute led a much-criticised past-player project from 2014 to 2019 investigating the brain health of former footballers.

World.title: Ambitious Scottish expat taking Missile shot for growing new stable
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Ambitious Scottish expat taking Missile shot for growing new stable Craig Kerry August 7, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rookie Scone trainer Liam Ruddy has already shown he’s not afraid to have a crack, whatever the odds, on or off the track, as he tries to build his stable. And while Ruddy did not expect Saturday’s group 2 Missile Stakes at Randwick to come up as strong as it has, the 26-year-old is not shying away from the challenge with $151 shot Aviatress. Aviatress, centre, winning the Doveton Stakes at Caulfield on November 29 last year. Racing Photos via Getty Images “She’s found probably the deepest Missile in probably the last 10 years,” Ruddy said. “I think off the last few years, a 102-rater like her would be about the top rater, and she’s found one that isn’t the case.



“She will run because the next week you’ve got a benchmark 94 and she’s a group 3 winner, so there’s no point going back to benchmarks. The week after there’s the Show County over 1200m, but she’s going to get some weight. There’s a 1100 mares race as well, but I don’t want to go back to 1100. “Three weeks between runs is the Mona Lisa Stakes at Wyong, which is probably the perfect race for her, over 1350m. The week after there’s the group 2 Sheraco over 1200. Liam Ruddy. Ruddy Racing “I think she’s got to run and if she gets beat four or five lengths by this lot, she’s probably the right horse for one of those mares races. I think she’ll hold her own.” Ruddy paid $360,000 for the mare, now six, at the Magic Millions National Broodmare Sale in May after she won more than $575,000 across 23 starts for Richard and Chantelle Jolly. On debut for Ruddy, she was six and half lengths off the pace in the July Sprint (1100m) three weeks ago on a heavy Rosehill track.



He said Aviatress’s “wheels spun” on the surface after tracking well into the race and he expected a better performance at Randwick, which was a soft 5 on Friday. Aviatress has been among many several horses, tried or yearlings, Ruddy has bought to kick-start his new stable, which had its first runner last December. That became possible when Ruddy, and Cade Hunter from Hunter Lodge, bought subsequent JJ Atkins winner Tron Bolt for $250,000 as a yearling then sold him for $900,000 to Hermitage. It was the major boost the former Ciaron Maher racing manager needed to go out on his own with partner Emily Kelly, an ex-assistant trainer to Annabel Archibald at Scone. But for the ambitious Ruddy, a former jumps jockey who came to Australia from Scotland seven years ago, it is only the beginning. “He was a good result and we had a few other little bits on the way, but when you try to set up training, if you want to get upscale, it takes a shit-ton of money to get on your way, so it’s all back in,” Ruddy said. “We bought some yearlings this year and probably 10 tried horses this last six months, so we’re chips in buying horses. It’s not sat in a bank, I can tell you. Hopefully we can find a good one the next few years and we’ll be away.



“I worked 48 horses this morning. I’ve got a farm and 10 boxes at the track, and I’m about to get another 30 at the track, so I’ll be up to 65 boxes. “It’s going to take a year or two, but hopefully we can be in the position where we’ve got 60-80 horses out there and be a decent force in the country.” Ruddy has had eight wins overall so far but six city runners without a placing, including $350,000 buy Melody Again running 10th in the group 1 Tatt’s Tiara. “It’s chewed me up and spat me out, to be honest, but that’s all right,” he said of metro racing. “We’ve had a group 1 runner and come four lengths off them, and finish fourth in a listed race. For me, seven or eight months into training, it’s good to put saddles on horses at that level.”



Apprentice ready to work after Crown Lodge call-up Apprentice Shannen Llewellyn stumbled into racing just five years ago because she wanted a second job. Now the 25-year-old former Woolworths assistant manager is ready to work even harder to make the most of a golden opportunity to ride for three-time Australian premiership-winning trainer Ciaron Maher. Shannen Llewellyn after winning on Lightning Glory at Scone in May. Getty Images Llewellyn is set to start on August 17 at Maher’s newly acquired NSW headquarters, Crown Lodge in Warwick Farm, after being offered a three-month loan stint.



The Wyong-based rider is set to move from Newcastle trainer Nathan Doyle and hopes to turn the chance into a long-term position with Maher. “I was shocked that there was interest because obviously you don’t expect people like that to be watching you and wanting you to come around,” Llewellyn said. “I’m just grateful that they offered it to me and I’m just taking it with a grain of salt. I don’t want to get too ahead of myself. “Going from 50 to 150 horse, it will definitely be a big change, but I like to work, and that’s what I’ll be doing. “I’ve had a pretty good stint with Nathan, but I think the opportunities are drying up with him, so it’s long overdue for a move.



“Ciaron has more numbers and he’s able to spread them around a bit and utilise me more. It’s a bit tougher when you’re with a smaller stable to get those opportunities.” Llewellyn had her first race ride in February 2024 for initial boss Brett Robb and has since racked up 152 winners, including seven at metropolitan level. One of those, Cherish Me, was for Maher last month at Randwick. She now hopes to maximise her two-kilogram provincial claim with Maher before focusing on the city. On Saturday, Llewellyn has the chance on eight-year-old Eliyass ($41) for Maher in the Premiers’ Cup Prelude (1800m). Third in the 2024 group 1 Turnbull Stakes and a two-time group 3 winner at Randwick, Eliyass is second-up from more than a year out with injury. He finished well back in his return in the Civic Stakes in June. “I trialled him on the Beaumont track as he was resuming after a long time off,” Llewellyn said.



“It’s really good to get on a nice horse like that. He was a good horse in his day, so it will good to take him around.” She also reunites with Paul Perry-trained Cosy Corner ($17) in the Midway Handicap. She was a close fourth on the mare two starts ago in a Rosehill Midway. “She’s a lovely little horse and she was very gallant and unlucky in the Midway at Rosehill to run into a horse of Cold Brew’s calibre,” she said. “She was beaten not even a length to him, so there’s some good form there. She tries her guts out.” Her other ride is Beaumista ($18) for Scone trainer Simon Casey in the Highway Handicap.

World.title: ‘The bill should not pass’: Australians with disability escalate fears over NDIS cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDisability ‘The bill should not pass’: Australians with disability escalate fears over NDIS cuts Natassia Chrysanthos August 7, 2026 — 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s biggest disability networks and the national legal aid service have made a private intervention to the health department, sounding the alarm that thousands of disabled Australians will be harmed under Labor’s push to save billions from the ballooning National Disability Insurance Scheme. In the week since their presentation to department officials, other disability groups, advocates and legal services have escalated their campaign against the government’s overhaul by providing evidence to an eight-week Senate inquiry about their fears for participants. Campaigners came to Parliament to protest NDIS cuts during budget week. Dominic Lorrimer The Australian Human Rights Commission added its weight on Wednesday, urging the Albanese government to pull its NDIS bill until “significant human rights concerns around process, accountability and the impact of the reforms are addressed”. A further 100 academics and community organisations – including former disability royal commissioner Alastair McEwin – also signed an open letter on Thursday to reject, specifically, the new powers that will allow Health Minister Mark Butler to make sweeping cuts to funding for participants’ personal social and community support budgets.





The Senate inquiry has heard that about 241,000 people will be removed from the scheme by mid-2031 under eligibility changes that will come in over the next few years. Of that group, 155,000 would be 18 and under – 60 per cent of whom would be autistic. The five peak disability organisations, National Legal Aid and other legal groups made a presentation to the health, disability and ageing department last Thursday to make their case that the bill will cause “significant and foreseeable harm”. They raised concerns about the bill’s drafting, saying it relied on broad and undefined concepts and future rules that would have uncertain impacts. They suggested legal amendments that would strengthen the bill’s language around access and permanency, bolster people’s right to reviews and embed strong protections for carers. “[We] were united in their position that the bill should not pass in its current form,” their communiqué, published on Friday, said.



Related Article Disability ‘Am I disabled enough?’ The question autistic participants are asking after NDIS overhaul The attendees included Disability Advocacy Network Australia, Children and Young People with Disability Australia, Inclusion Australia, People with Disability Australia and Women With Disabilities Australia. The Human Rights Commission, meanwhile, said it recognised the need for NDIS reforms so the scheme met its intended purpose, was sustainable, and market failures were fixed. But it said all seven commissioners as well as the president were jointly urging the government to slow down the process and “take a more considered approach to modifying the scheme in a way that protects and promotes human rights”. Visible gold in quartz veining at Saturn Metals Apollo Hill project 60 kilometres south east of Leonora in WA. Saturn Metals (ASX: STN)



Raised: $105 million Price: $0.40 Discount: 11.1 per cent to the pre-raise closing price. Post-raise performance +15% Joint lead manager: Petra Capital/Canaccord Genuity



One of the reporting period’s standout resource transactions belonged to Saturn Metals, which secured firm commitments for a $100 million placement before launching a fully underwritten $5 million share purchase plan to accelerate development of its Apollo Hill gold project in Western Australia. Petraand Canaccord assembled one of the strongest institutional books of the fortnight, reinforcing confidence in what is increasingly viewed as one of Australia’s more significant undeveloped heap leach gold projects. The size and quality of the book suggests the brokers had little difficulty finding institutional support despite the nine-figure raise. An 11.1 per cent discount was sufficient to attract strong demand without signalling distress, an important distinction in today’s market. Since the raise, Saturn’s shares have traded 15 per cent above the issue price, suggesting investors have strongly endorsed the company’s strategy. For Saturn, the raising wasn’t simply about strengthening the balance sheet. It was another step towards becoming a mine developer rather than just another explorer. Lotus Resources’ Kayelekera uranium project in Malawi.



Lotus Resources (ASX: LOT) Raised: $138.1 million Price: $0.22 Discount: 66.7 per cent to the pre-raise closing price. Post-raise performance -Steady



Lead Manager: Canaccord Genuity If Saturn Metals demonstrated where institutions were prepared to back quality, Lotus Resources highlighted the price investors still demand for taking on additional risk. The company assembled one of the reporting period’s largest and most sophisticated funding packages, combining fresh equity, convertible notes and inventory-backed finance to support the restart of its Kayelekera uranium mine in Malawi. Canaccord’s clients were basking in the glow of one of the larger discounts to market in the $60 million equity raise portion which went out at 22c, a whopping 66.7 per cent below the previous closing price. On face value it looked brutal. Context, however, matters. Restarting a uranium mine requires significant capital, carries execution risk and demands patient investors prepared to look well beyond the next quarter. The discount reflected those realities just as much as it reflected market conditions.



Despite the pricing, investors still committed more than $138 million to the Lotus raise, underlining continued confidence in uranium’s longer-term outlook. Lotus shares traded as high as 38 cents post raise, giving Canaccord’s nimble punter’s a quick turn for those who took it before the slide back to 22.5 cents. Vysarn (ASX: VYS) Raised: $65.3 million Price: $1.05 Discount: 0.5 per cent to the pre-raise closing price.



Post-raise performance +11% Lead managers: Unified Capital Partners/Morgans/Canaccord Genuity Canaccord also had its hand in the Vysarn raise recently along with Unified Capital Partners and Morgans. The integrated water services company Vysarn tapped the market for a fully underwritten $65.3 million placement to help fund its acquisition of Welltech, a water and sewage management business. The deal was priced at just0.5 per cent below the previous closing price, one of the tightest discounts of the period. In a market where many companies were still offering double-digit discounts simply to complete a book, Vysarn barely needed to sharpen its pencil.



The transaction, jointly managed by sole underwriter Unified Capital Partners, Morgans and Canaccord Genuity, suggested investors were far more interested in securing stock than negotiating a cheaper entry price. Since the raise, Vysarn’s stock has traded as high as $1.19, a nice little earner against the $1.05 entry price. It is currently holding up at$1.16.5. Taken together, Saturn Metals, Lotus Resources and Vysarn probably tell the story of the fortnight better than any market statistic. One attracted more than $100 million at a moderate discount to advance a flagship gold project. Another secured a transformational uranium funding package, but only after investors demanded a substantial margin of safety. The third barely needed to discount its stock at all. Three very different transactions. Three very different prices for capital. One unmistakable message. Investors are writing sizeable cheques again. They’re simply demanding much better reasons to do it and the price has to be spot on to reflect the risk. At the lower end, Euroz Hartleys and Taylor Collison managed to put away a lazy $13 million for Pacgold at 15 cents a pop to accelerate work at its White Dam North gold project.



Priced at a 12 per cent discount, Pacgold’s stock has held at the issue price and is still going out the door at 15c. Petra Capital has seen a busy year with its clients taking a well-timed punt on Kalamazoo Resources nailing some big numbers during infill drilling at its Mt Olympus gold deposit in WA. Petra led an oversubscribed $8 million placement at 12 cents for Kalamazoo on July 20th and by the 3rd of August Kalamazoo had tabled some stellar numbers like 74m at 4.1g/t gold and 10m going a serious 49g/t gold. In fact, it was hard to see a dud number in the latest drill results and not hard to see why the stock is now trading at 17c a share, a handy 41% hike for the Petra faithful. Casting the broking world aside, Western Mines Group quietly secured a modest $2.74 million at 16.3 cents per share, introducing cornerstone insto Lowell Resources Fund to its register. The arrival of a strategic 10.6 per cent shareholder shouts more about confidence in a project than the amount of money raised. Since the placement, Western Mines has traded as high as 19.5 cents, although the longer-term significance of the cornerstone investment may ultimately prove more important than the market’s initial reaction. If one transaction in the last fortnight illustrated the value investors are still prepared to place on conviction, it belonged to Golden Dragon Mining.



While much of the market continued to rely on discounted placements, Chinese player Chengtun Gold filled its boots with Golden Dragon stock at, wait for it.......a 17.65 per cent premium with a$2.2 million hit out. The outcome will see Chengtun sitting purposefully on Golden Dragon’s register with a 19.9 per cent stake. Premium placements are like hen’s teeth however, they generally occur when investors believe the market has materially undervalued the opportunity. Since completing the transaction, Golden Dragon has traded slightly below its 20-cent placement price at 18.5 cents, most likely just chump change for the Chinese. Golden Dragon wasn’t the only company able to command premium pricing though. Jade Gas ($11 million), Cambium Bio ($1 million) and RooLife Group ($1.06 million) also completed raisings above their prevailing market prices. Not every company had the luxury of getting cap raises away at a premium, however. The clients of West Perth mover and shaker Leeuwin Wealth are in the process of picking up a 2 for 1 entitlement offer in mining services firm Babylon Pump and Power at a 35 per cent discount to the last traded price when Babylon slipped off the ASX boards back in April this year.



Leeuwin is looking to plug about $12.7 million into Babylon at 5 cents a pop and will put its money where its mouth is with a $7.27 million underwriting package. The market has not yet been able to deliver its verdict on the raise with Babylon’s stock remaining suspended pending the outcome of the raise. Meanwhile, biotech firm Radiopharm Theranostics put away $12.5 million through Bell Potter and is currently down 20 per cent, Dalaroo Metals slotted $2.5 million via 62 Capital and is currently up 15 per cent, Greenvale Energy placed $3.25 million via Alpine Capital Partners and is down 24 per cent and finally G50 Corp raised $26.25 million through Bell Potter and Morgans Corporate, with Hancock Prospecting tipping in $7.95 million, which is now worth 16 percent less, not that Hancock would notice. Notably, July was also the busiest month for IPO’s so far in 2026 with nine new companies and one AI trust hitting the boards with retail investors continuing to prove they have an important role to play outside of providing sufficient shareholder spread for a company to be able to list. In the final 2 weeks of July, Lux Copper Corp was up 30 per cent after its IPO, Ceretas Limited hiked128 per cent and Gwardar Resources shot the lights out at 187 per cent. It wasn’t all peaches and cream however with Alurion Resources tracking down by about 27 per cent.



UBS Securities and MA Moelis along with Ord Minnett handled the biggest IPO for July which went to construction and infrastructure player FDC Consolidated with $400 million raised and is currently up 20per cent on its $3.00 subscription price. All things considered, it appears as though the IPO market is back in the black. Different sectors. Different commodities. Different strategies. The common thread was easy to spot. Companies that clearly articulated where the money was going generally found stronger support than those asking investors simply to extend the corporate runway. One other truth quietly emerged as the fortnight unfolded; the market doesn’t waste time delivering its verdict. Some companies have already moved comfortably above their issue prices, suggesting punters believe management will deliver exactly what was promised.......well almost. Brokers largely have an unenviable task - on the one hand they need to extract a decent discount to market for their investing clients and on the other hand, they need to keep the listed companies onside to secure a constant flow of business.



It is essentially a soft shoe shuffle and a high wire act that is not for the faint hearted. Convincing your listed client that the discount was appropriate when the market ran the stock hard post the raise is no mean feat. At the end of the day however, a stock that is heading north tends to be the only tonic that matters. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Second Liberal frontbencher called to ICAC
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Second Liberal frontbencher called to ICAC Michael McGowan Updated August 7, 2026 — 4:53pm ,first published 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A second Liberal frontbencher has received a summons to provide evidence to the anti-corruption watchdog’s bombshell investigation into allegations senior Liberal figures took illegal donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for political favours. Eleni Petinos, the shadow minister for jobs and industry, received a summons to appear at the Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry in the coming weeks. Former NSW fair trading minister Eleni Petinos has received a summons to appear at the ICAC inquiry. Rhett Wyman Petinos, who is on maternity leave, would be the second member of NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane’s frontbench to give evidence to the inquiry after shadow attorney-general Damien Tudehope appeared this week. Petinos was not named as a person of interest by the ICAC. However, her involvement in the resignation of former NSW building commissioner David Chandler is likely to be a key focus of the inquiry. She was not included on the list of witnesses to appear at the inquiry next week.



The ICAC has previously heard that Nassif paid significant funds to a group of Liberal Party apparatchiks, in part to seek Chandler’s removal. Related Article Operation Rosny Secret $2m deals, phone taps and ‘filthy money’: Explosive claims aired at ICAC They include one of the then-premier’s brothers, Charles Perrottet, and two other men: Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood. In phone taps played to the commission, Nassif bragged to a developer associate that he had “hands on the state government” and would “step on [the] neck” of Chandler by having “one of my girls” appointed fair trading minister. Two months after the recorded call, Petinos replaced Kevin Anderson as fair trading minister in a reshuffle.



By July 2022, Chandler had resigned as NSW building commissioner after an investigation into his conduct ordered by Petinos’ office. In her opening address to the commission, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, said: “Over the course of this public inquiry the commission will examine whether Mr Nassif’s predictions to his associate were an incidence of wishful thinking that serendipitously came to pass, or whether Mr Chandler’s resignation was, in fact, the result of work Mr Nassif had paid Charles Perrottet, Mr Greenwood and others to do for him.” Dwyer said she anticipated the inquiry would hear evidence Charles Perrottet sought assistance from both Petinos and Christopher Spence, then the chief of staff to planning minister Anthony Roberts, in seeking Chandler’s removal. Neither Petinos nor Spence have been named as persons of interest in the inquiry.



Petinos did not respond to a request for comment. However, senior party sources familiar with the December 2021 reshuffle told The Sydney Morning Herald that Petinos had not requested the fair trading portfolio. Charles Perrottet was involved in internal factional discussions about the reshuffle at the time, two Liberal Party sources said. Sloane has previously said she would not be commenting on Petinos’ potential involvement in the ICAC inquiry. On Friday she confirmed Petinos would be a witness but said she was “assisting the inquiry”. “She’s not a person of interest. I would encourage any of my team or people within the Liberal Party or outside of the Liberal Party to assist the inquiry to help provide support their evidence,” she said.



Related Article Operation Rosny Intercepted calls, leaked reports and cafe meetings: What we learnt from Rosny week two “That doesn’t mean they’ve done anything wrong. It means that they’re doing a very good job of supporting the inquiry. And you know, if anything comes up that isn’t that, then I’ll consider it at the time. But being a witness is being supportive of the inquiry. Nothing else.” Tudehope stood down from the frontbench ahead of his appearance, citing his “close relationships” with several of the people at the centre of the probe. He is not a focus of the inquiry but this week he conceded that he leaked a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a key witness who deliberately avoided giving evidence to a parliamentary inquiry into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council. The commission has previously heard evidence from Dylan Whitelaw, a NSW Reformers member who worked in Roberts’ office, that Spence had wanted to “get rid” of Chandler. Whitelaw told the commission Spence had wanted Petinos to raise a video of Chandler during a budget estimates hearing, with the goal of damaging his career.



The video, Whitelaw said, allegedly included the imputation Chandler was “racist” and included a reference to a list of building certifiers and developers he had given to banks. “I believe his [Spence’s] words were something to the effect of ‘we’ve just got to get rid of this guy’,” Whitelaw said. He told the commission that Spence and Petinos were “close” but did not know why she would want to have Chandler dismissed. Whitelaw said Spence later complained that Petinos had “f---ed it up” by not raising the video in her budget estimates appearance. Further reading Here are some of the highlights of our coverage.

World.title: Concern Wellington ratepayers will refuse to ration water
World.content:
An advocate for ratepayers says there is a risk Wellington residents will refuse to follow water restrictions, with growing frustration over pricey bills.

Tiaki Wai's first quarterly bills were sent out over the past few weeks, leaving residents shocked at the pricetag, some over $1000.

Come September, Wellington region will be asked to only use sprinklers every second day, and just between the hours of 6-8am and 7-9pm. The Upper Hutt area was already under those restrictions.

James Ross from the Wellington Rates Payers Alliance said the rationing had been unfair for a long time, but had been hidden away in rates bills.

Now, with water charges under a spotlight in a separate Tiaki Wai bill, he said restrictions would likely not be taken well.

"There's a very real concern that people won't be motivated to follow those water restrictions, because frankly I think a lot of people will see them as unfair.

"You've now got these huge water bills ... and yet we're still being told the assests are in such a bad way that you can't use your sprinklers when you need to."

For Ross, this would be solved with water meters, which he said would motivate residents to ration water.

Tiaki Wai planned to roll out water meters so bills reflected actual water use, rather than a fixed rate based on capital value.

However, its draft strategy said installing meters could take between five and seven years, and may cost upwards of $500 million.

Ross said the entity needed to begin this roll out sooner - and cheaper.

He said restrictions were a reality of mismanaged water systems, but meters would allow people to pay for what they actually use.

Tiaki Wai said there was no correlation between water conservation and the amount Wellington property owners have paid for water as part of their rates or will pay as part of their water services bill.

Upper Hutt was always on level one restrictions, following a decision made by the council years ago, a spokeperson said.

Wellington, Porirua and Hutt City were on the restriction during daylight saving months.

The restrictions were to conserve the region's finite water supply, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Wellington, Wairarapa mayors agree to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers
World.content:
Wellington and Wairarapa mayors have agreed to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers by Sunday.

Mayors from the eight councils in the region met this afternoon to discuss plans for a super-merger for local government reforms.

One proposal supported by Wellington, Lower Hutt, Porirua and South Wairarapa District Councils calls for a region-wide merger of all eight councils,

Caterton and Masterton District Councils are proposing a separate Wairarapa-only authority.

Some mayors opposed these ideas but proposals can be submitted against other councils' wishes.

Upper Hutt and Kapiti District Councils have opposed amalgamation.

Kapiti District wanted to submit their own proposal to be a singular unitary authority.

But individual councils cannot submit a proposal to become singular authorities without being part of a larger submission to the ministers.

And other councils disagreed on the grounds that the proposal did not meet the rules of the Head Start programme for local government overhaul.

World.title: Firefighters battle house fire in Auckland's Milford
World.content:
Emergency crews are battling a house fire on Auckland's North Shore.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) says it was called to the house in Milford about 3.30pm.

At 6.30pm, FENZ told RNZ the fire had been contained to the upper floor.

Two crews were still at the scene, alongside a fire investigator to determine the cause.

At its height, six fire trucks were at the scene.

World.title: Monty Knight's alleged killer's hearing adjourned to determine if she's mentally fit for trial
World.content:
A court hearing for a Northland woman accused of murdering well-known Kaitāia identity Monty Knight has been adjourned so an expert can determine if she is mentally fit to go on trial.

The 57-year-old, who has interim name suppression, was to have had a trial callover hearing in the High Court at Whangārei on Friday.

However, at the request of Crown prosecutor Richard Annandale, the hearing was rescheduled to early December.

He said that was to give psychiatrist Erik Monasterio time to work on a report examining "the issue of insanity".

Annandale said the extra time was needed because Dr Monasterio had much to do.

"The expert is a busy expert and has a large number of matters to attend to," he said.

The judge set a new callover date in December to monitor progress on the report.

Monty Knight was a well-known Kaitāia businessman, wine-maker and local politician. Supplied

A jury trial date had already been set for 5 July next year.

The accused was represented by Sharlene Pilkington, acting for high-profile Whangārei lawyer Arthur Fairley.

Monty Knight died at his home near Kaitāia in November last year. He had recently turned 80.

Ever the entrepreneur, Knight started his retail career with a record shop on the town's main street, then expanded into electronics, appliances and beds.

He took over the family business, Knights the Jewellers, and opened a second outlet in Kerikeri.

When told it was impossible to grow grapes in Kaitāia, Knight proved the doubters wrong by establishing an award-winning winery, Okahu Estate.

He was inducted into the Northland Business Hall of Fame in 2010.

Knight was elected to the Far North District Council in 2010 and the Northland Regional Council in 2015, and ran for the Far North mayoralty a number of times.

He had another tilt at winning a seat on the Far North District Council in the 2025 local elections.

World.title: Pacific Forum fails to reach consensus on anti-missile statement
World.content:
Disagreement from some China-aligned Pacific Islands countries has prevented regional countries wihtin the Pacific Islands Forum issuing a joint statement against missile testing in the Pacific

At their meeting in Suva today, Pacific Islands Forum foreign ministers failed to agree on a unified statement against China after it fired a nuclear-capable missile into Pacific waters last month, despite deep concern among most countries about China's actions.

It's understood there was a majority of countries represented at the meeting who wanted a clear joint regional statement condemning such missile testing in the nucelar-free Pacific.

However, the Forum's usual Pacific decision-making by consensus couldn't be met. it's understood Kiribati and Nauru were opposed to a strong statement condemning the testing.

New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters told media some Pacific nations were using the consensus because they were more concerned with external partners' wishes than those that belong to the Pacific Islands Forum, something he described as an "unsual view".

"They didn't actually lay out any reasons, apart from their disagreement, and not wishing for us to make the clear statement such as 'we are opposed to missiles being fired into the Pacific'.

"That's what the statement should have said, and we're still waiting for that to get laid out."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters speaking to reporters in Fiji ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Ministers' meeting on Friday. Supplied / screenshot

Some governments have pointed out that China is not the only country testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific. The US regularly conducts tests into the Marshall Islands.

Peters pointed out that testing in the Marshall Islands was done with the country's consent.

Security agenda

The Pacific Islands Forum foreign ministers meeting was held to set the agenda for the annual Forum leaders' summit in Palau later this month.

A Solomon Islands proposal for a regional security treaty was one of the discussion points, althohg it's clear more consultation is required on the matter.

The Solomon Islands Permanent Secretary for Foreign Affairs and External Trade, George Hoa'au, noted to RNZ Pacific that there's already a range of regional security mechanisms in the Forum fale.

"The missing part is to have a common thatched roof over them. The proposal for this single security treaty by Solomons is to provide an umbrella on top of what is already regional MOUs which are non-binding."

World.title: 'My heart went into my throat': Dog falls into sinkhole on Porirua walkway
World.content:
A dog owner says a sinkhole in Porirua is a serious injury waiting to happen, after her pet fell into the hole during a walk.

The fizzing sinkhole was coming from a leaking pipe on the Camborne Walkway. RNZ measured it as being just under a metre deep.

Jo Jones said her staffy, Missy, sank into the hole up to her neck.

"It looked like a puddle of water, and as we walked across it ... she just slid into it.

"My heart went into my throat."

Jones managed to pull her pet out before her head went under. The dog was left covered in silt and sand, and smelling like decomposing plants.

"She was very wide-eyed, it gave her a fright."

Missy had swelling on her paws on Friday, but was otherwise okay, Jones said.

The walkway was busy and needed to be cordoned off until it could be repaired, she added.

"It's a serious injury waiting to happen. It's not small, and if a small child or a small dog falls in there, I don't think you'd be able to get them out very easily."

A retaining wall sat beside the hole next to the beach shore, with water falling down it.

RNZ measured the hole as being just under a metre deep. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Residents told RNZ the leak had been growing for weeks, along with the hole, which they had reported to the council.

A Porirua City Council spokesperson said it was concerned about the area, and the section of the path would be closed for the weekend. But it was unclear whose problem it was to fix.

"There will be a further investigation as to who carries responsibility for the leak, which will include talking to nearby boatshed owners."

A spokesperson from the Parks team said Tiaki Wai had worked on repairs on the site last week, however, the hole had come back worse.

A Tiaki Wai spokesperson said they had attended and inspected the site.

"As it is a private leak, we will need to work with the responsible owner for them to make the repair," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Advertising watchdog finds Wegovy used font too small for billboard
World.content:
Should drug companies advertise direct to consumers? Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

A billboard for weight loss drug Wegovy used a font that was too small for the mandatory information required for advertising prescription medicines, the advertising watchdog has found.

The case has sparked renewed debate about advertising of prescription medicines direct to consumers.

The Advertising Standards Authority investigated a complaint about the ad, featured on a 30-second rotation digital billboard in Wellington, and advertiser Novo Nordisk Pharmaceuticals agreed to make changes in future.

The authority found the information was "not sufficiently accessible enough to be read and understood by consumers" but the advertiser had agreed to changes to the font and layout in future, which settled the complaint.

Dr Janet Joek, Professor of Public Health at the University of Otago, said there was a need for "clear, balanced, and well-explained information" about the risks, side effects and potential benefits of medicines before speaking with their doctor.

She argued that a 30-second  with key details displayed in small print or scrolling across a screen do not provide that information.

Meanwhile, David Menkes, associate professor of psychological medicine at the University of Auckland, said the case highlights a bigger issue around advertising of prescription drugs.

New Zealand and the United States are the only high-income countries that let drug companies advertise directly to consumers.

"This New Zealand policy, just like the one in the US, has done more harm than good and should be ditched as soon as there's political will to do so," Menkes told Checkpoint.

The Council of Medical Colleges does not support the practice and considers it can lead to increased costs, inappropriate prescribing, overtreatment and medicine-caused harm.

The Council also says it may put the doctor-patient relationship at risk.

Menkes said the net effect on public health from direct-to-consumer advertising is overall harder to determine but decades of research did show over diagnosis and over treatment.

Medicines New Zealand, representing the industry, and said companies follow a rigourous process when they're producing advertising to consumers.

It includes checks that promotional claims are accurate and substantiated by references, along with ensuring the advertising complies with legislation and regulations.

"Whilst in this case the compliance checks that will undoubtedly have been undertaken by the advertiser in advance of the billboard going up, may not have been 100 percent full proof, overall, this case demonstrates the system of self-regulation and checks and balances works to ensure that expected standards are met for public advertising," said Medicines NZ chief executive Dr Graeme Jarvis.

He said the Ministry of Health had conducted two independent reviews and found that on balance there was no evidence to justify banning direct-to-consumer advertising.

New Zealand also approached the advertising process differently to the US.

"It is our view that a ban would see the New Zealand public at the mercy of seeking or obtaining unregulated, unbalanced, and harmful information from overseas sources and illicit domestic purveyors of prescription medicines using the internet, rather than from well-regulated sources such as regulated s and regulated consumer information websites here in New Zealand."

World.title: Councils across country meet to finalise amalgamation proposals ahead of deadline
World.content:
Councils face deadline to propose amalgation agreements Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Councils across the country have been meeting to finalise their amalgamation proposals or face the process being dictated to them by central government.

Sunday marks the deadline for district councils to submit their proposals to amalgamate with at least one other nearby authority.

On announcing the three-month Head Start process in May, Local Government Minister, Simon Watts and Resource Management Act Reform Minister, Chris Bishop had a stark message for councils.

"Today we are giving council's a clear choice. Lead your own reform or we will do it for you," Bishop said.

This week, Hamilton District Council voted 12 to three to not participate - meaning the district would end up in a backstop process controlled by central government to ensure reforms still went ahead.

Councillor Andrew Bydder told Morning Report council didn't want to put forward a proposal and have the government think they were happy with it.

"Getting into the tent might leave us stuck in the tent which is not desirable when the tent is a brothel with a minister who wants to pimp us out," Bydder said.

Earlier in the month, Hamilton mayor Tim Macindoe told RNZ he was reluctant to cede control of the process but could not support rushing into an arrangement which did not suit his city.

Tim Macindoe. RNZ / Richard Tindiller

However this week he told councillors he received a phone call from Watts which ruled out his council's involvement in back stop decisions if they did not take the first step of submitting a proposal ahead of the deadline.

"He was also quite clear during our discussion that back-stop councils will not be at the table for that process," Macindoe said.

Down south, Christchurch City Council unanimously agreed to submit on the Head Start process.

They chose to retain the city's current city boundaries while taking on Canterbury Regional Council's functions.

But earlier in the week, councillor Melanie Coker warned the changes could cost millions to implement.

"Functions between councils that join will need to reviewed, combined, resized and this doesn't come for free. Any savings may be decades away and are not guaranteed," Coker said.

But in a Wellington City Council meeting yesterday, mayor Andrew Little said council reform was a necessary step to help address existing problems with long term infrastructure plans, economic growth and the region's ability to cope with the challenges of climate change.

Andrew Little. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"Put aside Head Start. Put aside the dodgy process. can we still address those challenges under the status quo? My view is not," Little said.

On Friday. a statement on behalf of the Wellington and Wairarapa Mayoral Forum outlined how the region could approach the merger.

Two proposals would come from councils of the region. One a region-wide proposal (supported by Wellington City Council, Hutt City Council, Porirua City Council and South Wairarapa District Council) and another proposal for Wairarapa (supported by Carterton District Council and Masterton District Council).

The statement said the proposals would convey the positions of individual councils and the forum was requesting the "door remains open" for alternative arrangements for Kapiti Coast District Council and Upper Hutt District Council.

Late last month, Taupo mayor John Funnell described a proposed Western Waikato Unitary Authority as a "hostile takeover" which would leverage his district's financial strength while ballooning ratepayer debt to nearly ten times current levels.

He said his council had decided not to engage in the Head Start process.

Funnell said he understood concerns that stepping away from the Head Start process could see a merger dictated by central government but said councils who wished to merge with Taupo should come through the front door.

"We're three months out from an election - I would say to Minister Watts 'be careful'.

"I've seen the communications from our residents of the district here and there's a fair bit at stake for everyone here.

"I think the residents are quite clear they want to have their concerns taken in consideration and they want to make sure that the investments that this council has made over many years can put them in a good position as protected - and there's many ways of doing that - but it needs time."

Watts has been approached for comment.

World.title: De Minaur haunted by Montreal Masters double-fault drama
World.content:
A double fault has proved costly for Alex de Minaur with the Australian star blowing a match point before falling to Briton Cameron Norrie at the Montreal Masters.

Third-seeded De Minaur was up 5-2 and 40-30 in the second set, but stumbled to allow Norrie back into their third-round match.

He had another chance when serving for the match at 5-4, but again double-faulted to surrender the game on Norrie's fourth break point.

World number 37 Norrie then dug deep to record a 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1 victory after two hours and 52 minutes in difficult, humid conditions.

Norrie said he had to weather de Minaur's early onslaught with the newly married Aussie starting with a bang.

"From the beginning, Alex came out firing and I was like, 'Woah, this is a crazy level', and I had to match it," Norrie said in his on-court interview.

"I managed to go up a break [in the first set], but he stayed really tough and I know he's so tough as a competitor and stole that first set.

"He was looking good in the second set, and I think he took the foot off the gas very slightly and I managed to free up, steal the tie-break and then it was just a battle.

"It was a great match to win, and to test my level and I can take so much confidence from this one."

Australians through in Montreal Alex de Minaur and fellow Australians Alexei Popyrin and Tahlia Gibson all record encouraging wins three weeks out from the US Open in New York.

Entering Thursday's (Friday AEST) match, de Minaur was the highest seed remaining at the hard court tournament, also known as the Canadian Open, with defending champion and fifth seed Ben Shelton taking over that title.

In some good news for de Minaur, because American Taylor Fritz and Italian Flavio Cobolli have also exited the event early, he can only possibly drop from seven to eight in the rankings, and that's only if Shelton wins the title.

That means the Australian, who broke through for a career-high number five ranking in July, will keep his top-eight US Open seeding intact for now.

De Minaur is looking to improve on quarter-final finishes at Flushing Meadows in the past two years.

Norrie will next take on 18th seed Arthur Fils, who earlier cruised past Mariano Navone 6-3, 6-2 to maintain his impressive record at Masters 1000 events this year.

World.title: Ex-AFLPA boss calls for independent tribunal over Cats concussion waiver
World.content:
Former Richmond player and AFL Players Association (AFLPA) chief Joel Bowden has criticised the AFL, Geelong and the AFLPA for their handling of the secret concussion waiver signed by an unknown Cats player, calling for a Senate committee hearing to investigate.

The Cats have avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Speaking to ABC Radio Melbourne on Friday, Bowden said he found it "absolutely outrageous that a young person's been taken advantage of", calling it "gambling with a young [player's] health and safety".

Dogs coach on concussion controversy Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge gives his view on concussion in the AFL following revelations of Geelong putting a waiver into a player's contract.

Bowden — who is also a former trade unionist and member of the Northern Territory parliament — pointed to the close ties between the club and the AFL, with former Geelong president Craig Drummond the chairman of the AFL Commission and Geelong chief executive Steven Hocking being the former general manager of football at the AFL.

"How this has got through, how people have thought that this is possibly OK is now ever more outrageous with the facts that have been put on the table," Bowden said.

Loading...

"It's conduct unbecoming. The AFL will fine players, they will fine people who are involved in the community sport — if you breach the code of conduct anywhere in the AFL at a game of community football you can be brought in front of a tribunal.

"And this AFL club, Geelong, have gone and signed a contract outside the standard playing contract and I would say outside of WorkSafe Victoria's legislative framework to provide a duty of care and a safe workplace.

"And now they're going to say: 'Nothing to see here, let's move on and watch the footy.'"

Bowden took aim at his former organisation the AFLPA for putting out a joint statement with the AFL over the issue and saying that the association had to "act more like a union, the union they are."

"They [the AFLPA] are too close [to the AFL] and this example says to me that the industry has got control of the Players Association," Bowden said, citing the AFL's funding of the AFLPA "to the tune of millions of dollars per year".

He called for Geelong to be brought in front of an independent tribunal to get to the bottom of the issue.

"I don't think there's been a press conference where anyone from the AFL or Geelong has stood there and taken questions," he said.

"Concussion is the nmber one issue in the AFL at this point of time. It's going to be huge in years to come, the CTE research and understanding now, the history that we know.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They're all too close and the industry is too close at times so maybe it needs to go to a Senate estimates committee hearing or something and get David Pocock to ask some questions and get independent senators and Sarah Hanson-Young to level these to the AFL.

"A young man has been put at risk and been asked to sign a secret waiver that says he'll exonerate the club from any future issues with his health. That needs to be investigated and that's not OK."

Asked if he thought Geelong would end up being sanctioned over the waiver, he replied:

"Yes I do. I think the court of public opinion will demand that they be sanctioned because this type of behaviour in modern AFL but also in workplace safety laws is not acceptable. Independent separate contracts are unacceptable."

A Victorian government spokesperson responded on Friday.

"Players safety must never be compromised," the spokesperson said.

"The AFL must have evidence-based policies and procedures in place to protect their players.

"The AFL, as the governing body for Australian rules football, has responsibility for managing concussion within the code."

World.title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Dogs coach says he would have signed concussion waiver to keep playing
World.content:
As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.
