World.title: Some of rugby league's truest believers await the NRL in Perth
World.content:
Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

A player's life at the outpost

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year. (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

The age of the Bear begins

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997. (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade. (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making. (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting. (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Loading Instagram content

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

World.title: Le Court wins Tour de France Femmes stage as Reusser keeps overall lead
World.content:
Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius overcame earlier difficulties to emerge victorious in a reduced sprint and win stage six of the Tour de France Femmes, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead with three stages remaining.

Le Court joined a small breakaway group 10 kilometres from the finish, launched her sprint with 300 metres to go and held off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands coming in third.

The 30-year-old Le Court suffered a mechanical before the final climb and had to change bikes, but, thanks to her teammates, made it back in time to launch her telling move.

"They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort," Le Court said.

"Then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front."

There was no change at the top of the standings after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, with Reusser holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney is third, 1:17 off the leader.

A group of three riders built an early lead of over two minutes but were brought back with 54km remaining.

World champion Magdeleine Vallieres set a blistering pace at the front on the penultimate climb of Col de Lalouvesc, which split the peloton, leaving a reduced bunch of about 30 riders to go for the stage win.

A group of six then got away, before they were joined by Le Court and Markus. The breakaway managed to hold off the chasing pack, and Markus made a move with one kilometre left.

The Dutch rider was unable to make her attack count, and it was left to Le Court to claim an almost carbon copy victory of her stage win last year when she outfought Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney in a seven-rider sprint to the line.

World.title: NRL and AFL 'saturated' with gambling and alcohol sponsors, report finds
World.content:
All NRL and AFL clubs have an alcohol sponsor this season, while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

The findings from the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (FARE) also show that both leagues have deals worth tens of millions of dollars each year with sports betting companies, which see them make money on every bet placed on their games.

The deals reportedly amount to $50 million per year for the NRL and $30 to $40 million per year for the AFL, FARE said.

SportsBet is a major sponsor of both codes as well, under deals worth about $10 million per year to the NRL and between $8 million and $10 million per year to the AFL.

With alcohol and gambling ads also becoming more prevalent in the leagues' women's competitions, FARE said its research showed these sponsorships were "deeply embedded across every level" of Australia's two largest sporting codes.

It comes as Labor's proposed crackdown on gambling advertising draws criticism from all sides of politics, with the Coalition, Greens, crossbenchers and some of its own party calling for stronger reforms during a Senate inquiry on the issue this week.

Labor's plan would limit gambling ads on TV to three per hour between 6pm and 8:30pm, on radio during school pick-up and drop-off, and ban logos on player jerseys or promotions in stadiums.

Labor MPs call for tougher gambling reforms The Albanese government faces internal pressure to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more MPs calling for sweeping amendments.

Alcohol ads cannot be shown on television until after 8:30pm when the media watchdog's designated children's viewing hours end, but an exemption exists for sporting matches.

However, the Australian Communications and Media Authority is currently reviewing that rule and is due to hand down a decision in the coming weeks.

FARE's State of Play report found that seven NRL clubs have gambling branding on their official playing uniforms this season — one more than the previous season — while betting advertising is part of 10 clubs' match-day promotions and across 12 clubs' digital channels.

Gambling sponsors are not on any AFL jerseys this season, but four clubs have digital gambling advertising and four clubs show betting ads at stadiums during matches.

Every AFL club advertises alcohol brands at stadiums during matches and through their digital channels, while five NRL clubs have alcohol logos on their jerseys and most clubs show alcohol ads in stadiums.

Every NRL club promotes alcohol brands through their digital channels.

Across the women's competitions, there are nine confirmed alcohol sponsorships for AFLW teams in this year's season and four for the NRLW, the report found.

Three AFLW clubs and seven NRLW clubs have gambling sponsors in the 2026 season.

FARE's research also found the volume of alcohol and betting ads during NRL and AFL broadcasts grew this year, with Seven and Nine both increasing their number of sponsors.

FARE chief executive Ayla Chorley said the report showed alcohol ads "saturate every part" of the sports and called on ACMA to take action.

Independent senator David Pocock, one of parliament's most vocal critics of Labor's planned reforms, has been calling for the government to implement all 31 recommendations of the Murphy Review — which includes a full ban on gambling advertising.

The Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs have an alcohol sponsor on their playing jerseys. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"We need a full gambling advertising ban — not some ineffective partial one that has been approved by the gambling industry, an end to harmful inducements and a national regulator to enforce the rules," he told the ABC.

Ex-NRL player alleges gambling staff offered drugs as he lost thousands Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs.

"Research shows that gambling and alcohol are huge accelerants to family and domestic violence.

"With 43 women murdered already this year, we should be doing everything possible to reduce and bring an end to this violence and the factors that exacerbate it."

Alcohol and Drug Foundation chief executive Erin Lalor said alcohol ads during sports broadcasting and at games influenced children and young people's attitudes towards drinking.

"Despite the significant harms that alcohol causes to individuals, families and communities, the alcohol industry continues to use sport to promote their unhealthy products," she said.

"That's why it's important to reduce children and young people's exposure to alcohol advertising, especially in the activities they love, like sport."

The NRL and AFL have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Richmond is facing a rebuild riddle — can it afford to stay the course?
World.content:
It's one of the most dreaded words in football: rebuild.

It's what's led Carlton into a search for its fifth senior coach in twelve seasons. It's why North Melbourne have been flirting with a seventh consecutive bottom-six finish and it's where Richmond finds itself six years after its drought-breaking dynasty.

The Tigers win over West Coast on Sunday was their 10th in their last 67 games. You could see how much it meant to former pick one Sam Lalor when he smashed through the sealer late at the MCG, whilst Willem Duursma's tears showed how devastating perennial losses can be.

Triple premiership-winning defender Nathan Broad, who announced his retirement this week, told ABC Sport's Alexia Pesce he was proud of the victory.

"It's reward for effort … the boys are working so hard, they have not thrown the towel in," he said.

" We're trying to win, we're not trying to get pick one. We're trying to build a winning culture. "

The 2017 grand final triumph broke a 37-year premiership drought. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Despite the win, Richmond will walk into the Adelaide Oval on Saturday night with a big decision looming.

If they're unable to salvage a win against Adelaide, St Kilda or Geelong in the final month, they'll finish their third season under coach Adem Yze with their worst record in history across three campaigns; surpassing the 1959-61 Tigers who managed 11 victories.

No-one in the AFL era has kept their job after winning fewer than 10 games over three seasons. Most, like David Noble in 2022 and Mark Neeld in 2013, exited during their second year of a disappointing run.

Brendon Bolton was given a fourth term at Carlton after a 14-41 start but managed just one win from his next 11 games and was sacked.

Justin Leppitsch departed Brisbane after just 14 wins across 2014-2016, whilst Stuart Dew survived an 11-61 record in the inaugural years of the Gold Coast Suns but was sacked three years later.

Richmond is at a fork in the road.

Their three flags across four years was only six years ago, and was built off a steely move to stick with coach Damien Hardwick when former players and Tiger identities were calling for change.

A disappointing 2016 campaign saw them finish 13th in Hardwick's seventh season, which followed three consecutive elimination final losses.

President Peggy O'Neal and CEO Brendon Gale backed their man and immediately found success in 2017 defeating Adelaide to snap a 37-year drought.

In 2017, the Tigers were flying high — but the three premierships in four years now feel like a distant memory. (AAP: Julian Smith)

The win sent their opponents, the Crows, spiralling out of their premiership window.

Once heavy flag favourites, Adelaide missed finals in consecutive campaigns and senior coach Don Pyke resigned.

'Two years into a significant rebuild'

Ironically the Crows, who face Richmond this weekend, found themselves in a similar situation to the 2026 Tigers. They signed a first-time coach in Matthew Nicks and were 0-13 to start his tenure.

Disconsolate Crows stars Taylor Walker and Rory Sloane in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 grand final. (AAP: Julian Smith)

They had progressed to 18-39 after three seasons and after narrowly missing finals in 2023, re-signed their figurehead twice in the space of two years, culminating in a minor premiership in 2025 and a potential return to the top four this season.

So should Richmond stick by Adem Yze who has the worst record of any coach in history after 67 games?

President John O'Rourke was emphatic Monday morning on 774 ABC Melbourne that the question isn't even being contemplated.

"He will coach to 100 games, I can assure you of that," he said.

"We're less than two years into a significant rebuild … [and] if you look at four of the top six teams they've all done a similar thing and they've taken four or five years to get back into contention so we do have to be a bit patient.

"We won't make judgement calls on where we sit until we see that through."

Richmond president John O'Rourke has spoken candidly about his side's form and fortunes. (AAP: James Ross)

The Tigers extended Yze's contract by another two years until 2028 in November last season after rising from two wins to five in 2025 and have shown some improvement statistically in 2026.

Richmond has risen from 17th to 12th for clearance differential; moving the delisted Thomson Dow's midfield minutes into first round pick Sam Cumming and rising star Jack Ross.

They've had small jumps with inside 50 differential as a result and scores from stoppage differential; but defensively are leaking 104 points per game compared to 95 last season.

Crisis or all is fair in footy? Pundits and fans alike talk about the AFL being an uneven competition — but does the data support that concern?

There has been a significant injury crisis that's likely to have played a role. Richmond have used a league-high 40 players this season with only one player, Seth Campbell, featuring in all 20 games.

Senior figures like spearhead Tom Lynch (12 games), captain Toby Nankervis (9 games) and midfielder Jacob Hopper (12 games) have barely featured; and young stars like Josh Smillie, Harry Armstrong, Taj Hotton, Josh Gibcus and Sam Lalor have managed just 21 games combined this campaign.

In football it's often believed rising stars find their rhythm around the 50-game mark. But of the Tigers nine first round picks in the last two years, only three have managed 18 matches or more out of a possible 43.

Former Richmond premiership player and Australian Football Hall of Famer Mick Malthouse, whom you can hear on AFL Saturday 12am AEST on ABC Sport, doesn't believe there's a universal number to development.

"The simple fact is, the more you play, the more experience you get and you become more aware of the game around you," he said.

"Is there a magical number? I've seen players 80 to 90 games in and they're as naive as they started and others have been street smart after 20 days.

" Today's football it's about whether you can keep the group together. I judge coaches on how their players improve. "

Mick Malthouse says player improvement should be the yardstick of coaching. (ABC Grandstand: Damien Peck)

Richmond's crippling injury toll led to an extensive internal review leading to the departure of high-performance manager Ben Serpell in July after two years in the role.

But will it be the only change at Punt Road following 2026? Or will the Tigers lean into their past success and their opponent Adelaide's current trajectory and stand by their embattled senior coach?

Richmond has a habit of upsetting Adelaide this decade, particularly at the Adelaide Oval where the 17th-placed Tigers jagged their second win of the season in Round 13, 2024, and in 2023 when they shocked the Crows with a 32-point win in Round 2.

Could another surprise be brewing Saturday night? Adem Yze will certainly be hoping so.

ABC Sport will be broadcasting Adelaide v Richmond live from Adelaide from 7pm AEST on Saturday, August 8, via ABC Listen.

Tech.title: Jony Ive’s first OpenAI gadget is reportedly a hockey puck-sized smart speaker
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The AI device OpenAI is developing with former Apple designer Jony Ive is “essentially a smart speaker without a display” that’s battery-powered, doughnut-shaped and roughly the size of a hockey puck, according to Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman. The device, expected to launch in 2027 for a price over $300, reportedly “will have a unique look, complete with moving parts,” including some that will move on their own to show when the device is responding or interacting with the user, along with lights, a camera system, and other sensors.

Gurman’s sources also say the “battery-powered” device is designed to be “easy to carry around the home with one hand,”similar to Amazon’s now-discontinued Tap speaker. Gurman says it will “work similarly to the company’s ChatGPT voice mode on smartphone apps, but with more advanced models for humanlike interactivity” but look and feel nothing like an Apple product — despite their ongoing lawsuit.

The speaker / pocket personal assistant could be the first in a “family of devices” OpenAI has planned, but we’ll probably hear a lot more about all of them before it eventually arrives.

Best Buy kicked off a sale on Apple products with discounts on its latest smartwatches to phones. The AirPods Pro are our favorite wireless earbuds to recommend for iPhone owners because they offer better sound quality than Apple’s entry-level AirPods. Tech.title: The Zelda movie’s Ganondorf casting hints at more movies
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Deadline reported Thursday that the upcoming The Legend of Zelda movie will feature Australian actor Uli Latukefu as the villain Ganondorf, and the publication notes that “We hear Latukefu inked a multi-picture deal.”

Nintendo or Sony haven’t formally confirmed that there’s more than one movie in the works, though it’s been rumored that Nintendo and Sony might be planning a trilogy. Still, it’s not exactly unexpected that more Zelda movies might be on the way, especially given the huge success of the recent Super Mario films at the box office.

Nintendo initially announced the live-action Zelda movie, which it’s making with Sony Pictures Entertainment, back in 2023, with Wes Ball directing with Shigeru Miyamoto and Avi Arad producing. Last year, Nintendo announced that Bo Bragason and Benjamin Evan Ainsworth had been cast as Princess Zelda and Link, respectively. The movie is set to release on April 30th, 2027, and filming has officially wrapped.

In a separate report published later on Thursday, Deadline says that Dichen Lachman, Yvonne Strahovski, and the late Sam Neill will be in the Zelda movie as well. Neill’s role is unclear, but the article says Lachman plays Impa while Strahovski has been cast as “a queen character.”

Nintendo is also preparing a big new Zelda game: the company has announced a Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time that’s set to launch sometime in 2026.

Update, August 6th: Adds new casting details from another Deadline report.

Tech.title: Suno shares plans to combat spammy AI music
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Suno announced plans to implement a new watermarking technology and download policy to limit the spread of spammy AI tracks and increase transparency. In a lengthy blog post, CEO and co-founder Mikey Shulman laid out the company’s principles and the next steps for the company as it seeks legitimacy.

The company is rolling out new transparency tools, along with new watermarking and fingerprinting tech. Shulman says it aligns with “emerging industry standards” that will make it easier to identify Suno-generated content. He also says the company is aiming to partner with “distribution platforms on combatting fraud and misuse.”

Last year, the company also announced it would change its download policy following a settlement with Warner Music Group (WMG), and in the wake of a similar settlement between WMG and Udio that ended downloads of outputs from that platform entirely. The company hasn’t offered specifics yet, but at the time it announced the plan last year, it said that downloads would be limited to paying subscribers, and users would be limited to a certain number of downloads each month.

Shulman’s post repeatedly mentions the company’s dedication to transparency, respect for rights holders, and the importance of human-made art. But he’s also careful to say it’s not Suno’s place to “pass judgment” on the value of individual pieces of art, and that it’s ultimately up to artists and platforms to decide whether they want to disclose the use of AI tools.

Suno didn’t immediately respond to a request for specifics about the new policies and technology.

Tech.title: Brendan Carr officially unleashes broadcast consolidation
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The era of set broadcast ownership limits is officially over, after the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted Thursday to end the national ownership cap rule.

The agency’s two Republicans, Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, voted to end the ownership cap, which restricts broadcast owners from holding stations that reach a combined more than 39 percent of US TV households, while Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez dissented. It formalizes a policy Carr has long criticized, and which he announced last month that he would seek to end at Thursday’s open FCC meeting. In place of a set limit, the FCC says, there will now be “granular, case-by-case review” to determine if broadcast consolidation is in the public interest. That will let the agency avoid having to “show special circumstances that would justify a waiver of a rule that no longer serves the public interest,” according to an FCC press release.

In place of a set limit, the FCC says, there will now be “granular, case-by-case review”

Carr has often criticized the rule as an artificial limit that restrains broadcast owners from competing with social media and streamers that can reach “100 percent of the country” without accessing broadcast licenses. This is happening at the same time Carr and President Donald Trump have threatened broadcasters for coverage they view as unfair. For example, the FCC demanded early renewal of ABC’s broadcast licenses shortly after Trump criticized the network for late night host Jimmy Kimmel’s joke about his wife. The agency said its decision was connected to an investigation into the company’s diversity, equity, and inclusivity (DEI) policies.

Those who oppose ending the ownership cap, including Gomez, say that allowing broadcast owners to gobble up as many stations as they can buy will disincentivize local reporting on public airwaves and drive up consumer costs. They also say that only Congress has the power to lift the ownership cap, since the figure was written into a 2004 law, leaving it open to legal scrutiny.

Still, the FCC under Carr has already found ways to work around the rule, even before voting it off the books. Carr agreed to waive the cap to approve the $6.2 billion merger of broadcasters Nexstar and Tegna. A federal judge has paused the merger pending a challenge by a group of state attorneys general.

Tech.title: OpenAI is giving ChatGPT free users unlimited text chats

OpenAI is making a big change for ChatGPT users on its free and Go tiers: Starting next week, users on those tiers will be able to have unlimited text chats with the chatbot, according to OpenAI. Right now, you may run into rate limits if you do too many text chats on those tiers, but those limits, just for text, will be going away soon. Messages that include things like file uploads and images will continue to have limits.

Next week, OpenAI is also adding a “Think” button for free and Go users that they can use to “access higher reasoning for harder questions.” This week, for those users, the company is additionally upgrading ChatGPT’s default AI model to the recently released GPT-5.6 Luna.

The “Think” button for free and Go subscribers. Image: OpenAI

For Plus and Pro subscribers, GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT is being updated to be “more reliable with facts,” OpenAI says. “The new GPT‑5.6 Sol is designed to make fewer mistakes — especially when answers depend on dates, numbers, sources, rules, or assumptions — by better using the sources it finds to answer your question.” The updated GPT-5.6 Sol will also give you “more direct responses” with “tighter formatting,” and OpenAI says ChatGPT will “avoid extra detail when it does not help.”

Plus and Pro subscribers can also use a new slider to decide “how much thought ChatGPT puts into an answer.” Both the updated GPT-5.6 Sol and the slider will be available starting Thursday.

Tech.title: TikTok blames ‘moderator error’ on slow response to Perez Hilton livestream
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

TikTok says a “moderator error” delayed the removal of a livestream that appeared to show blogger Perez Hilton harming himself, as reported earlier by Wired. Jamie Favazza, a spokesperson for TikTok US, tells The Verge that the platform notified law enforcement about the situation and banned Hilton’s account for violating its community guidelines.

Hilton, or Mario Armando Lavandeira Jr., is known for the celebrity gossip blog he started in 2004, where he often posted photos of stars featuring his own often obscene or cruel drawings layered on top.

Though some users claimed Perez’s livestream aired for more than 30 minutes, Favazza disputes this, saying it lasted around 15 minutes. Favazza adds that TikTok’s automated content moderation team flagged the video “within minutes” and routed it to US moderation teams. TikTok also took down the subsequent livestreams started by Hilton within 90 seconds. Screenshots and clips from the livestream are still floating around on some platforms like X.

The livestream aired on Tuesday night, with the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office responding to Hilton’s home after saying they received “multiple calls regarding an individual who was livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media,” according to CNN. The authorities transported Hilton to a local hospital.

The slow response to Hilton’s livestream has raised concerns about moderation on TikTok, which some creators have found to be unevenly applied. TikTok’s policies strictly prohibit content that “shows, promotes, or provides instructions for suicide or self-harm,” along with “extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content.” On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that TikTok US is laying off 250 employees and shutting down its Nashville office, where part of its content moderation team is based.

If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help. In the US: Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well. The Trevor Project: Text START to 678-678 or call 1-866-488-7386 at any time to speak to a trained counselor. Outside the US: The International Association for Suicide Prevention lists a number of suicide hotlines by country. Click here to find them. Befrienders Worldwide has a network of crisis helplines active in 48 countries. Click here to find them.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s new AI smart speaker will reportedly sell for between $300 and $400
Tech.content:
In Brief

More details continue to trickle out about OpenAI’s mysterious new hardware device — described previously as an AI-fueled smart speaker that will be the “physical manifestation” of ChatGPT.

Bloomberg now reports that the device will be “donut-shaped,” designed thusly to allow users to carry it around their home and place it in different locations, like a bedside table or a kitchen counter.

It will be constructed from “high-quality metal,” have a “premium look,” and (in a detail that mystifies) will have distinct “moving parts,” sources told Bloomberg.

It also could be slightly more expensive than your average smart speaker, perhaps $300 to $400 per unit, according to this report. For comparison, most of Amazon’s smart home speakers range in price from $40 on the low end to $240 on the high end.

So, to sum up: an expensive talking AI donut that has … moving parts? OpenAI releasing a smart home device has a certain logic to it, in that it would further integrate ChatGPT into users’ lives. However, historically speaking, smart speakers have not always been profitable and may prove a difficult market to break into. The potentially high price point also might not help.

The device, which is being developed in partnership with LoveFrom, the design studio founded by famous former Apple developer Jony Ive, will likely be released at some point in 2027, Bloomberg writes.

The company’s attempt to enter the hardware market has not gone off without a hitch. OpenAI is being sued by the current king of hardware, Apple, which has accused the AI lab of stealing trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing.

Tech.title: Vogue just gave another nod of approval to the tech world
Tech.content:
Vogue World is coming to San Francisco next year — perhaps another indication that tech billionaires have become leaders in the fashion zeitgeist.

Of course, the announcement of the enormous fashion/art/music event doesn’t say that. Instead, Anna Wintour wrote that Vogue believes in celebrating cities and “San Francisco is a city like none other.”

“It’s a place of diverse communities living side by side, a place that loves the arts, loves creativity, and isn’t afraid of change.” She also noted the city’s history of rebelliousness and innovation.

“I love that San Francisco has always stood up for values and the things it believes in,” Wintour wrote. “Vogue World will support San Francisco’s creative minds and strengthen the entire ecosystem — and it will offer another opportunity to show San Francisco is on the rise.”

There were rumors that Vogue World would head to San Francisco after Winter was seen having meetings with the city’s mayor, Daniel Lurie.

Plus, in the past year, Wintour has cozied up to the most powerful names in tech, culminating in this year’s Met Gala, which saw Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, serve as lead sponsors for the event. Google’s Sergey Brin and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg were also spotted at the event (the latter’s first, that is). In fact, OpenAI bought a table, as did Meta and Snap (for $350,000 a pop). It’s true that TikTok, Apple, and Instagram previously sponsored the event, but the presence of the tech crowd was so considerable that the Met Gala this year was dubbed the “tech gala” in some places.

Last year, Vogue put Lauren Sanchez on the cover of the magazine after her wedding to the Amazon founder. To the fashion world, this was Wintour’s stamp of approval — not just for Sanchez’s ascent into the fashion world, but that tech and its leaders were worthy of cultural recognition.

Though Bezos and Sanchez reportedly live in Florida (and Amazon is, of course, headquartered in the Seattle area), there is no city more associated with tech than San Francisco. By locating Vogue World there, this is another indication of Wintour’s approval.

Vogue, as a media publication, is always following the money, and as a cultural bible, is always looking for ways to stay relevant. Turning toward the worldwide headquarters of AI, good or bad, is brilliant for business (and Wintour is nothing if not brilliant).

But Vogue World was previously held in New York, London, Paris, and this year, Milan. Maybe because I live in an East Coast bubble, but I’ve not heard anyone in recent years refer to San Francisco as a beacon of style to rank alongside these other cities.

While the city has a reputation as the land of the free-spirited bohemian, tech and its workers have a reputation for hoodies, Patagonia vests, and expensive athletic shoes, if they even dress up that much.

For instance, billionaire Alexandr Wang, who is now running Meta’s all-important Superintelligence Labs, just did an interview with Y Combinator’s Garry Tan in front of a packed stadium wearing a faded Nintendo T-shirt and what looked like a pair of Crocs. Comfy? Yes. High fashion? Decidedly no.

But maybe that’s changing. Wang’s boss, Mark Zuckerberg, who once always appeared in a plain gray T-shirt and jeans, has made efforts in recent years to become more fashionable. Zuck and his wife Priscilla Chan were spotted front row at a Prada show this season. The new campaign for Meta Glasses has a slew of celeb ambassadors and looks like it could be a Saint Laurent or Balenciaga ad.

OpenAI and Palantir have recently released merch collabs, playing on the minimalist style of tech workers (the merch line of the latter, I would argue, looks inspired by Virgil Abloh’s Off-White).

I concede that creatively there is much to be done with the understated, Northern California style. Surrounded by beautiful nature and cooler temperatures, plenty of fashion designers could be motivated by San Francisco’s tech industry. I look forward to seeing Claude-inspired terra cotta-colored gowns and Vogue-emblazoned quarter-zips soon.

Tech.title: Google says hackers are calling financial firm employees to hack and extort victims
Tech.content:
Even in the age of AI-powered autonomous cyberattacks, the crude, tried and tested hacking techniques of tricking victims into doing things they shouldn’t are still producing great results.

Groups of unknown hackers are targeting and breaking into large financial and investment firms in the United States with the goal of stealing sensitive data to extort the victims with the threat of publishing it, Google’s security researchers wrote in a report on Thursday.

The company did not name the victims, but Reuters reported that among them there are leading private equity firms such as Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, CME Group, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG.

The hacking groups, which Google dubbed Falcon, Helix, Pink, and Redact, are using an old-fashioned technique to break into those firms: phone calls to employees’ personal cellphones in which the hackers pretend to be co-workers or IT helpdesk staffers, during which they try to trick targets into entering their credentials and multi-factor codes on spoofed websites, according to Google. In cybersecurity parlance, this technique is known as voice phishing, or vishing.

Some of the groups identified by Google run websites where they publicize their hacks and threaten to leak the stolen data as a way to extort the victims into paying a ransom, a common strategy among cybercriminals.

Image Credits:Google /

“We conduct every negotiation on professional terms. The publication of your data is never our preferred resolution; it is the consequence of refusal to engage, deliberate stalling, or failure to honor an agreement,” read one of the sites. “Respond promptly and in good faith, and the matter is resolved without further incident.”

Google researchers said that the different groups may all be part of a larger umbrella collective the company tracks under the name UNC6671. But it’s unclear if they are affiliates, splinter groups, or they all use the same Phishing-as-a-Service infrastructure.

“We believe that this most likely reflects a coordinated group of threat actors operating multiple public extortion brands possibly in an effort to compartmentalize operations, hide overall breach volumes, and isolate any negotiation fallout,” read the report.

According to Google, the hacking groups have also previously targeted large companies in the manufacturing, real estate, healthcare, and insurance sectors, as well as tech, transportation, and hospitality companies with the goal of stealing “valuable intellectual property, software source code, or sensitive VIP client data.”

More recently, the hackers have targeted legal and financial organizations such as private equity firms. “Concentrating on organizations involved in mergers, acquisitions, capital deployment, and litigation may reflect a strategy to target high-value corporate and confidential data to maximize leverage extortion demands,” wrote Google’s researchers.

Google said that one cryptocurrency wallet associated with one of the hacking groups received around $10 million in bitcoin in the first few months of this year, and that the hackers usually demand from $750,000 to $3 million from victims.

Laurie Bischel, a spokesperson for CME Group, declined to comment.

Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: China-linked LightSpy spyware caught targeting victims in 13 countries, including the US
Tech.content:
Security researchers say they have evidence that a Chinese-linked spyware has expanded from mainland China to now target victims in over a dozen countries, including across Europe and the United States. The previously identified spyware also has new functionality capable of stealing troves of data and remotely bricking devices.

The researchers at cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf said that the LightSpy spyware, first discovered in 2018 and previously linked to Chinese state-backed hackers, has since evolved into a commercial spyware platform operated by a single threat actor who caters to governments, enterprises, and militaries.

The platform is said to feature custom branding, billing, and demos for advertising it to prospective customers.

The findings underscore how the use of spyware continues to proliferate beyond governments and nation-backed hackers, and more broadly into the private industry.

LightSpy is a modular spyware platform that allows whoever is controlling it to attack a multitude of different devices, including smartphones, Apple devices, Linux servers, and Windows PCs. By using exploits for each device, the spyware can steal large amounts of sensitive information from its targets, including precise location data, chat messages, screen recordings, and stored passwords. The researchers also said the code is capable of remotely wiping and destroying data on a compromised device.

The researchers said that LightSpy has now been identified infecting routers, which researchers say they had not seen before. By attacking routers, the hackers can gain visibility and access to any other device on the same network.

Some of the compromised routers are associated with NATO member countries, said Arctic Wolf.

According to the company, LightSpy operates a network of at least 117 servers in several countries around the world.

The researchers said they were able to link the latest activity to a Chinese contractor after one of the spyware’s operators used the LightSpy administrator’s panel to place an order with Kentucky Fried Chicken using his real name and office address.

Tech.title: Ford needs another Taurus, and the $30K Fathom EV pickup isn’t it
Tech.content:
Few automotive companies are as dependent on breakout hits as Ford. It’s almost as though it’s baked into the company’s DNA: From the Model T and the Taurus to the F-150 and the Explorer, Ford has lurched from one success to another.

Recently, though, the automaker has been coming up empty handed. While its U.S. vehicle sales rose 6% year-over-year to 2.08 million in 2025, they’re today less than half their peak of 4.48 million in 2000. Of the new vehicles that Ford has introduced in recent years, none have become a sensation.

Ford CEO Jim Farley is betting its forthcoming EV pickup, Fathom, will change its fortunes, calling the introduction of the truck and its Universal EV platform a “Model T moment” for the company. Ford needs a product that can compete with Chinese EVs, which have been taking the world by storm. Yet, for reasons that are both within and beyond Ford’s control, the Fathom is unlikely to be another Taurus or Explorer, two hits that drove Ford sales in the 1990s.

Now, Fathom could be a minor success. Any way you spin it, the base model will be a good deal. On Thursday, Ford said the Fathom would start at $29,945, including the destination fee. That’s significantly below the $50,000 average for new vehicles and the $56,000 average for EVs. It’s also about $5,000 lower than the Keating Line — the average listing price of the largest price segment available at dealers.

But consumers don’t decide to buy a car based on price alone. Here’s where Ford could run into some challenges.

The Fathom will be a compact pickup truck, a form factor that the market largely ignored until Ford started selling the Maverick in 2021. The Fathom is entering an under-exploited niche, but it doesn’t appear to be one with enormous potential either. Sales of the Maverick offer a clue: they’ve been brisk, but at 155,000 last year, the small truck is not a blockbuster, either. The Taurus sold more than twice as many at its peak in 1992.

Now, the Fathom appears to have a few advantages over the Maverick. For one, passengers should enjoy a bit more interior space, according to Ford. The EV will also have a frunk, which could sway some buyers of traditional cars who have overlooked pickup trucks for lack of closed storage.

But the Fathom is still a pickup, and not everyone loves that look. The majority of the market today is dominated by SUVs, with just over 70% of prospective buyers looking for an SUV, compared with 33% for pickups, according to Cox Automotive.

Even among pickup fans, the Fathom may struggle to draw buyers. For many, trucks are a vibe. They want them to look ready to tackle the Rubicon trail, even if they never make it beyond the city limits. Every automaker is aware of this. GM, in a recent briefing I attended, made a point to mention how it is delivering the “lifted trucks” that its customers are demanding. The Fathom, from the little we’ve seen so far, doesn’t scream “rugged.”

Then there’s the EV thing. Most people who buy an EV, myself included, would never buy an internal combustion vehicle again, but a lot of people don’t love change. They’re content with gas-powered cars and trucks, and many dealers are happy to keep them in one.

The Fathom’s success won’t be dictated entirely by the whims of the market, though. Ford can spend on marketing and dealer training to overcome the EV hurdle, and may even convince people that a truck with a frunk is an ideal replacement for a sedan. And it’s almost a guarantee that Ford will introduce a ruggedized version of the Fathom.

Will that be enough to make the Fathom a breakout hit? Probably not. But maybe Ford doesn’t need it to be.

Maybe the Fathom is a test of its new production process, a toe in the water at a part of the beach that hasn’t been overrun. Compact trucks aren’t setting sales records, but the market for them is still growing. Ford can use that demand to soak up every Fathom it makes while it refines its new platform and process. Then, once it’s confident it has the kinks sorted out, it can expand it to other segments, including SUVs.

The Fathom may not be Ford’s swing for the fences. Maybe the company’s merely hoping to get on base and lay the groundwork for the next model rolling off the Universal EV platform — the one it really needs to be a home run.

Tech.title: Meta Ordered to Pay $567M in New Mexico Child Exploitation Lawsuit
Tech.content:
A New Mexico court has ordered Meta to pay $567 million for failing to warn the public about the dangers its social media platforms posed to children. The judgment is in addition to the $375 million the Instagram and Facebook parent company was ordered to pay in March as part of the trial’s first phase.

In a ruling late Thursday, Judge Bryan Biedcheid wrote that New Mexico teens are in the midst of a mental health crisis and found that “Meta’s platforms are a significant contributing cause to the crisis.” The $567 million will fund awareness and prevention, screening and assessment, and referral programs, with the bulk — $420 million — going to treatment.

Biedscheid’s ruling called Facebook’s platforms a “public nuisance” and compared Meta to a factory, with advertising and other content displayed on the platforms as its product and “the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated.”

The court ordered Meta to implement private-by-default settings for users under 18 and limit Friends for users under the age of 18 to users who are also under 18. Also, accounts belonging to users under 18 shall not show up in search or appear in recommendations, according to the order.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said Thursday’s verdict is a victory for parents worried about the effects social media is having on their children.

“This case has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence,” Torrez said in a statement.

Meta said in a statement that it disagreed with the ruling and would appeal it.

“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement. “We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.

This isn’t the only legal scrutiny Meta has faced over how it handles underage users on its platform. In March, a California jury found both Instagram owner Meta and Google’s parent company Alphabet liable in a lawsuit brought by a 20-year-old woman who alleged that YouTube and Instagram were designed to be addictive to children.

Social media platforms have introduced specific settings and tools for their youngest users, such as Instagram’s teen accounts, but many of these were launched relatively recently, in just the past few years.

Tech.title: Price Hikes May Be Coming for PC Motherboards Next
Tech.content:
PC gaming sites and social media discussions were buzzing this week after a report from a Chinese forum claimed PC motherboard prices could soon rise significantly.

Websites including VideoCardz, Guru3D and Digital Foundry, among others, cited what appears to be a supply chain report on a Chinese forum called Boards Channels, suggesting that PC motherboard makers could raise prices for consumers as material costs climb by as much as 50% in the coming months.

The link to the Board Channels report no longer seems to work, but a screenshot posted on these sites suggests that Taiwanese motherboard manufacturers, including ASUS, Gigabyte and MSI, will be trying to address the effects of rising component costs.

Whether the report is legitimate or not, we have some bad news, especially if you plan to build a PC or perform an upgrade. PC gamers, builders and upgraders have already seen the price of hard drives and SSDs skyrocket following massive cost jumps for RAM (dubbed by some as RAMageddon) over the last year due to AI data center needs and component shortages. Experts consulted by CNET said the implications of the Board Channels report for motherboard pricing are not only credible but also highly likely to materialize.

Why these price increases could happen

One reason analysts believe motherboards are likely to go up in price is that practically all electronic components are being affected by the AI data boom, with data centers gobbling up memory and storage products, creating supply constraints. There is also a reduced supply of materials such as copper, as well as chemicals manufactured in parts of the Middle East, said Cassandra Cummings, CEO of the electronics design and manufacturing company Thomas Instrumentation Inc.

“You can’t make PC motherboards without memory chips or copper, so its base pricing will follow what’s happening in those markets,” Cummings said in an email.

The war in Iran is also hurting supply chains.

“Some of those factories have been damaged in the war, and shipping logistics are struggling, so I believe those chemicals are also in short supply these days, causing more cost increases for the industry,” Cummings said.

Gaming enthusiasts may also be competing for motherboard parts with big PC makers, such as Dell and Apple, which could have a lock on certain supplies and components from some of the same motherboard manufacturers.

Joshua Goshorn, senior director at Quandary Peak Research, said in an email that he found the Board Channels report credible.

“With so much demand generally for PCBs (printed circuit boards) and materials and processes needed to create the PC motherboard, it seems reasonable that the cost of the PC motherboard from MSI, ASUS, etc. will increase,” he said.

But Goshorn believes those cost increases could be modest compared to the increases the market has seen in RAM and hard drive prices.

Companies that make PCs have an advantage over solo builders and upgraders because they have access to volume purchasing, and some of them have stockpiles of components ahead of any price shifts.

Although he hears that production of circuit boards is continuing to ramp up, that may not mitigate the rising cost of materials.

“I don’t believe that pricing relief to the consumer will come any time soon,” Goshorn said.

Calm before the storm

PC component costs don’t just affect DIY PC owners; they also create cost headaches for companies that make pre-built PCs for gamers and power users. The head of one of those custom builders, Maingear, says that while we haven’t seen a cost jump for motherboards just yet, it could be coming.

“Motherboards have stayed relatively flat” compared to storage and memory,” William Santos, CEO at Maingear, said in an email. “If you’re looking into upgrading your PC, we recommend acting sooner rather than later to avoid the next component cost increase. Waiting doesn’t seem to pay off in this market.”

Tech.title: Fare Is Fair: Zoox Launching Robotaxi Service in Las Vegas
Tech.content:
Autonomous ride-hailing company Zoox will start charging for rides in Las Vegas next week, ending its free pilot program. Starting Aug. 10, the Amazon-owned startup will begin offering a paid service for its pod-shaped, purpose-built robotaxis — a bummer for free riders, but the next logical step for the company in its growth from a flashy startup to a viable business model.

Zoox’s road from pilot program to paid rides has been more of an expressway. CNET Senior Writer Abrar Al-Heeti was one of the first to test ride Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxi in 2024. The pilot program opened to the public in 2025 with free rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco, later expanding to Austin and Miami. The pod-shaped autonomous vehicles were among the highlights of CES 2026, roaming the Vegas strip. Since launch, Zoox claims it has carried nearly 1 million riders across its pilot cities, covering over 3 million miles on public roads.

Last week, Zoox announced that it had received the Part 555 commercial exemption from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, giving the company federal regulatory approval to charge for rides in its purpose-built robotaxi. According to a Zoox representative, the next step was completing “the necessary notifications in Nevada to begin charging for rides.”

Starting Aug. 10, Zoox will flip the switch and start charging for rides in Las Vegas.

Optimized pricing

According to Zoox, fares will initially be calculated based on a base fare, distance traveled, time traveled from pickup to drop-off and applicable taxes. Destination fees — for trips to or from the airport or to high-traffic events at the Sphere or T-Mobile Arena, for example — may also apply, following a structure similar to that of other ride-hailing and traditional taxi services. To start, Zoox says it’s aiming to be competitive with ride-hail “comfort” tier pricing (think Uber Comfort or Lyft Extra Comfort), which averages around 20% to 30% more expensive than standard UberX or Lyft Standard.

This initial fare calculation, visible at the time of booking, is the price, not an estimate. Unlike other services that may update the final price based on actual distance and time traveled, Zoox says its optimal-route price is fixed and will not change, even if the robotaxi takes a longer route (for example, to avoid traffic or accidents) or the trip takes longer than expected.

CNET reached out to Zoox regarding the specifics of next week’s transition from free to paid service, changes to the Zoox app and what customers should expect. We will update this space when we hear back.

Zoox’s robotaxi is purpose-built for passengers — no pedals and no steering wheel required. Zoox

No more free rides

Las Vegas is the first stop for paid Zoox rides, but it won’t be the last. Eventually, payments will launch in other cities, such as San Francisco, but Zoox says it doesn’t have any additional details to share yet. For now, service for riders in the San Francisco Zoox Explorers program remains free.

Earlier this year, Zoox and Uber announced a multiyear strategic partnership to feature Zoox robotaxis on the Uber app, marking Zoox’s first third-party platform integration. Zoox will continue operating its own separate app in these launch markets alongside the Uber integration.

For tourists and Vegas locals, the end of free rides in Sin City is sure to be a disappointment (who doesn’t love free stuff?), but Zoox frames this as an important step toward becoming a self-sustaining business, rather than just another startup running on venture capital. That positive cash flow will help fuel the company’s continued testing, mapping and research and development work that extends well beyond the pilot cities.

Zoox is also conducting manual mapping and autonomous testing with safety drivers in Seattle, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Washington, DC, Dallas and Phoenix using a fleet of retrofitted Toyota Highlanders.

The company also said that iOS customers can link an iPhone to their accounts.
